title: Soft-Boiled Eggs with Toast Soldiers
summary: A soft-boiled egg with a set white and a runny yolk, served in a cup with buttered strips of toast for dipping. It opens the course because time and temperature decide everything in a kitchen, and an egg shows the effect of thirty seconds more clearly than any other food.
skills: timing an egg to the minute
equipment: 2 quart (1.9 litre) saucepan with a lid
bread knife and a small serrated or paring knife

ingredients.item: large eggs, straight from the fridge
ingredients.note: Use eggs at least a few days old if you can; very fresh eggs are harder to peel but fine for eating from the shell.

ingredients.item: white or wholemeal sandwich loaf, thickly sliced
ingredients.note: A sturdy bloomer or sourdough holds its shape when dipped.
Leave it out for 30 minutes so it spreads without tearing the toast.
For the yolk at the table.
Enough to cover the eggs by 1 inch (2.5 cm).

mise: Take the butter out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead.
Fill the saucepan with the water and set it on the largest burner.
Put the eggs in a bowl beside the stove with the slotted spoon.
Slice the bread if it is a whole loaf and put it by the toaster.
Set out the egg cups, a plate for each person, salt and pepper.
Fill a bowl with cold tap water for the eggs.

timeline.do: Water on to boil over high heat with the lid on.
Water at a full boil: lower the eggs in, start the timer at 6 minutes, turn the heat down to a steady simmer.
Bread into the toaster.
Butter the toast and cut the soldiers.
Timer done: eggs into cold water for 20 seconds, then into the cups.
Take the tops off at the table and serve with the soldiers.

steps.do: Bring the 6 cups (1.4 litres) of water to a full rolling boil in the saucepan over high heat with the lid on. There must be enough water to cover the eggs by about 1 inch (2.5 cm), so that adding four cold eggs does not stop the boil for long.
steps.look: Large bubbles break across the whole surface and keep breaking when you lift the lid; the pan roars rather than hisses.
steps.mistake: Starting the timer in water that is only steaming, so every egg comes out underdone and the timing is never repeatable.
steps.fix: Wait for the full boil before the eggs go in; the boil is your fixed starting point, so treat it like a starting gun.

steps.do: Lower each egg gently into the water on the slotted spoon, one at a time, letting the spoon touch the bottom before you tip the egg off. Start a 6 minute timer the moment the last egg is in.
steps.look: The eggs settle on the bottom without a crack; a thin stream of tiny bubbles may rise from the round end, which is just air escaping from the air pocket.
steps.mistake: Dropping eggs in from height, which cracks the shell and lets a white ribbon of egg leak into the water.
steps.fix: If an egg cracks, add a splash of vinegar to the water to help the leak set quickly, and serve that egg to yourself.

steps.do: Turn the heat down to medium so the water holds a steady simmer: small bubbles rising constantly, the surface trembling but not churning. Leave the lid off.
steps.look: Bubbles the size of a lentil rise all over the base; the eggs rock very slightly but do not knock against each other.
steps.mistake: Leaving the water at a violent boil, which bangs the eggs together, cracks them and toughens the outer white.
steps.fix: Lower the heat further; a simmer cooks the egg in the same time, because water at sea level cannot get hotter than 212°F (100°C) however hard it boils.

steps.do: With 4 minutes left on the timer, put the bread into the toaster, or under a hot overhead grill about 4 inches (10 cm) from the element, turning once, until both sides are deep golden.
steps.look: An even golden brown edge to edge, smelling of toasted grain, not of smoke; the slice is rigid when you lift it by one corner.
steps.mistake: Pale toast that flops when dipped and tears in the yolk.
steps.fix: Give it another 30 to 60 seconds; a soldier must be crisp enough to stand up in a yolk.

steps.do: Spread the hot toast with the softened butter right to the crusts. Cut off the crusts if you like, then cut each slice into strips about 3/4 inch (2 cm) wide with the bread knife, using long single strokes rather than sawing.
steps.look: Strips of equal width with clean edges, the butter melted into a shine, about 5 soldiers per slice.
steps.mistake: Uneven strips, some too thick to fit into the egg, some so thin they snap.
steps.fix: Lay a ruler or the width of two fingers alongside the first cut and match every strip to it; even cuts are the first knife habit.

steps.do: When the timer sounds, lift the eggs out with the slotted spoon straight into the bowl of cold tap water for 20 seconds. This stops the shell being too hot to hold and arrests the cooking just enough; do not leave them longer or the yolk cools.
steps.look: The shell is warm, not scalding, after 20 seconds; the eggs feel firm at the ends.
steps.mistake: Leaving the eggs in the hot pan while you finish the toast, so carryover heat sets the yolk.
steps.fix: Next time start the toast earlier; this time, serve the firmer eggs and note the extra minute in your notebook.

steps.do: Stand each egg pointed end up or round end up in its cup. Holding it steady, tap a knife sharply around the shell about a quarter of the way down, or slice the top cleanly off with one firm stroke of a serrated knife.
steps.look: A neat circular opening revealing an opaque white that is just set at the cut and a deep yellow yolk that moves when you nudge the cup.
steps.mistake: Tapping too timidly so the shell shatters in small pieces into the yolk.
steps.fix: Use one decisive stroke, then lift any shell fragments out with the tip of a teaspoon, which shell sticks to better than a finger.

steps.do: Season the open yolk with a pinch of flaky salt and a turn of pepper and serve at once with the soldiers. Judge the result: white set and tender, yolk runny and warm. Note the minutes and adjust next time by 30 seconds either way.
steps.look: The first soldier comes out coated in a thick, glossy yolk that runs slowly down the toast.
steps.mistake: Watery, translucent white near the top of the egg, meaning it was undercooked.
steps.fix: Add 30 seconds next time; very large or very cold eggs need 6 minutes 30 seconds.

science: An egg is two proteins with different setting points. The white is mostly water and proteins such as ovotransferrin, which begins to set around 140°F to 145°F (60°C to 63°C), and ovalbumin, which needs about 176°F (80°C) to firm completely. The yolk thickens from about 149°F (65°C) and turns crumbly above 158°F (70°C). Heat moves from the shell inward, so after six minutes in boiling water the outer white has passed 176°F (80°C) while the centre of the yolk is still around 140°F (60°C). Starting the eggs in boiling water rather than cold makes the time repeatable, because every egg meets the same temperature from the first second. A simmer cooks as fast as a boil, since water cannot exceed 212°F (100°C) at sea level, but it stops the shells cracking.
plating: Serve each person two eggs in matching cups on a warm side plate with the soldiers fanned beside them, crusts all facing one way. Put a small mound of flaky salt and the pepper mill on the plate, and the egg tops, if kept, upside down next to the cup so the shell does not litter the plate.

pairing.drink: A Bucks Fizz of one part fresh orange juice to two parts dry sparkling wine: the acidity cuts the richness of the yolk and the bubbles lift the butter.
pairing.brennans: Brandy Milk Punch: Brennan's classic morning drink is the dairy-rich, gently boozy counterpoint to a simple egg breakfast.

variations: Asparagus soldiers: blanch thick asparagus spears in boiling salted water for 3 minutes and dip them instead of toast.
Marmite soldiers: spread a thin layer of Marmite over the butter for a salty, savoury dip in the British manner.
Jammy eggs: cook for 7 minutes, cool in iced water, peel and halve for a set but soft yolk on toast.
safety: A runny yolk has not reached 160°F (71°C), the temperature at which eggs are considered fully cooked. Anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with a weakened immune system should use pasteurised eggs or cook the eggs until white and yolk are firm, about 10 minutes.
Lift eggs in and out of boiling water with a spoon, never your fingers, and keep the pan handle turned inward.

title: Fried Eggs, Basted and Over Easy
summary: Two eggs fried two ways in one session: basted with spoonfuls of hot butter until the top of the white sets, and flipped over easy so the yolk stays liquid under a thin film. Frying eggs teaches the cook to read a pan by sound and by the edge of the white before anything more costly goes into it.
equipment: 10 inch (25 cm) nonstick or well seasoned cast iron frying pan
thin, flexible fish slice or offset spatula

ingredients.item: large eggs, as fresh as possible
ingredients.note: Fresh eggs have firmer whites that spread less in the pan.
For basting; a mix of 2 tbsp (28 g) butter and 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil gives more margin before browning.

ingredients.item: neutral oil, such as rapeseed or sunflower
ingredients.note: For the over easy eggs.
Optional.

mise: Crack each egg into its own ramekin, checking for shell and broken yolks.
Measure the butter and oil.
Warm two plates in a low oven at 200°F (95°C) or under hot tap water, dried.
Put salt, pepper, spatula and spoon beside the stove.

timeline.do: Crack the eggs into ramekins, warm the plates.
Heat the pan for the basted eggs over medium heat with the butter.
Cook and baste the first pair of eggs.
Wipe the pan, add oil, cook and flip the over easy pair.
Season and serve both styles side by side.

steps.do: Crack each egg on a flat surface, not the rim of a bowl, and open it into its own ramekin. A flat crack pushes less shell into the egg. Pick out any shell with a larger piece of shell, which slices through the white better than a fingertip.
steps.look: Four whole yolks sitting up in thick, clear whites; the thick white hugs the yolk and the thin white runs around it.
steps.mistake: Cracking straight into the hot pan, which leaves no chance to remove shell or rescue a broken yolk.
steps.fix: Always use a ramekin; a broken yolk can go into scrambled eggs tomorrow.

steps.do: Set the pan over medium heat with 3 tbsp (42 g) of butter. Wait until the butter melts, foams up and the foam starts to subside, about 2 minutes. That is the moment it is hot enough but not yet browning.
steps.look: A gentle steady sizzle, large foam bubbles turning to small ones, butter pale gold and smelling nutty but not burnt.
steps.mistake: Butter turning brown and smoking before the eggs go in, giving bitter, blistered whites.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds, wipe it out if the butter is black, and start again with fresh butter at a lower setting.

steps.do: Slide two eggs into the pan from the ramekins, holding the ramekin close to the surface so the yolk does not drop. Lower the heat slightly to medium low. Leave them untouched for 1 minute.
steps.look: The white sets opaque from the edge inward with a soft, steady sizzle, not spitting; the edge stays white or barely golden.
steps.mistake: Too much heat, so the white bubbles up into large blisters and turns brown and crisp while the top is still raw.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and move to basting sooner; a crisp lacy edge is a different style, which comes later in the course.

steps.do: Tilt the pan towards you about 20 degrees so the butter pools at the lower side. With a tablespoon, scoop the hot butter and spoon it over the raw white around the yolks, again and again, for 1 to 2 minutes. Spoon mostly over the white; a little over the yolk gives a pale film.
steps.look: The translucent jelly around each yolk turns opaque white as the butter lands; the yolk keeps its gloss and colour.
steps.mistake: Spooning only over the yolk, which sets it while the white beside it stays raw.
steps.fix: Aim each spoonful at the clear patches of white first; finish with one or two spoonfuls over the yolk only if you want it veiled.

steps.do: When no clear white remains, slide the spatula under each egg and lift it onto a warm plate. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.
steps.look: Fully set white, tender rather than rubbery, with a yolk that wobbles when the plate is moved.
steps.mistake: Breaking the yolk while lifting because the spatula is pushed at the egg from the side.
steps.fix: Slide the spatula flat under the white from the edge furthest from the yolk, then lift in one level motion.

steps.do: Wipe the pan out with paper towel held in tongs, return it to medium heat and add 1 tbsp (15 ml) of oil. Heat for 1 minute until the oil shimmers, then slide in the second pair of eggs. Cook untouched for 2 to 2 1/2 minutes.
steps.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze; the eggs sizzle steadily and the white sets almost all the way across, with just a thin film of clear white near the yolk.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, when the white is still loose, so it folds over itself and tears.
steps.fix: Wait until the white is set right up to the yolk and the edge lifts freely when you nudge it with the spatula.

steps.do: Slide the spatula fully under one egg, lift it about 1 inch (2.5 cm) and turn it over with a quick roll of the wrist, laying it down close to the pan rather than dropping it. Repeat with the second egg. Cook for 20 to 30 seconds only, then turn it back over onto the plate.
steps.look: The underside carries a pale gold edge; after the flip, the yolk under its thin film still moves like liquid when gently pressed.
steps.mistake: Flipping from height, so the yolk bursts on landing.
steps.fix: Keep the turn low and fast; if a yolk breaks, call it over medium and cook it 1 minute more on the second side.

steps.do: Season the over easy eggs and serve them beside the basted pair. Taste both and note the difference: the basted egg is buttery and tender throughout, the over easy egg has a firmer base and a hidden liquid yolk.
steps.look: Two styles side by side, both with whole yolks and no brown, crisp edges.
steps.mistake: Letting the plates sit while you clean up, so the yolks thicken from the heat of the plate.
steps.fix: Eat straight away; eggs are always cooked last on a breakfast plate for this reason.

science: Pan heat changes the egg white as much as time does. Below about 300°F (150°C) the water in the white turns to steam slowly and the proteins set quietly into a tender sheet. Hotter than that, steam forms so fast that it inflates the white into blisters, and the dry edges brown through the Maillard reaction, giving a crisp, lacy rim. Butter's milk solids start to burn at around 250°F to 300°F (120°C to 150°C), which is why the foaming stage is the signal: the water in the butter is boiling off and the fat is hot enough. Basting carries heat to the top of the egg by conduction from fat at roughly the pan's temperature, setting the white without turning the egg, while flipping uses direct contact for a few seconds.
plating: Use warm plates. Set the basted eggs and the over easy eggs side by side with whites trimmed tidy if the edges spread, yolks centred. Add a slice of buttered toast cut on the diagonal and leaning against the eggs, and finish with a few grains of flaky salt and pepper on the yolks only.

pairing.drink: A classic Bloody Mary: the tomato, lemon and spice wake up rich buttery eggs, and the salt in the drink seasons every bite.
pairing.brennans: Egg Any Style: the side Brennan's lists on the breakfast menu, and the server's chance to ask exactly how the guest wants it cooked.

variations: Sunny side up: cook covered with a lid over low heat for 3 minutes so steam sets the top without flipping or basting.
Over hard: flip and cook 1 1/2 minutes on the second side until the yolk is completely set, for sandwiches.
Olive oil fried egg in the Spanish style: shallow fry in 1/4 inch (6 mm) of hot olive oil for crisp lacy edges, spooning oil over the top.
safety: Runny yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or immune compromised, use pasteurised eggs or cook over hard.
Hot butter and oil spit when wet eggs go in: slide eggs in away from you, keep sleeves back and the pan handle turned inward.
Wash hands after handling raw eggshells.

title: Oeufs Brouillés (French Scrambled Eggs)
summary: French scrambled eggs cooked slowly over low heat with constant stirring until they form tiny, creamy curds, then finished with cold butter off the heat. The dish teaches patience at the stove and how far carryover heat continues to cook food after the pan comes off.
skills: finishing with butter off the heat
equipment: small heavy saucepan, about 1 1/2 quart (1.4 litre), or a nonstick pan
heatproof silicone spatula or wooden spoon

ingredients.item: unsalted butter, cold, cut in small cubes
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp (14 g) for the pan, 2 tbsp (28 g) cold to finish.
Salting the eggs a few minutes ahead gives a more tender set.
Optional, stirred in at the end to stop the cooking.
White pepper keeps the eggs unspeckled, the French habit.
To serve.

mise: Cube the butter and keep 2 tbsp (28 g) in the fridge until needed.
Crack the eggs into the bowl, add the salt and beat with a fork for 30 seconds until no streaks of white remain; leave for 10 minutes.
Snip the chives.
Warm the plates and have the toast ready to go in.

timeline.do: Beat and salt the eggs; cube the butter.
Melt 1 tbsp (14 g) butter over low heat and add the eggs.
Toast the bread while you keep stirring.
Off the heat while still loose; beat in the cold butter and crème fraîche.
Spoon onto toast, finish with chives and pepper, serve at once.

steps.do: Beat the eggs with the salt using a fork, lifting and cutting through the white rather than whipping air in, for about 30 seconds until the mixture is an even yellow and falls from the fork in a smooth stream. Let it stand 10 minutes.
steps.look: Uniform colour, no clear threads of white, a few small bubbles on top.
steps.mistake: Under-beating, leaving streaks of white that set into rubbery white flecks.
steps.fix: Keep beating until the stream from the fork has no clear strands; push the mixture through a sieve if you want it perfect.

steps.do: Melt 1 tbsp (14 g) of butter in the saucepan over the lowest heat your burner gives, or medium low on a stubborn stove. Swirl it so the base is coated. It should melt without sizzling.
steps.look: Butter melted and glossy, no foam and no sizzle; you can rest your hand 2 inches (5 cm) above the pan comfortably for several seconds.
steps.mistake: A pan already hot enough to sizzle, which will set the eggs into large curds within seconds.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat and let it cool for a minute before the eggs go in.

steps.do: Pour in the eggs. Stir constantly with the spatula in a slow figure of eight, scraping the base and the corners of the pan every few seconds so no layer sets undisturbed. Keep going for 6 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: For the first 3 or 4 minutes nothing seems to happen; then the mixture thickens like a custard and the spatula leaves a trail across the base.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat because nothing is happening, which turns slow cream into lumps in the next 30 seconds.
steps.fix: Hold your nerve. If you see lumps forming, lift the pan off the heat for 20 seconds while stirring, then return it.

steps.do: Manage the heat by moving the pan, not the dial: whenever you see curds forming quickly at the edges or the base, lift the pan clear of the heat for 10 to 20 seconds while stirring, then set it back down.
steps.look: Tiny curds the size of couscous suspended in a creamy, glossy mass; the eggs look like loose porridge.
steps.mistake: Letting a layer stick on the base, which browns and adds dry, tough scraps to the eggs.
steps.fix: Scrape the base on every pass; with a nonstick pan this is easier, so use one until the habit is formed.

steps.do: Put the bread in the toaster now, while you continue stirring.
steps.look: You are still stirring; the eggs have not been left alone at any point.
steps.mistake: Walking away to the toaster for a minute, during which the eggs set into a solid sheet.
steps.fix: Set everything within arm's reach before you start. A scrambled egg is a dish you stand over.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat when the eggs are still slightly looser than you want to eat them: creamy, just holding their shape when pushed into a pile, with a little liquid egg still visible. Carryover heat will finish them.
steps.look: A soft mass that slumps slowly when you pile it at one side of the pan; glossy, never dry or matte.
steps.mistake: Cooking until they look perfect in the pan, so they are overdone and weeping by the time they reach the plate.
steps.fix: Pull them earlier next time by about 30 seconds; the eggs keep cooking from the pan's heat for at least a minute.

steps.do: Off the heat, add the 2 tbsp (28 g) of cold cubed butter and the crème fraîche, if using, and stir until melted and absorbed. The cold dairy lowers the temperature and stops the cooking while adding richness.
steps.look: The eggs turn glossier and slightly looser, with a pale, creamy sheen.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter while the pan is still on the heat, so it melts into grease and the eggs carry on cooking.
steps.fix: Always finish off the heat; if the eggs look oily, stir in another teaspoon of cold cream to bring the emulsion back.

steps.do: Taste and add a pinch more salt if needed and the white pepper. Spoon onto the warm toast or into a warm dish, scatter with chives and serve immediately.
steps.look: Soft, spoonable eggs that hold a gentle mound, pale yellow, glistening, without any liquid pooling around them.
steps.mistake: Watery liquid weeping onto the plate, the sign of overcooking: the proteins squeezed out their water.
steps.fix: Note the time off the heat for next attempt and pull earlier; for now, serve on toast, which soaks up the liquid.

science: Egg proteins are long chains folded into balls. Heat unfolds them and lets them bond into a mesh that traps water. If heated fast, they bond tightly into large curds that squeeze out water, which is why fast scrambled eggs weep. Low heat with constant stirring breaks the mesh into tiny pieces as it forms, each one holding its water, so the result is creamy rather than lumpy. Salting the beaten eggs ten minutes ahead helps, because salt ions get between the proteins and stop them binding too tightly. The finished eggs sit around 150°F to 160°F (65°C to 71°C); off the heat, the pan and the eggs themselves hold enough energy to raise them several more degrees, so the cook takes them off early and uses cold butter as a brake.
plating: Spoon the eggs into a loose mound across the centre of the toast or in a warmed shallow bowl, using the back of the spoon to make soft folds rather than a flat layer. Scatter chives in a thin line along the top, add a light dusting of white pepper, and serve the toast cut in half on the diagonal beneath.

pairing.drink: A glass of Blanc de Blancs Champagne: its chalky acidity and fine bubbles slice through butter and cream without overwhelming delicate eggs.
pairing.brennans: Crab & Corn Omelette: Brennan's richer egg dish, built on the same principle of eggs cooked soft and finished with butter.

variations: Truffled: fold in a few drops of truffle oil or a little grated truffle with the finishing butter.
Smoked salmon: fold in 2 oz (55 g) of smoked salmon strips off the heat so it warms without cooking.
Fines herbes: finish with 1 tbsp (3 g) each of chopped chervil, parsley, chives and tarragon.
safety: Soft scrambled eggs may not reach 160°F (71°C) throughout; use pasteurised eggs for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or immune compromised, or cook until no liquid egg remains.
Do not keep scrambled eggs warm for more than a few minutes; cook them to order.

title: Masala Omelette
summary: An Indian street and home breakfast: eggs beaten with a fine dice of onion, green chilli, tomato and coriander, cooked flat and folded. It is the first knife drill with a reward, since a fine, even dice is the only way the vegetables soften in the time the eggs take to set.
skills: fine dice of onion, chilli and tomato
equipment: chef's knife, 8 inch (20 cm), freshly sharpened
large chopping board with a damp cloth underneath

ingredients.note: Diced 1/8 inch (3 mm).
Diced 1/4 inch (6 mm); seeding keeps the omelette from going watery.

ingredients.item: green chilli, such as a Thai or Indian finger chilli
ingredients.note: Seeded for mild, minced fine.

ingredients.item: fresh coriander, leaves and tender stems
Kashmiri chilli powder or mild paprika
ingredients.note: For colour more than heat.
1 tbsp (14 g) per omelette.
Optional, loosens the eggs slightly.

ingredients.item: buttered toast or soft white bread rolls (pav)
ingredients.note: To serve, with ketchup or green chutney.

mise: Set the board on a damp cloth so it cannot slide.
Halve the onion through the root, peel and dice it 1/8 inch (3 mm).
Seed the tomato and dice it 1/4 inch (6 mm).
Halve, seed and mince the chilli; wash your hands straight afterwards.
Chop the coriander.
Measure spices, salt and ghee; warm the plates.

timeline.do: Knife work: onion, tomato, chilli, coriander.
Beat eggs with spices, salt and milk; fold in the vegetables.
Cook the first omelette.
Cook the second omelette; keep the first warm on its plate.
Serve with toast or pav and chutney.

steps.do: Learn the claw grip before you cut: curl the fingertips of the hand holding the food under, so the knuckles face the blade and the flat of the knife rests against them. Keep the knife tip on the board and rock the blade forward and down through the food.
steps.look: Fingertips are hidden behind your knuckles at all times; the blade slides against the knuckles without lifting higher than them.
steps.mistake: Flat fingers spread across the food, with fingertips in the path of the knife.
steps.fix: Stop, curl the fingers and slow down. Speed comes with months of practice; safe uniform cuts come first.

steps.do: Dice the onion: halve it through the root, peel, lay one half flat. Make thin vertical cuts 1/8 inch (3 mm) apart towards the root without cutting through it, then one or two horizontal cuts, then slice across to release a fine dice.
steps.look: Even little squares about 1/8 inch (3 mm), all much the same size, with the root end left whole to throw away.
steps.mistake: Cutting through the root on the first cuts, so the onion falls apart and cannot be diced evenly.
steps.fix: Stop short of the root by 1/4 inch (6 mm); the root holds the layers together while you cut.

steps.do: Quarter the tomato, scoop out the seeds and jelly with a teaspoon, then cut the flesh into strips and across into 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice. Halve the chilli, scrape out seeds and pith for less heat, slice into thin strips and mince. Chop the coriander finely, stems included.
steps.look: Firm red cubes with no wet seeds; chilli in pieces smaller than a grain of rice.
steps.mistake: Leaving the tomato seeds in, which floods the eggs with water and stops them setting.
steps.fix: Seed the tomato; if it is already in, tip the bowl and pour off any pooled liquid before cooking.

steps.do: Beat the eggs in the bowl with the salt, turmeric, chilli powder and milk for 30 seconds until even. Stir in the onion, tomato, chilli and coriander.
steps.look: A bright yellow mixture flecked evenly with red, green and purple, smelling fresh and peppery.
steps.mistake: Adding all the vegetables to one omelette's worth, so they are unevenly shared.
steps.fix: Stir well just before pouring each omelette and ladle half the mixture each time.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (14 g) of ghee in the nonstick pan over medium heat for about 1 minute until it shimmers and a drop of egg sizzles gently on contact. Swirl to coat the whole base.
steps.look: Ghee rippling, pan coated edge to edge, a soft sizzle rather than a loud spit when tested.
steps.mistake: A cold pan that lets the egg soak in the fat and stick.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer and the test sizzle every time.

steps.do: Give the egg mixture a stir and pour in half. Tilt the pan so it spreads into an even round about 8 inches (20 cm) across. For the first 30 seconds, push the set edges towards the centre with the spatula and tilt raw egg into the gaps. Then leave it flat and untouched for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes.
steps.look: The omelette sets from the edges inward; the top goes from liquid to just moist; the underside turns golden with light brown freckles, which is right for this style.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the base burns before the onion has softened and the top has set.
steps.fix: Drop to medium low and cover the pan with a lid for 30 seconds to steam the top.

steps.do: When the top is nearly set, slide the spatula under one half and fold it over, or flip the whole round and cook the second side for 30 seconds, then fold. Slide it onto a warm plate.
steps.look: A golden half-moon, firm enough to hold its shape, the vegetables tender, with no runny egg leaking from the fold.
steps.mistake: Tearing on the fold because the base stuck.
steps.fix: Loosen the edges all the way round with the spatula before folding, and add a little more ghee next time.

steps.do: Repeat with the remaining ghee and egg mixture. Serve with buttered toast or soft rolls and ketchup or green chutney, the way Indian street stalls do.
steps.look: Two even omelettes with the vegetables spread through each, golden outside and soft inside.
steps.mistake: The second omelette darker than the first because the pan has built up heat.
steps.fix: Lower the heat a notch for the second one; a pan gains heat over a session.

science: Small dice is not just about looks: heat penetrates a cube roughly in proportion to the square of its thickness, so a 1/8 inch (3 mm) piece of onion cooks about four times faster than a 1/4 inch (6 mm) piece. In an omelette that sets in two minutes, only a fine dice can soften and lose its raw bite in time. Seeding the tomato removes the watery jelly that would otherwise dilute the egg, because egg proteins need to touch each other to form a set mesh. Turmeric and chilli powder are fat soluble, so they disperse into the yolk fat and the ghee, colouring the omelette evenly. Ghee has had its milk solids removed, so it can take medium heat for longer than butter without burning, giving a golden base with a toasty flavour.
plating: Fold each omelette into a neat half-moon and lay it slightly off centre on a warm plate. Lean two triangles of buttered toast against its straight edge, add a small pool of green chutney or ketchup in a ramekin, and scatter a few coriander leaves and a pinch of chilli powder over the top.

steps.mistake: Streaks of unbeaten white, which set into rubbery white ribbons on the surface.
steps.fix: Beat longer or push the eggs through a fine sieve; the surface of a French omelette must be a single colour.

steps.do: Put the pan over medium heat for 1 minute, then add 1 tbsp (14 g) of butter and swirl it around the base and up the sides. Wait until the foam rises and just begins to subside, but before any colour appears.
steps.look: Butter foaming evenly, pale and sweet smelling, with no brown flecks; a drop of egg sets around its edges within 2 seconds.
steps.mistake: Browned butter, which gives a freckled tan omelette that in France counts as a mistake.
steps.fix: Wipe the pan and start again on lower heat; the butter must never pass pale gold.

steps.do: Pour in the eggs. Immediately start stirring rapidly with the flat of the spatula or the back of a fork held parallel to the base, in small fast circles, while with the other hand shaking the pan back and forth over the burner. Keep both moving for about 20 to 30 seconds.
steps.look: The eggs thicken quickly into very fine, creamy curds like loose porridge, with liquid egg still flowing between them.
steps.mistake: Stirring too slowly, so the eggs set into large lumps rather than fine curds.
steps.fix: Stir faster and smaller; think of whisking cream, not folding.

steps.do: As soon as the curds are mostly set but the surface is still wet and glossy, stop stirring. Use the spatula to smooth the eggs into an even layer and push any curds clinging to the sides back down. Lift off the heat and leave it still for 10 seconds.
steps.look: An even round of soft curds, wet on top, set underneath into a thin skin no thicker than a coin; no colour on the base.
steps.mistake: Stirring for too long, so the whole thing is dry before the skin forms and it will not roll.
steps.fix: Stop when it looks underdone; the ten still seconds and the plate finish it.

steps.do: If using cheese, scatter it in a line across the middle now. Tilt the pan away from you at about 45 degrees and, with the spatula, fold the third of the omelette nearest the handle over towards the centre.
steps.look: The skin folds cleanly without tearing; the top edge stays soft and creamy.
steps.mistake: Base stuck to the pan, so the fold tears.
steps.fix: Run the spatula around the edge and under the omelette before you begin the fold; use a reliable nonstick pan for this dish.

steps.do: Hold the warm plate in one hand and the pan in the other, with the handle gripped from underneath, palm up. Bring the far edge of the omelette to the plate and tip the pan over so the omelette rolls onto itself and lands seam side down.
steps.look: A neat cigar shape, closed at both ends, sitting seam down on the plate.
steps.mistake: Tipping from too high, so it flops open on landing.
steps.fix: Touch the pan lip to the plate before you turn; shape the roll with a clean towel over your hand if needed.

steps.do: Rub the 1 tsp (5 g) of butter over the top to give it a shine, scatter with chives and serve at once. Wipe the pan with paper towel and repeat with the second bowl of eggs.
steps.look: A glossy, pale blond surface without a single brown patch; cut across, the inside is creamy and moist, top to bottom.
steps.mistake: A dry, overcooked middle.
steps.fix: Next time move the pan off the heat 10 seconds earlier. Make a dozen of these over a month; it is the repetition that teaches the wrist.

steps.do: Judge the omelette against the standard: uniform pale colour, cigar shaped and closed at both ends, unbroken skin with no liquid weeping onto the plate, creamy curds throughout, seasoned evenly. Write down what went wrong and what you will change next time.
steps.look: When the plate is tilted, the centre slumps once and stops rather than running.
steps.mistake: Judging it by taste alone and forgetting the visual standards a chef would mark you on.
steps.fix: Photograph each attempt; the comparison over several weeks shows progress you cannot feel in the moment.

science: The French omelette works by making tiny curds fast and then letting them knit. Rapid stirring breaks setting proteins into fine pieces before they can bond into large lumps, giving a creamy texture. The ten seconds of stillness at the end lets the base, where heat is highest, set into a thin continuous skin that can be rolled. Medium heat is the balance point: hot enough to cook three eggs in under a minute, but cool enough that the surface never reaches the temperatures, around 300°F (150°C), where the Maillard reaction browns proteins and sugars. Browning adds a roasted note that French tradition considers a fault here because it masks butter and egg. Salting ahead loosens protein bonds so the curds stay moist.
plating: Turn the omelette out seam side down across the centre of a warm white plate, angled slightly. Glaze the top with soft butter for shine, scatter a narrow band of chives along the ridge, and keep the plate otherwise clean: a French omelette is presented alone, perhaps with a small green salad on the side.

pairing.drink: A glass of unoaked Chablis: clean, mineral Chardonnay that echoes the butter without weighing down the eggs.
pairing.brennans: Crab & Corn Omelette: Brennan's own omelette, a good comparison for a server explaining how a soft French omelette differs from a filled American one.

variations: Omelette aux fines herbes: beat 1 tbsp (3 g) mixed chopped chervil, parsley, tarragon and chives into the eggs.
Mushroom omelette: fill with 1/2 cup (40 g) mushrooms sautéed in butter until golden.
Boursin filling: a spoonful of soft herbed cheese laid down the middle before rolling.
safety: A creamy omelette may not reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre; use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests or cook until fully set.

title: Çılbır (Turkish Poached Eggs)

Or 1/2 tsp (1 g) sweet paprika plus a pinch of chilli flakes.
Optional, for the poaching water.
Optional.

Make the chilli butter.

steps.mistake: Fridge cold yoghurt, which makes the hot eggs go lukewarm and stiff the moment they land.
steps.fix: Stand the bowl of yoghurt in a larger bowl of warm water for 10 minutes, stirring once.

steps.do: Bring the water in the wide pan to a gentle heat where the surface just shivers and small bubbles cling to the base, about 180°F to 190°F (82°C to 88°C). Add the vinegar if using. The water must not be boiling.
steps.look: Tiny bubbles forming on the bottom and occasionally rising; a wisp of steam; the surface trembles but does not break.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which tears the whites into ragged strands and toughens them.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down and wait a minute; add a splash of cold water to bring it down quickly.

steps.do: Crack one egg into the fine sieve set over a bowl and swirl gently for 10 seconds so the thin, watery white drains through. Tip the egg into a ramekin. Repeat with each egg.
steps.look: The thin white runs through the mesh; what remains is the yolk wrapped in a firm, jelly-like dome of thick white.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve with eggs that are not very fresh, which leaves wispy clouds of white floating in the pan.
steps.fix: Always strain; it costs ten seconds and gives a neat oval egg every time.

steps.do: Lower each ramekin until its lip touches the water and tip the egg in gently. Add the eggs one at a time in different parts of the pan, noting the order. Set a timer for 3 minutes for a runny yolk, 3 1/2 minutes for jammy.
steps.look: The white wraps around the yolk and turns opaque within a minute; the egg rests on the base without spreading.
steps.mistake: Dropping the egg from a height, which splits the white and lets the yolk tear.
steps.fix: Get the ramekin right down to the surface. If an egg sticks to the base, nudge it free with the slotted spoon after 1 minute.

steps.do: While the eggs poach, toast the bread. At 3 minutes, lift the first egg with the slotted spoon and press gently on the yolk with a fingertip: it should feel soft beneath a firm white. Lift each egg in the order it went in and rest it on the paper towel for a few seconds to drain.
steps.look: A smooth white oval, fully opaque with no clear jelly near the yolk, and a yolk that yields like a water balloon.
steps.mistake: Plating straight from the water, which floods the yoghurt with poaching water.
steps.fix: Always drain on paper towel; trim any ragged edges with kitchen scissors for a clean shape.

steps.do: Put the butter in the small saucepan over medium heat. Let it melt, foam and turn light hazelnut brown with a nutty smell, about 2 to 3 minutes, swirling the pan so it colours evenly.
steps.look: Fine foam on top, golden brown flecks on the base, a smell of toasted nuts.
steps.mistake: Taking it past hazelnut to dark brown and acrid, with black flecks.
steps.fix: If it smells burnt, start again with fresh butter; burnt butter will make the whole dish bitter.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and immediately stir in the Aleppo pepper and dried mint. Let them sizzle for about 10 seconds only; the butter turns brick red.
steps.look: The butter stains deep orange red and smells fruity, warm and minty.
steps.mistake: Adding the spices over the flame, where they scorch in seconds and turn bitter.
steps.fix: Always off the heat. The residual heat of the butter is enough to bloom them.

steps.do: Set two eggs on each nest of yoghurt, spoon the red butter over and around them, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and the dill if using, and serve at once with the toast.
steps.look: White yoghurt, white eggs, a red butter pooling at the edges; when a yolk is broken it flows into the yoghurt and butter to make a sauce.
steps.mistake: Pouring all the butter on the eggs, so the yoghurt stays plain.
steps.fix: Spoon most of the butter on the yoghurt around the eggs, a little on top for colour.

science: Egg white proteins begin to set around 140°F to 145°F (60°C to 63°C), well below boiling. Water held at 180°F to 190°F (82°C to 88°C) sets the white steadily from outside in while the yolk stays liquid, and its stillness keeps the white in one piece. Very fresh eggs hold more thick white, a dense protein gel, which clings to the yolk; the thin white is mostly water and spreads into wisps, so straining it off produces a compact egg. Vinegar slightly speeds the set at the surface but can taste sharp, so it is optional. Browning butter cooks its milk solids, giving nutty Maillard flavours, and the spice compounds in chilli and mint are fat soluble, so a few seconds in hot butter carries their aroma through the dish.
plating: Use shallow bowls. Spread the yoghurt into a wide, swirled bed, set the two eggs side by side slightly off centre, then spoon the red butter in a ring around them so it pools in the swirls. Finish with a pinch of Aleppo pepper over the eggs, a few dill fronds, and the toasted bread on a board alongside.

pairing.drink: A dry, crisp rosé from Provence: red fruit to meet the chilli butter, acidity for the yoghurt, and no tannin to clash with the eggs.
pairing.brennans: Eggs Sardou: Brennan's poached eggs on creamed spinach and artichoke, the same poaching skill served the New Orleans way.

variations: Add a spoon of sautéed spinach under the eggs for a greener plate.
Swap the mint for a pinch of sumac and the butter for olive oil for a lighter, sharper finish.
Top with crisp fried sage leaves and toasted pine nuts.
safety: Poached eggs with runny yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); use pasteurised eggs for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or immune compromised, or poach 5 minutes for a set yolk.
Raw garlic in yoghurt should be eaten the same day; do not store the garlic yoghurt for more than 24 hours in the fridge.
Browned butter is far hotter than boiling water; keep it away from the edge of the stove.

title: Bánh Mì Ốp La

steps.look: Even sticks that bend without snapping after salting, and a little liquid squeezed out.
steps.mistake: Thick, uneven sticks, which stay hard and do not take up the brine.
steps.fix: Use a julienne peeler for speed, or slice the thick ones in half lengthways.

steps.do: Whisk the warm water, vinegar, sugar and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt until clear. Pack the vegetables into the jar and pour the brine over until covered. Leave at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, or refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

steps.mistake: Brine that is too sharp because the sugar has not dissolved.

steps.do: Warm the baguettes directly on the oven rack at 375°F (190°C) for 4 to 5 minutes, until the crust crackles when squeezed. If using pâté, have it at room temperature.
steps.look: Thin, glassy crust that shatters, soft warm crumb inside.
steps.mistake: Leaving the bread too long, so it dries into a rusk.
steps.fix: Set a timer; a slightly stale baguette revives best with a quick spritz of water before it goes in.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) of oil in each small pan over medium high heat for about 2 minutes, until the oil shimmers and just begins to smoke at the edges. This is hotter than for basted eggs, deliberately.
steps.look: Oil ripples freely and a faint wisp of smoke appears; a drop of water flicked in spits immediately.
steps.mistake: A pan not hot enough, which gives a flat white with no crisp edge.
steps.fix: Wait another 30 seconds; the lace only forms when the oil instantly boils the water at the edge of the white.

steps.do: Slide two eggs into each pan from the ramekin, keeping the yolks apart. Stand back slightly; they will spit. Let them fry undisturbed for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes.
steps.look: The white bubbles up immediately into blisters, the edges turn golden brown and lacy, the sizzle is loud and steady.
steps.mistake: Panicking and turning the heat right down at the first spit, which stops the crisping.
steps.fix: Hold the heat at medium high; tilt the pan and spoon a little hot oil over the raw white near the yolks if the top is slow to set.

steps.do: In the last 30 seconds, scatter the spring onions into the whites and add the pâté or pork roll to the side of the pan to warm. Season the eggs with pepper.
steps.look: The whites set completely with crisp brown frills, the yolks glossy and trembling, the spring onion just wilted.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the yolks cloud over and set.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat the moment the white around the yolk turns opaque; the cast iron keeps cooking for a minute.

steps.do: Set each hot pan on a trivet or wooden board at the table. Shake a few drops of Maggi over the eggs, add chilli sauce to taste, and serve with the warm baguette, the drained pickle, cucumber and coriander.
steps.look: Sizzling eggs with brown lacy edges in the pan, dark drops of Maggi pooling on the whites.
steps.mistake: Putting a hot cast iron pan straight onto a table or a plastic surface.
steps.fix: Always use a trivet or board, and warn everyone that the pan handle is hot; wrap it in a cloth.

steps.do: Eat by tearing the bread, breaking the yolk and dragging the bread through yolk and seasoning, with bites of pickle between to cut the richness. Taste and adjust with soy or more Maggi.
steps.look: A pan wiped clean by the end; the pickle's sourness balances each rich, salty mouthful.
steps.mistake: Too much Maggi at once, which is intensely salty.
steps.fix: Start with a few drops; add at the table rather than in the kitchen.

science: This egg is fried hotter than the basted egg on purpose. When oil is above about 350°F (175°C), water at the thin edge of the white flashes to steam so violently that it puffs the white into bubbles, and once the water is gone the dry protein browns through the Maillard reaction, giving a crisp, lacy frill and a roasted flavour. The quick pickle relies on salt and acid: rubbing the vegetables with salt draws out water by osmosis so they soften and absorb the brine, while vinegar and sugar season them through within half an hour. plating: Serve the eggs in the pan they were cooked in, set on a wooden board, with the warm baguette split along one side and laid beside it. Put the pickle in a small bowl with a fork, the cucumber spears and coriander sprigs in a little stack, and the Maggi bottle and chilli sauce within reach.

pairing.brennans: Café Glacé de la Maison: Brennan's chicory cold brew is the New Orleans cousin of the iced coffee drunk with this breakfast in Saigon.

steps.mistake: Pale, barely blistered tomatoes, which give a raw, flat tasting salsa.

steps.mistake: Cold, stiff tortillas that crack when folded and taste raw.

Slide in four eggs from the ramekins and fry for about 2 to 3 minutes, tilting the pan and basting the whites with the hot oil, until the whites are set and the yolks are still runny. Lift onto a warm plate and repeat with the rest of the oil and eggs.
steps.look: Fully set white with a little golden lace at the edge, yolks glossy and liquid.
steps.mistake: Frying all eight eggs at once in a crowded pan, so the whites run together and steam.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches; the first batch waits on a warm plate under an upturned bowl for the 3 minutes the second takes.

steps.do: Build each plate: two warm tortillas overlapping, a thin spread of warm beans over them, two fried eggs on top, then ladle salsa around and over the whites, leaving the yolks uncovered.
steps.look: Yellow yolks standing clear above red salsa; the tortillas visible at the edges.
steps.mistake: Drowning the yolks in salsa, so the dish loses its contrast and the yolks go unseen.
steps.fix: Spoon salsa around the eggs and over the whites only; offer extra at the table.

steps.do: Finish with crumbled queso fresco, avocado slices, coriander leaves and a lime wedge. Serve at once.
steps.look: Red, white, green and yellow; the cheese softening slightly on the hot salsa.
steps.mistake: Letting the plates sit while the tortillas soak up the salsa and go soft.
steps.fix: Assemble at the last minute and serve immediately; that is why the salsa is made first.

science: Charring tomatoes, onion, garlic and chilli under intense heat does two things. It browns sugars and amino acids through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, building smoky, sweet flavours, and it softens the flesh so it blends easily. Mexican cooks then fry the blended salsa in very hot oil, a step that concentrates it quickly as water boils off and develops further browning, turning a bright raw flavour into a rounder, deeper one. Simmering reduces the water so the sauce thickens and clings. Warming corn tortillas matters because the starch in nixtamalised corn becomes stiff and brittle as it cools; reheating gelatinises it again so the tortilla turns soft and flexible, while light toasting adds aroma.
plating: Use a warm, wide plate. Overlap two tortillas slightly off centre, spread the beans thinly so the tortilla edge shows, set two eggs side by side, and spoon the salsa in a ring around the yolks. Scatter cheese across the salsa, fan three slices of avocado at one side, add a few coriander leaves and set the lime wedge at the edge.

pairing.drink: A Michelada, beer with lime, salt and hot sauce, or a classic Paloma of tequila, grapefruit and soda: both have salt, citrus and fizz to match the smoky salsa.
pairing.brennans: Bloody Bull: Brennan's beef broth and tomato eye opener matches the chilli and tomato of a ranch breakfast.

variations: Huevos divorciados: serve one egg with red salsa and one with a green tomatillo salsa.
Add crumbled fried chorizo over the beans before the eggs go on.
Bake the eggs in the salsa in a covered pan for 6 minutes for a one pan version.
safety: Frying salsa spits hard: use a deep pan, stand back and add the salsa all at once, away from you.
Blending hot liquids can blow the lid off; let the charred vegetables cool 5 minutes and fill the blender no more than half full.
Runny yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests.
Wash your hands after handling chillies, before touching your eyes.

title: Shakshuka
summary: Eggs poached under a lid in a thick sauce of sweated onion, red pepper, tomato and warm spices, served in the pan with bread. It joins two earlier lessons, sweating aromatics and poaching eggs, in one pan, and adds a third: reducing a sauce until it is thick enough to hold a well.
skills: poaching eggs in sauce under a lid
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) frying pan or shallow casserole with a lid
small bowl or ramekin for cracking eggs

ingredients.item: red pepper, seeded and sliced into thin strips
ingredients.note: A mix of red and yellow is fine.
Or smoked paprika for a smokier pan.
Or 1 tsp (6 g) harissa paste.

ingredients.item: whole peeled tomatoes, crushed by hand, with juice

ingredients.note: Plus a pinch for the eggs.
Only if the tomatoes are sharp.

ingredients.item: flat leaf parsley or coriander, chopped

ingredients.note: To serve.

mise: Slice the onion and pepper into even 1/4 inch (6 mm) strips.
Slice the garlic thinly.
Measure the spices into a small dish together.
Crush the tomatoes by hand in a bowl, removing any hard cores.
Crumble the feta and chop the herbs.
Crack each egg into a cup just before you add it.

timeline.do: Slice onion, pepper and garlic; crush the tomatoes.
Sweat the onion and pepper for 10 to 12 minutes.
Garlic, spices, tomato paste, then tomatoes; simmer to thicken.
Make wells, add the eggs, cover and cook gently.
Feta and herbs on top; serve in the pan with bread.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the 12 inch (30 cm) pan over medium low heat. Add the onion and pepper with a pinch of salt and stir to coat. Cook gently, stirring every minute or two, for 10 to 12 minutes, covering the pan for the first 5 minutes to help them soften.
steps.look: Onion translucent and floppy, pepper strips soft and bending, both glossy with oil and sweet smelling, with little or no browning.
steps.mistake: Medium high heat that browns the edges before the insides soften, giving a harsh, uneven sauce.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a tablespoon of water if anything starts to catch; sweating is about softness, not colour.

steps.do: Add the garlic and cook 1 minute. Then add the cumin, paprika and cayenne and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 1 minute more, pressing it against the pan.
steps.look: The oil turns red, the spices smell toasted and warm, the tomato paste darkens slightly to brick red.
steps.mistake: Spices scorching black in a dry pan.
steps.fix: Keep the heat at medium low and move quickly to the tomatoes; if the spices burn, they will taste bitter, so start that step again with fresh spices.

steps.do: Pour in the crushed tomatoes with all their juice and 3/4 tsp (4.5 g) salt. Bring to a lively simmer, then lower the heat to medium low and simmer uncovered for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick.
steps.look: The sauce reduces by about a third, turns glossy and a deeper red, and bubbles thickly rather than splashing.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs to a thin, watery sauce, which turns the whole pan into soup as the eggs release their own water.
steps.fix: Use the well test: drag a spoon through the sauce to make a crater. If it holds its shape for a few seconds, the sauce is ready.

steps.do: Taste the sauce and adjust: more salt, the 1/2 tsp (2 g) sugar if it is sharp, more cayenne for heat. It should taste bold, because the eggs will soften it.
steps.look: A balanced sauce: sweet from the pepper, warm from cumin, bright from tomato, with a gentle heat.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, so the finished dish tastes flat once the eggs are in.
steps.fix: Season the sauce firmly now; the eggs need only a pinch of salt on top.

steps.do: Turn the heat to low. With the back of a spoon, make six wells in the sauce, evenly spaced around the pan with one or two in the middle. Crack one egg at a time into a cup and slide it into a well.
steps.look: Each egg sits in its own crater; the white spreads slightly but the yolk stays in place.
steps.mistake: Cracking eggs directly into the sauce, which risks shell and broken yolks you cannot fish out.
steps.fix: Always use a cup first; a broken yolk can be stirred into the sauce.

steps.do: Sprinkle a pinch of salt over the eggs. Cover the pan with its lid and cook on low for 5 to 8 minutes, checking after 5, until the whites are set and opaque but the yolks still jiggle when you shake the pan gently.
steps.look: Opaque whites with no clear jelly around the yolks; yolks still glossy and slightly domed, wobbling like jelly when the pan moves.
steps.mistake: Cooking uncovered, so the whites near the yolks stay raw while the bottoms overcook.
steps.fix: Keep the lid on so steam sets the tops; spoon a little sauce over stubborn whites to speed them.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat a minute before the eggs look perfect, since the pan keeps cooking them. Scatter the feta and herbs over and bring the pan to the table on a trivet.
steps.look: White feta, green herbs and yellow yolks over a deep red sauce.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on the heat while you crumble cheese, so the yolks set hard.
steps.fix: Have garnishes ready before the eggs go in.

steps.do: Serve straight from the pan, spooning an egg and plenty of sauce into each bowl, with bread to mop up.
steps.look: When an egg is broken, the yolk runs into the sauce and thickens it.
steps.mistake: Plating the eggs dry with little sauce.
steps.fix: Lift each egg with a large spoon, taking the sauce beneath it.

science: Reduction is evaporation with a purpose. As water leaves the tomatoes, their sugars, acids and savoury glutamates concentrate, and the pectin and fibres left behind thicken the sauce. Eggs release water as their proteins set and tighten, so a thin sauce becomes thinner once they are in; a sauce thick enough to hold a well can absorb that water and still cling. Sweating the onion and pepper slowly breaks down cell walls and converts sharp sulphur compounds into sweeter ones without browning. Spices bloomed in oil release fat soluble aroma compounds. The lid traps steam at about 212°F (100°C), which cooks the top of each egg while the bottom poaches gently in sauce that sits below boiling on low heat.
plating: Serve the shakshuka in the pan on a wooden board, with the eggs evenly spaced like a clock face. Scatter feta in small crumbles between the yolks rather than on them, sprinkle herbs over everything, add a final thread of olive oil and a pinch of paprika, and set bread in a basket alongside.

pairing.drink: A Moroccan style mint tea for the morning, or for a cocktail a Bloody Mary made with a little harissa: both meet the spice and tomato head on.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Bloody Mary: tomato and spice in a glass, a natural partner for eggs in a spiced tomato sauce.

variations: Green shakshuka: use spinach, leeks and courgette in place of tomato and pepper.
Add sliced merguez sausage, browned first, to the sauce before the eggs.
Finish with dollops of garlic yoghurt from the çılbır lesson.
safety: Runny yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); for vulnerable guests, cover and cook 10 to 12 minutes until the yolks are set.
The pan and its handle stay very hot at the table; serve on a trivet and cover the handle with a cloth.
Lift the lid away from you to avoid a face of steam.

title: Gyeran-jjim (Korean Steamed Egg)
summary: A savoury Korean custard of eggs beaten with stock, gently steamed until it sets with a soft wobble and finished with spring onion and sesame. It is the course's first custard, set by steam so the cook learns what a wobble means and how a precise ratio of egg to liquid governs the texture.
equipment: heatproof bowl holding about 3 cups (700 ml), or a Korean earthenware ttukbaegi
large pot with a lid that fits over the bowl, or a steamer
small rack, trivet or folded cloth for the base of the pot
plate or foil to cover the bowl

ingredients.note: Measure them: about 2/3 cup (150 ml).

ingredients.item: anchovy and kelp stock, dashi or light chicken stock, cool
ingredients.note: Water works; stock tastes far better.
Or 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) fine salt plus 1/2 tsp (2.5 ml) fish sauce.
Optional.
To serve.

mise: Put the rack in the pot and add water to 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep, below the top of the rack.
Measure the stock.
Chop the salted shrimp very finely.
Slice the spring onion; keep the green tops separate.
Check that the bowl fits inside the pot with the lid closed.

timeline.do: Water into the pot and heat to a simmer.
Beat the eggs, mix with stock and seasoning, strain.
Bowl into the steamer, covered; steam gently 12 to 15 minutes.
Test the set; add the spring onion tops for the last minute.
Sesame oil and seeds; serve with rice.

steps.do: Set the rack in the pot, add water to 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep, cover and bring to a boil over high heat, then lower to a gentle simmer. The water must not touch the bowl.
steps.look: Steady wisps of steam escaping from the lid, a soft simmer audible but not a hard rattling boil.
steps.mistake: Too much water, which bubbles up into the bowl and makes the custard watery.
steps.fix: Pour some out; there should be a clear gap between the water and the bowl's base.

steps.do: Crack the eggs into a jug and beat them gently with chopsticks or a whisk until the whites and yolks are fully combined but not foamy, about 30 seconds. Measure: note the volume, then add 1.2 times as much stock, about 3/4 cup (180 ml) for 3 large eggs, plus the salted shrimp. Stir gently.
steps.look: An even, pale yellow liquid with very few bubbles.
steps.mistake: Whisking hard, which beats in air that becomes holes in the custard.
steps.fix: Stir rather than whip; skim off any foam with a spoon.

steps.do: Pour the mixture through the fine sieve into the heatproof bowl. Skim off any bubbles on the surface. Stir in the white part of the spring onion.
steps.look: A smooth, glassy surface with no bubbles and no strands of white.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, which leaves chalazae and white strands that set into tough threads.
steps.fix: Always strain; it is the difference between a home custard and a silky one.

steps.do: Cover the bowl with a small plate or a sheet of foil to stop condensation dripping onto the surface. Lower it onto the rack, cover the pot and steam over low to medium low heat, so the water simmers gently, for 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: Gentle steam; when you peek after 10 minutes, the edges are set and the centre is still liquid.
steps.mistake: Steaming at a fierce boil, which overheats the egg so it puffs, bubbles and sets full of holes like a sponge.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and the lid on; a gentle steam takes longer but sets the custard smooth.

steps.do: Test after 12 minutes: lift the cover and gently shake the bowl. Then insert a thin knife or skewer near the centre.
steps.look: The whole surface wobbles as one, like a just set jelly, and the liquid that rises in the knife hole is clear, not yellow and raw.
steps.mistake: Taking it out when the centre still ripples like liquid.
steps.fix: Cover again and steam 2 to 3 minutes more, then test again. Remember the bowl keeps cooking for a minute after it comes out.

steps.do: For the last minute, scatter the green spring onion tops over the surface so they wilt and set into the custard. Then lift the bowl out carefully with an oven glove, opening the lid away from your face.
steps.look: Bright green onion pressed lightly into a smooth yellow surface.
steps.mistake: Reaching in with bare fingers; steam burns quickly.
steps.fix: Use oven gloves or a folded cloth, and tilt the lid away from you as you open it.

steps.do: Drizzle the sesame oil over the surface, sprinkle with sesame seeds and a pinch of chilli flakes if you like. Serve hot in the bowl with rice, eating it with a spoon.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth custard that shivers when the spoon goes in and is soft and silky in the mouth, savoury with a gentle sea saltiness.
steps.mistake: Holes and a weeping, watery layer at the bottom, a sign of overheating.
steps.fix: Lower the heat next time and steam for longer; the ratio and the temperature are the two levers.

science: A custard is egg proteins forming a loose mesh that traps liquid. Diluting eggs with stock spreads the proteins further apart, so the custard sets at a higher temperature, around 175°F to 180°F (79°C to 82°C), and becomes softer. The ratio sets the texture: about 1.2 parts stock to 1 part egg gives a tender set that still holds a spoonful. Heat speed matters as much as temperature. If the custard heats too fast, water in it boils into steam bubbles before the mesh is firm, leaving holes, and the proteins tighten and squeeze out liquid, which weeps. Gentle steam heats the bowl evenly from all sides. Salted shrimp and stock provide glutamates and sodium for a deep savoury taste without making the custard heavy.
plating: Serve in the bowl or ttukbaegi it was steamed in, set on a small plate with a folded napkin under it for grip. Scatter the spring onion in a loose ring, finish with a few drops of sesame oil and seeds in the centre, and put a bowl of rice and a spoon beside it.

pairing.drink: A chilled glass of dry sake or a light, crisp Korean lager: both are gentle enough to let the delicate custard show.

variations: Ttukbaegi gyeran-jjim: cook the mixture directly over the flame in a Korean earthenware pot, stirring until half set, then cover so it puffs up like a soufflé.
Add finely chopped carrot and shiitake to the mixture for colour and texture.
Japanese chawanmushi: use three parts dashi to one of egg, add a prawn and a piece of chicken, and steam in cups.
safety: Steam burns: open lids away from you and use gloves to lift the bowl out.
Never let the pot boil dry; check the water level if steaming longer than 20 minutes.
The custard is cooked through when set, reaching well above 160°F (71°C); serve it hot.

title: Kaya Toast with Soft-Boiled Eggs
summary: The coffee shop breakfast of Malaysia and Singapore: crisp toast sandwiching a slab of cold butter and kaya, a stirred custard jam of coconut milk, eggs, sugar and pandan, with very soft eggs seasoned with soy and white pepper. Kaya must thicken without scrambling, which is the core skill behind every sweet custard to come.
skills: a stirred coconut and egg custard
equipment: heatproof glass or stainless steel bowl that sits snugly over a saucepan
clean jar with a lid, about 1 1/2 cups (350 ml)
small saucepan with a lid for the eggs
4 small bowls or saucers for the eggs

ingredients.item: full fat coconut milk, well shaken
pandan leaves, tied in a knot
ingredients.note: Fresh or frozen from an Asian grocer; or 1/4 tsp (1.25 ml) pandan extract.
Soft, plain white bread is traditional.
Cut into slabs 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick.

ingredients.item: large eggs, at room temperature, for soft-boiling
ingredients.note: Out of the fridge for 30 minutes.

ingredients.item: dark soy sauce and light soy sauce

mise: Put 2 inches (5 cm) of water in the saucepan and check the bowl sits over it without touching the water.
Knot the pandan leaves; take the soft-boil eggs out of the fridge.
Measure eggs, sugar, coconut milk and salt for the kaya.
Slice the cold butter into thin slabs and keep it in the fridge on a plate.
Have the sieve set over the clean jar.

timeline.do: Make the kaya: about 25 to 35 minutes of stirring.
Strain the kaya into its jar and let it cool and thicken.
Boil a kettle; put the room temperature eggs in a pan and cover with boiling water off the heat.
Toast the bread.
Assemble the toast with kaya and cold butter; crack the eggs into bowls.
Season the eggs with soy and white pepper and serve.

steps.do: In the heatproof bowl, whisk the 3 eggs, sugar and salt for 1 minute until the sugar mostly dissolves, then whisk in the coconut milk. Drop in the knotted pandan leaves.
steps.look: A smooth, pale mixture with no streaks of egg white and no gritty sugar at the bottom when you scrape.
steps.mistake: Leaving the sugar undissolved, which can give a grainy kaya.
steps.fix: Whisk a little longer, or warm the bowl over the water for a minute while whisking.

steps.do: Bring the water in the saucepan to a bare simmer over low heat, then set the bowl on top. The base of the bowl must not touch the water, and the water should only steam gently, never boil hard.
steps.look: Wisps of steam from under the bowl, small bubbles on the base of the saucepan, the mixture warming slowly.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil under the bowl, which overheats the eggs at the bottom and scrambles them.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; if you see curds forming, lift the bowl off at once and whisk hard.

steps.do: Stir constantly with the spatula, scraping the base and sides of the bowl in a figure of eight. Keep going for 25 to 35 minutes. For the first 15 minutes it stays thin; then it thickens steadily.
steps.look: The mixture goes from milky to slightly glossy, then coats the spatula; a line drawn through it on the spatula holds its edges. On a thermometer, aim for 180°F to 185°F (82°C to 85°C).
steps.mistake: Walking away and letting the custard set in lumps against the hot sides of the bowl.
steps.fix: Keep stirring. If small lumps form, whisk vigorously off the heat; the sieve will catch the rest.

steps.do: When the kaya is as thick as loose custard and coats the spatula heavily, take the bowl off the heat. Remove the pandan, squeezing the leaves against the side of the bowl to release their juices.
steps.look: Thick enough that a spoonful dropped back onto the surface holds a mound for a second before sinking; pale green-gold, smelling of vanilla, coconut and grass.
steps.mistake: Taking it too far until it is thick as paste while hot, which sets rubbery once cool.
steps.fix: Stop at thick custard; it thickens considerably as it cools. If it becomes grainy, blend it smooth with a stick blender.

steps.do: Push the kaya through the fine sieve into the jar with the spatula. Press a piece of baking parchment onto the surface to stop a skin and let it cool for at least 30 minutes, then refrigerate if not using the same day.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, spreadable jam that sets to the thickness of soft peanut butter when cool.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, leaving small cooked lumps of egg white.
steps.fix: Always strain; it takes a minute and guarantees silkiness.

steps.do: For the soft eggs, put the 4 room temperature eggs in the small saucepan and pour over enough boiling water from the kettle to cover them by 1 inch (2.5 cm). Cover with the lid, off the heat, and leave for 6 to 7 minutes.
steps.look: After 6 minutes the white is milky, just set close to the shell and still soft and translucent near the yolk; the yolk is warm and liquid.
steps.mistake: Using fridge cold eggs, which cool the water so the whites stay raw.
steps.fix: Use room temperature eggs, or add 1 minute; this style is meant to be very soft and is eaten with a spoon.

steps.do: Meanwhile toast the bread until crisp and golden. Spread a thick layer of kaya on one slice, lay slabs of cold butter over it, top with a second slice, press gently and cut into halves or thirds.
steps.look: Hot crisp toast, a dark golden layer of kaya and a clearly visible slab of butter that is still cold and only melting at its edges.
steps.mistake: Softened butter spread thinly, which melts away and loses the contrast that defines the dish.
steps.fix: Keep the butter in the fridge until the last second and slice it thick.

steps.do: Crack two soft eggs into each small bowl. Add a few drops of dark and light soy sauce and a dusting of white pepper. Stir lightly and dip the toast into the eggs, or drink them from the bowl.
steps.look: Silky, barely set eggs streaked with brown soy; the toast crisp, sweet, salty and buttery.
steps.mistake: Over-boiled eggs that are firm, which cannot be dipped.
steps.fix: Reduce the time next attempt by 1 minute, and note how many minutes your pan and your eggs need.

science: A stirred custard thickens because egg proteins unfold and link as they heat, trapping liquid in a loose mesh. Sugar and coconut fat get between the proteins and raise the setting point, so kaya thickens around 180°F to 185°F (82°C to 85°C), but scrambles if any part passes about 190°F (88°C). A bain-marie limits the temperature: water at a gentle simmer heats the bowl slowly and evenly, and constant stirring keeps the hot layer against the bowl moving so it never overcooks. Long, gentle cooking also lets the sugar and proteins brown very slightly, adding a caramel note. The custard keeps thickening as it cools because the protein mesh tightens and the coconut fat sets. Pandan leaves contain an aromatic compound with a vanilla and rice-like scent that infuses into the warm fat.
plating: Stack the kaya toast in two triangles, cut edge facing out so the green-gold layer and the white butter slab show clearly, on a small plate. Serve the soft eggs in a small bowl or saucer beside it with soy and pepper on the table, and a cup of strong sweet coffee.

pairing.drink: Strong Malaysian kopi with condensed milk is the tradition; as a cocktail, a Painkiller of rum, pineapple, orange and coconut cream picks up the coconut and pandan.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the roasted, slightly bitter cup is close in spirit to the dark roasted kopi served with kaya toast.

variations: Hainanese brown kaya: caramelise 2 tbsp (25 g) of the sugar to deep amber, cool slightly, then whisk it into the coconut milk before cooking.
Kaya on steamed bread: steam soft white rolls and spread them with kaya and butter.
Kaya French toast: sandwich kaya between bread, dip in egg and fry in butter.
safety: These soft-boiled eggs are well below 160°F (71°C); anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or immune compromised should use pasteurised eggs or cook the eggs 10 minutes.
Kaya is an egg custard: cool it within 2 hours, keep it covered in the fridge and use it within 1 week, with a clean spoon each time.
Lift the bowl off the bain-marie with a cloth; steam escapes around its edge.

title: Scottish Oat Porridge
summary: Oats toasted, then simmered in salted water and stirred until they release their starch into a smooth, loose porridge, served with cold milk or cream. Grains begin here: the ratio of liquid to grain, the salt that makes it taste of oats, and the stirring that turns cereal into a creamy bowl.
skills: stirring to a smooth, loose set

ingredients.item: rolled oats (porridge oats) or medium oatmeal
ingredients.note: See the variations for pinhead (steel cut) oats.
Or 1 cup (240 ml) water and 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk for a richer bowl.
Scottish porridge is salted, never sweetened in the pan.
For toasting; optional.

ingredients.item: cold whole milk or single cream, to serve
toppings: brown sugar, honey, berries or toasted seeds
ingredients.us: to taste, about 1 tbsp per bowl
ingredients.note: Optional.

mise: Weigh or measure the oats, water and salt.
Warm the bowls with hot water.
Pour the cold milk or cream into a small jug and keep it in the fridge until serving.
Set out toppings.

timeline.do: Toast the oats in the pan for 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the water, bring to the boil, then simmer and stir.
Add the salt; keep stirring.
Check consistency; rest off the heat 1 minute.
Serve in warm bowls with cold milk on the side.

steps.do: Put the saucepan over medium heat, add the butter if using, then the oats. Toast them, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: The oats darken by a shade to pale gold and smell like warm biscuits; you hear a gentle crackle.
steps.mistake: Leaving them unstirred so the oats against the base burn while the rest stay raw.
steps.fix: Stir continuously; if any blacken, tip the oats out and start again, as burnt oats flavour the whole pot.

steps.do: Pour in the 2 cups (480 ml) of water; it will hiss. Bring to the boil over medium high heat, stirring.
steps.look: The water turns cloudy straight away as starch starts to leach out; bubbles break across the surface.
steps.mistake: Adding the oats to cold water and walking off, so they stick in one mass on the base.
steps.fix: Stir from the moment the liquid goes in until it boils.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium low so the porridge bubbles lazily, with a plop every second or two. Stir steadily with the wooden spoon or spurtle, drawing it across the base of the pan, for 5 minutes.
steps.look: The mixture thickens and turns creamy as the oats swell and release starch; the spoon leaves a brief trail.
steps.mistake: Too high a heat, which makes the porridge spit and catch on the base.
steps.fix: Turn it down; porridge should simmer gently, and the spoon should keep the base clean.

steps.do: Add the 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) of salt and stir it in. Continue simmering and stirring for 2 to 3 minutes more for rolled oats, or 5 for medium oatmeal.
steps.look: The grains are swollen and soft, the porridge glossy, and it tastes clearly of oats rather than flat starch.
steps.mistake: Leaving the salt out, which makes the porridge taste bland however much sugar goes on top.
steps.fix: Taste and add a pinch more salt; it should be seasoned, not salty.

steps.do: Check the consistency: lift a spoonful and let it drop back. It should flow slowly from the spoon and settle level in the pan within a few seconds. Add a splash of hot water to loosen, or simmer a minute longer to thicken.
steps.look: A loose, pourable porridge that settles flat, like thick double cream; it will firm up in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Cooking until it stands in a stiff heap, which sets into a solid lump by the time it is eaten.
steps.fix: Stop while it still flows; stir in a little hot water if it has become too thick.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and let it stand for 1 minute so the oats finish absorbing water.
steps.look: A thin skin forming at the edges, the surface settling glossy and smooth.
steps.mistake: Leaving it to stand longer, which turns it gluey.
steps.fix: Stir in a splash of hot water to bring it back.

steps.do: Ladle into the warm bowls. Serve the cold milk or cream in a jug on the side, to be poured around the edge, so each spoonful is hot porridge dipped into cold milk. Add a sprinkle of brown sugar or honey if wanted.

science: Oats are rich in starch and in beta glucan, a soluble fibre that becomes viscous in water. Stirring rubs the swollen grains against each other and the pan, releasing starch and beta glucan into the liquid, which thickens it into a creamy suspension. The ratio decides the final texture: roughly three parts water to one part rolled oats by volume gives a loose porridge. Toasting first browns the bran through the Maillard reaction, adding nutty flavours. Salt does not just season; it suppresses bitterness and makes the cereal taste sweeter and fuller.

title: Bircher Muesli
summary: Rolled oats soaked overnight in milk and apple juice, then loosened with yoghurt, lemon and honey and folded with freshly grated apple, toasted hazelnuts and fruit. chef's knife and paring knife, board

ingredients.note: Not instant oats, which turn to mush.
From about half a lemon; some for the apple, some for the mix.
Adjust to taste.

ingredients.item: fresh berries, such as raspberries or blueberries

ingredients.note: Optional.

Toast the hazelnuts and rub off the skins.
Squeeze the lemon.
Wash the apples and berries; dry the berries on a towel.
