Skin and chop the nuts; stir yoghurt, lemon and honey into the oats.
Grate one apple into the mix; slice the second for garnish.
Spoon into bowls, top with apple slices, berries and nuts.

steps.do: The night before, stir the oats, milk, apple juice and a pinch of salt together in the bowl, making sure every oat is wet. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, or up to 2 days.
steps.look: In the morning the oats have swollen to almost double, absorbed most of the liquid and turned soft and creamy but still have a slight chew.
steps.mistake: Soaking at room temperature, which risks the milk spoiling.
steps.fix: Always soak in the fridge; it works just as well, only slightly more slowly.

steps.do: In the morning, spread the hazelnuts on the tray and toast at 350°F (175°C) for 10 to 12 minutes, shaking once halfway, until the skins crack and the nuts are golden under the skin.
steps.look: Skins blistered and flaking, nut flesh light gold when one is cut open, a rich roasted smell.
steps.mistake: Forgetting them, so they burn; nuts go from toasted to burnt in about 2 minutes.
steps.fix: Set a timer. If they are dark brown inside, start again with a new batch.

steps.do: Tip the hot nuts into the tea towel, fold it over and rub vigorously for 30 seconds. Pick out the nuts, leaving most of the papery skin behind. Roughly chop them on the board with the chef's knife, holding the tip down and rocking the heel through the pile.
steps.look: Golden nuts with most of their skins gone, chopped into pieces about the size of a lentil, with a few larger halves for garnish.
steps.mistake: Chopping before they cool slightly, which makes them oily and crumbly.
steps.fix: Let them cool 3 minutes first; a few stubborn skins do no harm.

steps.do: Stir the yoghurt, 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the lemon juice and the honey into the soaked oats. The mixture should be loose and spoonable. Add a splash of milk if it is stiff.
steps.look: A creamy, loose mixture that drops easily from a spoon, rather than a stiff paste.
steps.mistake: Muesli thick as cement because the oats absorbed everything.
steps.fix: Stir in milk or yoghurt a spoonful at a time until it loosens.

steps.do: Grate one apple straight into the bowl on the coarse holes of the box grater, skin on, turning it as you go and stopping at the core. Hold the apple with your fingertips curled and stop when it gets small, to protect your knuckles. Fold in at once.
steps.look: Fresh, juicy shreds of apple with flecks of skin, folding in without browning.
steps.mistake: Grating the apple in advance, which turns it brown and soft.
steps.fix: Grate at the last minute directly into the lemony mixture; the acid slows browning.

steps.do: Taste and balance: it should be gently sweet and noticeably fresh and sour. Add more honey for sweetness, more lemon for brightness, a pinch of cinnamon if you like.
steps.look: Sweet, sour and creamy in balance, with no one flavour shouting.
steps.mistake: Adding lots of honey to cover a flat taste that actually needs acid or salt.
steps.fix: Try a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt first; they make fruit taste fruitier.

steps.do: For the garnish, quarter the second apple, cut out the core with the paring knife, and slice each quarter into thin wedges about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Toss them in the remaining lemon juice. Fan a few slices on each portion by overlapping them in a curve.
steps.look: Even, thin slices with clean edges, overlapping evenly, staying white.
steps.mistake: Thick, uneven slices that look clumsy and brown quickly.
steps.fix: Slice with the whole length of the blade in one smooth stroke rather than pressing straight down.

steps.do: Spoon the muesli into bowls, add the fanned apple slices, scatter the berries and toasted hazelnuts over and serve cold.
steps.look: A pale creamy base, a fan of green-skinned apple, bright berries and golden nuts.
steps.mistake: Adding the nuts too early, so they go soft.
steps.fix: Scatter nuts just before serving for crunch.

science: Soaking replaces heat as the way to soften the oats. Rolled oats have already been steamed and flattened during processing, so their starch is partly gelatinised and they absorb cold liquid readily, softening over several hours as water moves into the flakes. The acid in apple juice and yoghurt keeps the flavour bright. Grated apple browns because cutting breaks its cells, letting the enzyme polyphenol oxidase meet oxygen and turn phenolic compounds brown; lemon juice lowers the pH and slows the enzyme. Toasting hazelnuts drives off moisture and develops roasted flavours through the Maillard reaction, while the skins, which are slightly bitter, loosen and can be rubbed off. Sweet and sour balance works because acid cuts through sweetness and cream, making the whole dish taste lighter.
plating: Spoon the muesli into a shallow bowl and smooth it level. Fan five or six thin apple slices in an arc across one side, pile the berries in the space beside them, and scatter the chopped nuts over the berries with two or three halves on top. Finish with a light dusting of cinnamon and a thread of honey.

pairing.drink: A Bellini made with white peach purée and Prosecco, or simply a glass of cloudy apple juice: fruit and bright acidity to match the apple.
pairing.brennans: Revive Cold-Pressed Juice: strawberry, apple and pineapple echo the fruit and freshness of the muesli.

variations: Use pear instead of apple and add a pinch of ground ginger.
Stir in 2 tbsp (20 g) of grated coconut and top with mango for a tropical bowl.
Make it dairy free with oat milk and coconut yoghurt.
safety: Soak the oats in the fridge, never at room temperature, and eat within 2 days.
Keep fingers clear of the grater: stop grating when the apple becomes small and use the last piece for snacking.
Hot nuts from the oven can burn; let them cool for a minute before rubbing in the towel.

title: Chicken Congee
summary: Rice simmered slowly in plenty of water with ginger and chicken until the grains break down into a silky porridge, then topped with spring onion, white pepper, soy and crisp garnishes. equipment: heavy 5 quart (4.7 litre) pot with a lid
wooden spoon with a flat end

ingredients.note: Or a mix with a little glutinous rice for extra silkiness.
Rubbed into the rice, a Cantonese habit.

ingredients.item: water or light unsalted chicken stock
ingredients.note: Plus more hot water to adjust.
Thighs stay juicier than breast during the long simmer.

ingredients.item: fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced
ingredients.note: Plus a little julienned for garnish.
To serve.
To serve.
Shop bought is fine.
Optional.

Toss the drained rice with the oil and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and leave 15 minutes.
Slice the ginger.
Prepare the garnishes in small bowls: spring onion, coriander, shallots, julienned ginger, soy, sesame oil, chilli crisp, white pepper.

timeline.do: Rinse and oil the rice; bring the water to the boil.
Rice, ginger and chicken in; return to the boil, then hold at a bare simmer.
Chicken at 175°F (79°C) in the thickest part: lift out to cool.
Shred the chicken; keep stirring the congee every 10 minutes.
Whisk the congee, adjust thickness, return the chicken, season.
Ladle into bowls and garnish.

steps.do: Rinse the rice in the sieve under cold running water, rubbing the grains between your fingers, until the water is only faintly cloudy. Drain well, then toss with the oil and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and leave for 15 minutes.
steps.look: Rinse water going from milky to nearly clear; the oiled grains glossy and separate.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rinse, which leaves loose surface starch that makes the bottom catch early.
steps.fix: Rinse three times; if the pot catches later, do not scrape the burnt layer into the congee.

steps.do: Bring the 9 cups (2.1 litres) of water or stock to a full boil in the heavy pot over high heat. Add the rice and ginger and stir well so nothing sticks. Return to the boil.
steps.look: Rice dancing in rapidly boiling water, the water turning cloudy.
steps.mistake: Putting the rice into cold water, which lets it settle and glue to the base.
steps.fix: Always add rice to boiling water and stir until it is back at the boil.

steps.do: Add the chicken thighs. When the pot returns to a gentle boil, skim off any grey foam, then turn the heat to low so the congee holds a bare simmer: a few lazy bubbles breaking the surface. Set the lid ajar.
steps.look: Occasional slow bubbles, steam rising gently, foam removed so the liquid stays clean.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil with the lid on, which boils over in a starchy flood and toughens the chicken.
steps.fix: Keep the lid ajar and the heat low; if it starts to rise, lift the lid and stir.

steps.do: Simmer, stirring and scraping the base every 10 minutes, for about 25 minutes, then check the chicken with the thermometer in the thickest part of a thigh, away from the bone. Lift the thighs out when they read at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are tenderest at 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Chicken firm, juices clear when pierced, meat beginning to pull away from the bone.
steps.mistake: Guessing the chicken is done; undercooked chicken is a real hazard.
steps.fix: Always probe the thickest part; if it is under 165°F (74°C), return it for 5 minutes and check again.

steps.do: Let the chicken cool on a plate for 10 minutes, then pull off the skin and discard it, and shred the meat into bite sized strands with two forks. Return the bones to the pot for flavour if you like, removing them before serving.
steps.look: Moist strands of chicken, no pink at the bone.
steps.mistake: Shredding too fine, so the chicken disappears into the porridge.
steps.fix: Pull into strips the size of a finger joint.

steps.do: Keep simmering the rice for a total of 60 to 75 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes and scraping the base each time. In the last 20 minutes stir more often, as it thickens.
steps.look: Grains swollen and bursting, the liquid thick and opaque, the whole pot turning into a smooth, silky porridge.
steps.mistake: Ignoring the pot so a layer sticks and scorches on the base, giving a burnt taste.
steps.fix: If it catches, do not scrape; pour the congee into a clean pot, leaving the burnt layer behind.

steps.do: When the grains have broken down, whisk the congee vigorously for 1 minute to break up remaining grains. Adjust the thickness with hot water: it should pour from a ladle like heavy cream. Return the chicken and season with up to 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the white pepper.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy porridge that flows slowly off the ladle and settles level in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Over-thick congee, stiff like mashed potato, which sets into a block as it cools.
steps.fix: Thin with hot water a ladle at a time; congee thickens as it stands.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls. Garnish each bowl with spring onion, julienned ginger, coriander, fried shallots, a few drops of soy and sesame oil, and chilli crisp if wanted. Let each person add more at the table.
steps.look: Pale, silky porridge with bright green, gold and red garnishes on top.
steps.mistake: Seasoning heavily in the pot, which leaves no room for the salty garnishes.
steps.fix: Season the pot lightly and let the garnishes add salt, crunch and fragrance.

science: Congee is starch gelatinisation taken to its end point. With about twelve times as much water as rice by volume, the grains have unlimited water to absorb. As they simmer, starch granules swell, soften and eventually burst, releasing amylose and amylopectin into the liquid, which thickens it into a smooth porridge. Rinsing removes loose surface starch that would settle and scorch; rubbing the rice with oil and salt is a Cantonese habit thought to help the grains break apart. A bare simmer is enough because water at 190°F to 200°F (88°C to 93°C) still breaks the grain down, without the violent boil that sticks rice to the pan. Chicken thighs, rich in connective tissue, release gelatin and flavour while staying moist.
plating: Ladle the congee into deep, warm bowls so it settles in a smooth, level surface. Place the chicken in a loose pile in the centre, then add the garnishes in small clusters around it: spring onion, ginger threads, coriander, shallots. Finish with a few drops of sesame oil and a dark swirl of soy at the edge.

pairing.drink: A pot of hot jasmine or oolong tea, or for a wine, a chilled glass of dry fino sherry, whose savoury, nutty edge matches ginger and soy.

variations: Pork and century egg congee: add marinated pork mince and chopped preserved duck egg in the last 15 minutes.
Fish congee: slide thin slices of white fish into the hot congee off the heat and let them poach for 2 minutes.
Freeze the rinsed rice overnight before cooking; ice crystals crack the grains and halve the time.
safety: Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part; check with a thermometer.
Rice can carry spores that survive cooking; cool leftover congee quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat until steaming hot throughout.
Starchy liquids boil over and spit; keep the lid ajar and stir with a long spoon.

title: Kiri Bath (Sri Lankan Milk Rice)
summary: Short grain rice cooked soft in water, then stirred with thick coconut milk until it sets firm enough to press flat and cut into diamonds, served with lunu miris, a pounded relish of red onion, chilli and lime. pressing and cutting a set rice
equipment: heavy 3 quart (2.8 litre) saucepan with a tight lid
flat plate or tray, about 9 inches (23 cm) across
offset spatula or the back of a wet spoon
large knife and a glass of water

ingredients.item: short grain white rice, such as Sri Lankan samba or Italian pudding rice
ingredients.note: Short grain gives the sticky set.

ingredients.item: thick coconut milk, the first press or full fat canned
ingredients.note: One standard can, shaken.

ingredients.item: red onion or shallots, for the lunu miris

ingredients.note: Sri Lankan lunu miris is hot; start with less.
Optional, for savoury depth; leave out for a vegetarian relish.

mise: Rinse the rice in the sieve until the water runs clear.
Shake the coconut milk can well and open it.
Line the plate or tray with a banana leaf or parchment.
Peel and roughly chop the onion.
Squeeze the lime.
Set the mortar on a folded towel so it cannot slide.

Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 to 18 minutes.
Stir in the coconut milk and salt; stir over low heat until thick.
Spread on the lined tray and smooth flat.
Pound the lunu miris while the rice sets.
Cut into diamonds and serve with the relish.

steps.do: Put the rinsed rice and 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of water in the saucepan and bring to the boil over medium high heat, stirring once to stop the grains sticking.
steps.look: Water bubbling across the surface, the rice moving, the water clouding with starch.
steps.mistake: Adding the coconut milk now, at the start.
steps.fix: Hold the coconut milk back; added early, its fat coats the grains and keeps them chalky while the milk scorches.

steps.do: Cover with the tight lid and turn the heat to the lowest setting. Cook for 15 to 18 minutes without lifting the lid, until all the water is absorbed.
steps.look: When you lift the lid, steam holes on the surface, no free water at the bottom when you tilt the pan, the grains soft and starting to burst.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid every few minutes, letting steam escape so the rice cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Trust the time; if there is still water, cover and cook 3 minutes more.

steps.do: Pour in the coconut milk and 1 1/2 tsp (9 g) salt. Stir steadily with the wooden spoon over low heat. The rice will first loosen into a porridge, then gradually thicken again, over 6 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The mixture turns glossy and creamy; the grains are very soft and sticky.
steps.mistake: Medium or high heat, which scorches coconut milk on the base in minutes.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and stir constantly, scraping the base.

steps.do: Keep stirring until a spoon drawn across the base of the pan leaves a clear track that closes slowly, and the rice clumps together and comes away from the sides as a mass. Taste: it should be creamy and gently salty.
steps.look: A thick, sticky, glossy mass that pulls from the pan sides and holds the track of the spoon.
steps.mistake: Stopping while it is still loose, so it will never set firm enough to cut.
steps.fix: Stir for 2 to 3 minutes more; the track test is the signal.

steps.do: Tip the hot rice onto the lined plate. Wet the offset spatula or the back of a spoon in water and press the rice into an even slab about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, smoothing the top and squaring the edges.
steps.look: A level, glossy slab with neat, straight sides and a smooth surface.
steps.mistake: Pressing with a dry spatula, which sticks and tears the surface.
steps.fix: Dip the spatula in water before every few strokes; a piece of banana leaf pressed on top works beautifully too.

steps.do: Leave the slab to cool and set for 20 to 30 minutes. Meanwhile, make the lunu miris: pound the chilli flakes and salt in the mortar for 30 seconds, add the onion and the Maldive fish if using and pound to a coarse, moist paste. Stir in the lime juice and taste.
steps.look: A rough, deep red paste that is wet but not soupy, sharp with onion and lime and hot with chilli.
steps.mistake: Pounding the onion first, so the chilli and salt never break down evenly.
steps.fix: Always pound dry, hard ingredients first, then add the wet ones.

steps.do: When the rice is firm and just warm, cut it into diamonds about 2 inches (5 cm) long with a large knife dipped in water: cut parallel lines one way, then diagonal lines across them. Wipe and wet the blade between cuts.
steps.look: Clean, straight edged diamonds that hold their shape when lifted.
steps.mistake: Cutting while it is too hot, which smears.
steps.fix: Wait 10 minutes more; for the cleanest cuts, cut once it is completely cool.

steps.do: Serve two or three diamonds per person with a spoonful of lunu miris on the side.
steps.look: White, glossy diamonds and a vivid red relish.
steps.mistake: Burying the rice under relish; lunu miris is very hot.
steps.fix: Serve a small spoonful and let each person add more.

science: Rice starch needs water to swell, and fat gets in the way. When coconut milk goes in at the start, its fat coats the starch granules and slows water absorption, so the grains stay chalky while the milk sugars and proteins scorch on the base. Cooking the rice in water first lets the granules swell and soften completely; the coconut milk then adds richness, and stirring drives off its water while the released starch and the coconut fat bind into a dense mass. As it cools, gelatinised starch molecules realign and bond, a process called retrogradation, which is why the slab firms enough to slice. Short grain rice is high in amylopectin, the sticky branched starch, so it holds together better than long grain. Pounding releases the onion's juices and sharp sulphur compounds.
plating: Arrange the diamonds in a neat overlapping row or a fan on a banana leaf or a white plate. Put the lunu miris in a small bowl at one end, with a single diamond topped with a little relish to show how it is eaten, and add a wedge of lime.

pairing.drink: A pot of Ceylon black tea with milk, or for a cocktail, an arrack sour made with coconut arrack, lime and sugar, Sri Lanka's own spirit.

variations: Serve with a mild chicken or fish curry for a celebration breakfast.
Sweet kiri bath: serve with grated jaggery and banana instead of lunu miris.
Add 1 tsp (2 g) cumin seeds or a cinnamon stick to the cooking rice for gentle spice.
safety: Cooked rice left at room temperature can grow bacteria from spores that survive cooking; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and reheat thoroughly.
Coconut rice is very hot and sticky; it holds heat like porridge, so take care when pressing it by hand.
Wash hands after handling chilli, and keep it away from eyes.

title: Tapsilog

steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which leaves long fibres and chewy tapa.
steps.fix: Turn the steak 90 degrees and cut the other way; thin and across the grain is what makes tapa tender.

steps.do: Whisk the soy, citrus, minced garlic, brown sugar and pepper until the sugar dissolves. Add the beef, massage it so every slice is coated, press out the air and refrigerate for at least 1 hour and no longer than 12 hours.

steps.mistake: Starting in hot oil, so the garlic browns in seconds and turns bitter.

steps.do: Turn the heat up to medium high under the remaining garlic oil. Add the cold, broken up rice and the salt. Toss and press the rice against the pan with a spatula for 4 to 5 minutes, letting it sit 30 seconds between tosses so it toasts lightly.
steps.look: Separate, glossy grains that hop in the pan, flecked with garlic, with a few lightly toasted bits; a toasty garlic smell.
steps.mistake: Using fresh warm rice, which turns into sticky clumps.
steps.fix: Use rice cooked the day before; in a pinch, spread fresh rice on a tray and refrigerate uncovered for an hour.

steps.do: Taste the rice and add salt if needed. Keep it warm in a low oven at 200°F (95°C), covered loosely, with the reserved crisp garlic set aside for the top.
steps.look: Fluffy, seasoned rice with a clear garlic taste.
steps.mistake: Stirring the crisp garlic in now, where it goes soft.
steps.fix: Scatter it on top at the end.

steps.do: Heat the cast iron pan over high heat for 2 minutes, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil, and when it smokes lightly, lay in half the beef in a single layer, shaking off excess marinade first. Sear 1 to 1 1/2 minutes per side without moving it. Repeat with the rest.
steps.look: Dark, caramelised edges, glossy and sticky from the sugar, a loud sizzle. The beef is cooked through but still juicy.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan with all the beef and marinade, so it boils grey in liquid instead of searing.
steps.fix: Cook in batches with room between slices; if liquid pools, pour it off and let the pan reheat.

steps.do: Wipe the egg pan, heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil over medium high until shimmering, and fry the eggs sunny side up with crisp, lacy edges, about 2 minutes, spooning a little hot oil over the whites to set them.
steps.look: Golden lacy edges, whites set, yolks runny and glossy.
steps.mistake: Frying the eggs first, so they are cold by the time the beef is done.
steps.fix: Always cook eggs last; they take two minutes.

steps.do: Plate a dome of garlic rice topped with the crisp garlic, the tapa beside it and the fried egg on the rice, with tomato and cucumber slices and the spiced vinegar in a small bowl for dipping the beef.

The sugar caramelises and joins the Maillard reaction on a very hot pan, giving tapa its sticky, dark edges. Day old rice fries well because, as cooked rice cools, its starch retrogrades and the surface dries, so the grains firm up and separate instead of gluing together. Garlic browns quickly because of its sugars; starting it in cold oil gives an even gold.

Lay the tapa in an overlapping row beside it, slide the egg onto the top of the rice dome, and scatter crisp garlic over the rice. pairing.brennans: Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak: Brennan's steak served with a sunny side up egg is the New Orleans cousin of tapa and egg.

potato masher or a large fork
mortar and pestle or a board and knife for the garlic

ingredients.note: Sold in Middle Eastern shops; see variations for canned.
Fresh water for the simmer.
From about 1 1/2 lemons.
Optional garnish.
Optional.
Optional, loosened with water.

Next morning, drain and rinse the beans.
Mash the garlic with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt to a paste.
Squeeze the lemons.
Dice tomato and onion, chop parsley, slice chilli.
Hard-boil the eggs if using; warm the bread.

Drain, cover with fresh water and bring to a simmer.
Hold at a bare simmer, lid ajar, 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours, topping up with hot water.
Prepare garnishes; hard-boil the eggs.
Drain most of the liquid; mash partly and dress while hot.
Into a shallow bowl, flood with olive oil, serve with garnishes and bread.

steps.do: Tip the dried beans onto a tray and pick through them, discarding any small stones, shrivelled beans or bits of husk. Rinse, then soak in a large bowl with three times their volume of cold water for 12 hours, or overnight.
steps.look: In the morning the beans have doubled in size, their skins smooth and taut, and a bean cut in half is evenly pale throughout.
steps.mistake: Not picking over the beans; small stones are common in dried pulses.
steps.fix: Spread them in a single layer on a pale tray where stones are easy to see.

steps.do: Drain and rinse the soaked beans. Put them in the pot with fresh water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm), with no salt or acid. Bring to the boil over high heat, skim off any foam, then turn down to a bare simmer with the lid ajar.
steps.look: Lazy bubbles breaking the surface now and then; the beans moving only slightly.
steps.mistake: A hard rolling boil, which splits the skins and leaves the outsides mushy while the centres stay hard.
steps.fix: Keep it gentle; patience is the only route to a creamy bean.

steps.do: Simmer for 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours, checking every 20 minutes and adding hot water to keep the beans covered. Start testing after 1 1/2 hours by pressing a bean between your finger and thumb.
steps.look: Done when a bean collapses into a smooth paste with no chalky centre when pressed, and the skin slips easily.
steps.mistake: Adding salt, tomato or lemon to the pot early, which can keep the skins tough so the beans never soften.
steps.fix: Season only once they are tender. If the beans are very slow, older beans can take 3 hours or more, so keep going.

steps.do: While the beans cook, hard-boil the eggs: lower them into boiling water, simmer 10 minutes, then cool in cold water and peel. Prepare the tomato, onion, parsley and chilli and set them in small bowls.
steps.look: Eggs with fully set, pale yellow yolks and no grey ring; neat little bowls of colourful garnishes.
steps.mistake: Boiling eggs too long, which gives a green ring around the yolk and a sulphur smell.
steps.fix: Ten minutes, then straight into cold water.

steps.do: When the beans are tender, drain them, keeping 1 cup (240 ml) of the cooking liquid. Return the beans to the pot with about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the liquid.
steps.look: Hot beans, some starting to split, in a little cloudy liquid.
steps.mistake: Throwing away all the cooking liquid, which holds starch that makes the ful creamy.
steps.fix: Always reserve a cupful before draining.

steps.do: Mash about half the beans with the masher or fork against the side of the pot, leaving the rest whole. Add more reserved liquid a little at a time until it is loose and creamy.
steps.look: A rough mix of creamy mash and whole beans, loose enough to spread on a plate but not soupy.
steps.mistake: Mashing everything into a smooth purée, which loses the texture that defines ful.
steps.fix: Stop at rubble; if you have gone too far, stir in a handful of whole beans held back.

steps.do: While the beans are hot, beat in the garlic paste, lemon juice, cumin, remaining 3/4 tsp (4.5 g) salt and half the olive oil. Taste and push it: it should be clearly lemony, garlicky and well salted.
steps.look: Glossy, fragrant beans that taste bright and bold, with the oil absorbed.
steps.mistake: Timid seasoning, which makes ful taste like plain porridge.
steps.fix: Add lemon and salt in small amounts and taste after each; hot beans soak up seasoning, so they need more than you think.

steps.do: Spoon into a shallow bowl, make a hollow in the centre with the back of a spoon and flood it with the remaining olive oil. Scatter with tomato, onion, parsley and chilli, add halved eggs and a drizzle of tahini, and serve with warm bread to scoop.
steps.look: A golden pool of oil on brown beans, crowned with red, white and green.
steps.mistake: Serving it lukewarm, when the oil sits heavily.
steps.fix: Serve hot; reheat gently with a splash of the reserved liquid if needed.

science: Dried beans are seeds sealed to keep water out. Soaking lets water enter slowly through the seed's small opening and its skin, so the bean swells evenly and later cooks in far less time. During simmering, heat dissolves pectin, the glue between the cells, and swells the starch inside, so the bean turns creamy. Acid and very hard water slow this, because they keep pectin bound with calcium and magnesium, which is why lemon and tomato go in only once the beans are soft. A gentle simmer matters because a hard boil tumbles the beans, splitting skins before the centres are cooked. Hot, freshly mashed beans absorb dressing readily because their broken starch soaks up oil and acid, so seasoning while warm flavours them all the way through.
plating: Use a wide, shallow bowl. Swirl the ful into an even layer with a hollow in the centre, pour olive oil into the hollow and let it run, then arrange the garnishes in neat sections around the rim: tomato, onion, parsley, chilli, eggs cut in half lengthways. Dust cumin over the centre and stack warm bread on the side.

pairing.drink: Sweet mint tea in the Egyptian way, or a glass of chilled, dry Assyrtiko from Santorini, whose salty lemon edge mirrors the dressing.

variations: Quick ful: use two 15 oz (425 g) cans of fava beans with their liquid, warmed for 10 minutes and mashed as above.
Ful with tahini: stir 3 tbsp (45 g) of tahini into the mash and finish with chilli oil.
Ful iskandarani: fold in sautéed tomato, peppers and onion, the Alexandria style.
safety: Keep cooked beans hot until serving or cool them within 2 hours and refrigerate.
Simmering pots hold steam; lift the lid away from you.
Hard-boiled eggs that are peeled should be eaten within 2 days and kept refrigerated.

title: Ndambé (Senegalese Bean Sandwich)
summary: A Senegalese street breakfast of black-eyed beans simmered into a thick, peppery tomato sauce built on onion softened in red palm oil, spooned hot into split baguette. It builds on the bean simmer of ful with a sweated onion base and a tomato paste fried until it darkens.
skills: cooking black-eyed beans in a tomato base
equipment: wide heavy saucepan or sauté pan, 10 inch (25 cm)

ingredients.note: Soaked overnight.
Or groundnut oil with 1 tsp (2 g) sweet paprika for colour.
Ndambé is peppery.
Optional, from West African grocers; adds deep savoury flavour.
Optional, traditional; reduce the salt if using.
Pierce once with a knife for more heat.
Adjust after tasting.
Each cut in half to make four sandwiches.

Drain and rinse in the morning.
Finely chop the onions and crush the garlic.
Measure tomato paste, pepper, netetou and stock cube into one small dish.
Cut the lime into wedges.
Warm the baguettes in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 minutes just before serving.

Simmer the beans with bay in unsalted water until tender, 40 to 60 minutes.
Soften the onion and garlic in palm oil; fry the tomato paste.
Fold in the beans and some cooking liquid with the chilli; simmer and partly mash.
Season, add lime; warm the bread.
Split the bread and fill with hot beans.

steps.do: Put the drained beans in the pot with the bay and enough fresh water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring to the boil, skim the foam, then simmer gently without salt for 40 to 60 minutes until a bean crushes easily between finger and thumb but still holds its shape. Drain, keeping 2 cups (480 ml) of the cooking liquid.
steps.look: Plump, creamy-white beans with their black eyes intact, soft right through, skins mostly whole.
steps.mistake: Salting or adding tomato to the beans' cooking water, which keeps the skins squeaky and tough.
steps.fix: Cook beans in plain water; all the seasoning goes into the sauce.

steps.do: Warm the palm oil in the wide saucepan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, only until it melts and turns clear and bright orange. Do not let it smoke.
steps.look: Clear, glowing orange oil with a fruity smell.
steps.mistake: Heating palm oil to smoking, which bleaches its colour and gives an acrid taste.
steps.fix: If it smokes, take it off the heat and let it cool before adding the onion; next time stay at medium.

steps.do: Add the onions and a pinch of salt. Cook over medium low heat, stirring often, for 10 to 12 minutes, until they are soft, slumped and sweet but not browned. Add the garlic for the last 2 minutes.
steps.look: Onions translucent, collapsed and glossy with orange oil, smelling sweet rather than sharp.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions at high heat, which makes a bitter edge in a sauce that should be sweet and peppery.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of bean liquid if they begin to catch.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato paste, pepper, netetou and stock cube. Fry, stirring constantly, for 3 to 4 minutes, until the paste darkens to brick red and oil begins to separate around the edges.
steps.look: The paste turns from bright red to a deep rusty brown, smells sweet and roasted, and the oil pools at the edges of the pan.
steps.mistake: Adding liquid before the paste has fried, which leaves a raw, tinny tomato taste.
steps.fix: Keep stirring until the colour deepens and the oil splits out.

steps.do: Fold in the beans with 1 cup (240 ml) of their cooking liquid and drop in the whole Scotch bonnet. Simmer gently for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
steps.look: A thick, rich red sauce coating every bean, bubbling slowly.
steps.mistake: Breaking the Scotch bonnet open, which can make the dish far too hot.
steps.fix: Keep the chilli whole and lift it out when the heat is right; taste from 10 minutes.

steps.do: Mash about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pan with the back of the spoon and stir them through. Add more cooking liquid if needed: the sauce should cling to the beans thickly, with no free liquid.
steps.look: Thick enough to sit in bread without soaking straight through, creamy from the mashed beans.
steps.mistake: A runny stew that turns the baguette to mush.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered for a few more minutes, or mash a few more beans to thicken it.

steps.do: Remove the chilli and bay leaves. Taste, add salt as needed, and squeeze in the juice of half the lime. The flavour should be peppery, savoury and bright.
steps.look: Bold, well seasoned beans with a clear peppery warmth and a lift from the lime.
steps.mistake: Under-salting, which leaves the beans tasting flat inside bland bread.
steps.fix: Season firmly; beans carried in bread need more salt than beans eaten from a bowl.

steps.do: Split the warm baguette pieces lengthways, leaving a hinge, and spoon in the hot beans generously. Serve with the remaining lime wedges.
steps.look: A crisp baguette packed with glossy, red-orange beans.
steps.mistake: Filling cold bread, which tastes stale.
steps.fix: Warm the bread for 5 minutes first so the crust crackles.

science: Black-eyed beans soften as heat dissolves the pectin that cements their cells, but acid, as in tomato or lime, and lots of salt early on can keep that pectin firm, so the beans are cooked in plain water and seasoned only once they crush easily. Frying tomato paste in oil until it darkens drives off water and caramelises its sugars, developing deep roasted flavours and removing the raw edge. Red palm oil is coloured by carotenoids, which break down at high heat, so it is warmed gently to keep its colour and fruity flavour. There is no flour in this sauce: mashing some of the cooked beans releases their starch into the liquid, which thickens it so the filling clings rather than soaking straight into the bread.
plating: Serve each half-baguette on a sheet of paper or a board, split side up and generously filled so the beans show along its length. Add a lime wedge at one end and, if you like, a few slices of raw onion and a pinch of black pepper over the top.

pairing.drink: Chilled bissap, the Senegalese hibiscus drink, or as a cocktail a hibiscus gin cooler: tart, floral and red to cut the earthy beans.

variations: Add a handful of sweet potato, diced small, to the sauce with the beans for a sweeter filling.

Use canned black-eyed beans for speed: two 15 oz (425 g) cans, drained, with 1 cup (240 ml) water.
safety: Scotch bonnet chillies are very hot; wash hands and the knife after piercing, and keep it away from eyes.
Hot palm oil and tomato paste spit; stir with a long spoon.
Cool leftover beans quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

title: Mangú with Pickled Red Onions
summary: Green plantains boiled until soft and mashed hot with butter and some of their cold cooking water until smooth, crowned with red onions softened in oil and vinegar. equipment: potato masher or a sturdy fork

ingredients.item: green plantains, skins hard, green and matte
ingredients.note: No yellow; green plantains are starchy, not sweet.
Some cooks add a little more for richness.

ingredients.item: red onion, sliced into thin rings

ingredients.note: To chill the reserved cooking water.

mise: Slice the onion into thin rings, about 1/8 inch (3 mm).
Fill the large pot with the water and 2 tsp (12 g) salt and bring to the boil.
Cube the butter and keep it cold.
Set a jug with the ice cubes beside the stove.
Warm the plates.

timeline.do: Water on to boil; peel and cut the plantains.
Plantains into the boiling water for 20 to 25 minutes.
Cook the onions in oil, then vinegar; set aside.
Reserve and chill cooking water; drain and mash the plantains with butter.
Spread on warm plates and crown with the onions.

steps.do: Cut off both ends of each plantain. With the paring knife, score the skin along each of its ridges from end to end, cutting only through the peel. Slide your thumb under the edge and peel each strip away. Cut the plantains into 2 inch (5 cm) lengths and drop them straight into the boiling salted water.
steps.look: Pale, cream coloured flesh with no green peel left on it.
steps.mistake: Trying to peel green plantain like a banana, which does not work and tears the flesh.
steps.fix: Score along the ridges and lever the peel off in strips; green plantain sap stains, so wear gloves or oil your hands.

steps.do: Boil the plantain pieces hard for 20 to 25 minutes, until a knife slides into the centre with no resistance and a piece breaks apart under light pressure from a spoon.
steps.look: Flesh turned from creamy white to slightly yellow and translucent, soft right through.
steps.mistake: Draining while the centres are still firm, which gives a lumpy mash that no amount of beating fixes.
steps.fix: Test the thickest piece; give it 5 minutes more if in doubt.

steps.do: While the plantains boil, heat the oil in the frying pan over low heat, add the onion rings and cook gently for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until they slump and turn translucent. Add the vinegar and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, stir, and cook 1 minute more. Take off the heat the moment the sharp vinegar smell in the steam softens.
steps.look: Soft, glossy, bright magenta-pink onions in a little vinegar dressing.
steps.mistake: Frying the onions until brown, which loses their pink colour and sharpness.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; they should soften, not colour.

steps.do: Before draining, scoop out 1 cup (240 ml) of the hot plantain cooking water into the jug of ice and stir until the ice has mostly melted, so the water is cold.
steps.look: A jug of cold, cloudy water.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to reserve any water, leaving nothing to loosen the mash.
steps.fix: Plain ice water works if you forget, though the cooking water adds a little starch and salt.

steps.do: Drain the plantains and tip them into the heatproof bowl at once. Add the cold butter and mash immediately and firmly while they are hot, adding the cold water a splash at a time, about 1/2 cup (120 ml) in total.
steps.look: The plantain breaks down into a smooth, heavy paste that turns paler and softer as the water goes in.
steps.mistake: Letting the plantains cool before mashing; their starch sets and they will not go smooth.
steps.fix: Mash straight away; if they have cooled, warm them in the pot for a minute first.

steps.do: Switch to the wooden spoon and beat the mash hard for 1 minute until there are no lumps or fibres and it holds a soft furrow when you drag the spoon through. Taste and add salt.
steps.look: Smooth, glossy, soft but thick, like soft mashed potato; it will firm slightly on the plate.
steps.mistake: Using a blender or food processor, which breaks the starch and turns it gluey.
steps.fix: Mash and beat by hand only; if it looks too stiff, beat in a little more cold water.

steps.do: Spread the mangú onto warm plates and top with the onions and a spoonful of their vinegar. Serve at once.
steps.look: Pale gold mash crowned with a tangle of pink onions glistening with vinegar.
steps.mistake: Holding the mash too long, so it sets into a firm block.
steps.fix: Serve immediately; reheat leftovers with a splash of water, beating well.

science: Green plantains are mostly starch with very little sugar. Boiling gelatinises the starch: granules absorb water, swell and soften, which is why the flesh turns translucent. Gelatinised starch begins to firm again as it cools, as molecules realign, so a mash that looks perfect on the stove can set stiff on the plate. Mashing hot breaks the swollen cells while they are soft, and adding cold water both loosens the paste and brings it down towards eating temperature, so what you see in the bowl is close to what reaches the table. Beating by hand keeps the starch granules mostly intact; a blender ruptures them, releasing loose starch that turns the mash sticky and gluey. Vinegar softens the onions' harshness while keeping their colour bright.
plating: Spoon the mangú onto the centre of a warm plate and use the back of the spoon to sweep it into a smooth round with a slight hollow on top. Pile the pickled onions high in the hollow, letting a little of the vinegar run down the sides.

pairing.drink: A rum Mojito with fresh mint and lime, or a crisp, light Caribbean lager: sharp and refreshing beside a rich, starchy plate.

variations: Los tres golpes: serve with fried Dominican salami, fried cheese and fried eggs, the classic breakfast plate.
Stir 2 tbsp (30 ml) of olive oil and a crushed garlic clove into the mash instead of butter.
Mofongo style: mash with crisp fried pork rind and garlic for a firmer, savoury mound.
safety: Green plantain peel is slippery and hard; cut on a stable board with the knife angled away from your hand.
Drain boiling water away from you, tilting the pot slowly.
Keep leftovers refrigerated and reheat until hot throughout.

title: Changua (Colombian Milk and Egg Soup)
summary: A breakfast soup from the Colombian highlands: eggs poached in a light broth of milk, water and spring onion, served over torn bread and fresh cheese with coriander. Poaching in milk rather than water shows how a gentler, more delicate liquid needs gentler heat.
equipment: wide saucepan or deep frying pan, about 10 inch (25 cm)

ingredients.note: Keeps the broth light and stops it boiling over.

ingredients.item: spring onions, thinly sliced, whites and greens kept apart

ingredients.note: Very fresh.

ingredients.item: fresh coriander, chopped leaves and fine stems
stale white bread or bread rolls, torn
ingredients.note: Colombian calado toasts are traditional.

ingredients.item: fresh white cheese (queso campesino, cuajada) or fresh mozzarella, crumbled

mise: Slice the spring onions, keeping the white and green parts in separate piles.
Chop the coriander.
Tear the bread into bite sized pieces and divide it between the bowls with the cheese.
Crack each egg into its own ramekin.
Warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Slice, chop, tear; bread and cheese into bowls.
Milk, water and spring onion whites heating to a shiver.
Poach the eggs in the milk for about 3 minutes.
Eggs into the bowls; season the broth off the heat.
Pour the broth over, scatter coriander and greens, serve.

steps.do: Put the milk, water and the white part of the spring onions in the wide saucepan over medium low heat. Heat slowly, stirring once or twice to stop a skin forming on the base, for 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: Steam rising, the surface beginning to shiver, a ring of tiny bubbles clinging to the edge of the pan. On a thermometer, about 180°F to 185°F (82°C to 85°C).
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry it, which makes the milk froth up and boil over in seconds.
steps.fix: Stay at medium low and never leave the pan; if it starts to rise, lift it off the heat immediately.

steps.do: Hold the broth at that shiver: small bubbles at the edge, no rolling boil. Adjust the heat up or down a little as needed.
steps.look: A calm surface that trembles and steams, with no large bubbles.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which scorches milk on the base and hardens the eggs.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; if the base has scorched, pour the broth into a clean pan without scraping.

steps.do: Lower each ramekin to the surface and slide the eggs in one at a time, spaced apart around the pan. Leave them completely untouched for about 3 minutes.
steps.look: The whites turn opaque and white against the milk, the yolks visible as golden domes beneath a thin veil.
steps.mistake: Stirring or prodding the eggs, which breaks the whites into the soup.
steps.fix: Leave them alone; nudge one gently with the slotted spoon only after 2 minutes to free it if stuck.

steps.do: Test an egg: lift it on the slotted spoon and press the yolk lightly with the back of a spoon. It should feel soft and wobble under a set white.
steps.look: Fully opaque white with no translucent jelly; yolk soft and moving.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the eggs to hard yolks because the milk was too hot.
steps.fix: Cook the next batch 30 seconds less, or at a slightly lower heat.

steps.do: Lift each egg out with the slotted spoon, let the broth drain off for a second, and set two eggs into each bowl on top of the bread and cheese.
steps.look: Two neat eggs resting on bread and white cheese.
steps.mistake: Cooking the bread in the pot, where it dissolves into paste.
steps.fix: Bread always goes in the bowl, never in the pan.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the salt, the coriander and the green spring onion. Taste: it should be gently salty and fresh with herbs.
steps.look: A pale broth flecked with bright green coriander and onion.
steps.mistake: Salting the milk while it heats, which can encourage curdling and makes the broth hard to judge.
steps.fix: Season off the heat at the end and taste.

steps.do: Ladle the hot broth over the eggs and bread, letting it soak the bread so it softens but keeps its edges. Add pepper and serve straight away.
steps.look: Bread swelling in the broth, cheese softening, eggs half submerged.
steps.mistake: Waiting before serving, so the bread turns to mush and the eggs overcook in the hot broth.
steps.fix: Serve the moment the broth goes in.

science: Milk is water carrying fat droplets, the protein casein and whey proteins, and lactose. Heated, the whey proteins at the surface set into a skin, which traps steam beneath it until it lifts and the milk foams over. Adding water dilutes the proteins and adds volume, so the broth is less likely to boil over and stays light enough to drink. Milk sugars and proteins scorch on a hot pan base at much lower heat than water would, so the broth is held at a shiver, around 180°F to 185°F (82°C to 85°C). plating: Use deep, warm soup bowls. Place the torn bread and cheese in the bottom, set two eggs side by side on top, and pour the broth around them so the yolks stay visible above the surface. Finish with a scattering of coriander and green onion and a turn of black pepper.

pairing.drink: Colombian hot chocolate made with water or milk is traditional; as a warming drink, a cup of strong Colombian black coffee.
pairing.brennans: Brandy Milk Punch: milk at breakfast in Brennan's style, a gentle partner for a milky egg soup.

variations: Add a few thin slices of cooked potato to the broth for a heartier bowl.
Use mild chicken stock in place of the water for more savoury depth.
Top with a few crisp croutons instead of soft bread for contrast.
safety: Milk boils over very quickly; stay at the stove and keep the heat moderate.
Soft poached yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests or poach 5 minutes.
Hot milk spills cause deep scalds; keep pan handles turned in and children away.

title: Buttermilk Pancakes

steps.mistake: Adding hot butter, which can partly cook the eggs.
steps.fix: Let the butter cool until just warm to the touch before adding it.

steps.look: A thick batter with many small lumps and no pockets of dry flour.
steps.mistake: Whisking until smooth, which develops gluten and makes rubbery, flat pancakes.
steps.fix: Stop early; small lumps hydrate during the rest. If you overmix, rest the batter 20 minutes to let the gluten relax.

steps.do: Leave the batter to rest for 5 to 10 minutes, without stirring.
steps.look: It thickens and puffs slightly, with small bubbles on the surface.
steps.mistake: Stirring after the rest, knocking out the bubbles that will lift the pancakes.
steps.fix: Ladle from the bowl gently without stirring.

steps.do: Heat the griddle over medium heat for 5 minutes, about 350°F to 375°F (175°C to 190°C). Test it by flicking on a few drops of water: they should skitter and dance before evaporating. Brush lightly with butter and wipe most of it off with paper towel.
steps.look: Water droplets bead and dance across the surface; the butter sizzles gently but does not brown instantly.
steps.mistake: A griddle too hot, which burns the outside while the inside stays raw; or too cool, which gives pale, dense pancakes.
steps.fix: Cook one small test pancake first and adjust: if it browns in under 1 minute, lower the heat; if it is pale after 3, raise it.

steps.do: Pour 1/4 cup (60 ml) of batter per pancake onto the griddle from just above the surface, leaving 2 inches (5 cm) between them. Do not spread it. Cook untouched for about 2 minutes.
steps.look: Rounds about 4 inches (10 cm) across; bubbles rise across the surface, pop and stay open, and the edges look dry and matte.
steps.mistake: Flipping when bubbles first appear but still close up, so the raw batter splatters.
steps.fix: Wait until the bubbles in the centre pop and leave holes that do not fill in, and the edges look set.

steps.do: Slide the turner fully under each pancake and flip it with one confident turn of the wrist, laying it down close to the griddle. Cook the second side for about 1 minute, until risen and golden.
steps.look: An even golden brown first side; the pancake rises noticeably after flipping, and the side feels springy when pressed lightly with a finger.
steps.mistake: Pressing the pancake down with the turner, which squeezes out the gas and makes it flat and dense.
steps.fix: Never press. If it looks raw in the centre, lower the heat and give it 30 seconds longer.

steps.do: Move finished pancakes in a single layer to the rack in the warm oven while you cook the rest, wiping and re-buttering the griddle lightly between batches.
steps.look: Pancakes stay warm and keep their texture, without sweating.
steps.mistake: Stacking them on a plate, where steam makes the lower ones soggy.
steps.fix: Keep them on the rack in a single layer until serving.

steps.do: Stack three pancakes per plate with a little butter between each, top with a pat of butter and pour over warm maple syrup at the table.
steps.look: A tall, even stack, golden on the outside, fluffy and moist inside when cut.
steps.mistake: Cold syrup that chills the pancakes.
steps.fix: Warm the syrup; a few seconds in the microwave or a pan of hot water is enough.

science: These pancakes rise by two chemical leaveners. Baking soda is an alkali that reacts immediately with the lactic acid in buttermilk, releasing carbon dioxide and giving a gentle tang. Baking powder holds its own acid and releases more gas when wet and again when heated, so the pancakes keep rising on the griddle. The gas inflates bubbles already in the batter, so the bubbles that pop and stay open on the surface tell you the top has set enough to flip. Mixing as little as possible matters because wheat proteins form gluten when stirred in water, and gluten makes a pancake chewy. Resting lets the flour absorb liquid and the lumps dissolve on their own. A steady griddle around 375°F (190°C) browns the outside through the Maillard reaction while the centre cooks through.
plating: Stack three pancakes neatly in the centre of a warm plate, each slightly offset so the edges show. Set a square of cold butter on top, pour warm maple syrup over so it runs down the sides, and add a few berries beside the stack.

pairing.drink: A Mimosa of fresh orange juice and dry sparkling wine: the acidity lifts butter and maple and the bubbles keep the plate light.
pairing.brennans: Framboise French Toast: Brennan's sweet griddled breakfast, a fine comparison for explaining a batter against a soaked bread.

variations: Blueberry pancakes: drop 6 to 8 blueberries onto each pancake right after pouring, before the flip.
Banana pancakes: lay thin banana slices on the poured batter and dust with cinnamon.
Cornmeal pancakes: replace 1/2 cup (60 g) of the flour with fine cornmeal for a crisp, Southern style edge.
safety: Hot griddles and pans stay hot long after cooking; keep handles turned in and cool them before washing.
The pancakes are cooked through when springy and no wet batter shows when one is cut, which takes the egg well past 160°F (71°C).

title: Swedish Pancakes with Lingonberries
summary: Thin, buttery Swedish pancakes made from an unleavened batter of eggs, milk and flour, swirled across a hot pan and served rolled with lingonberry compote and whipped cream. Thin batter teaches pan coating and the difference eggs make when there is no baking soda to lift anything.
equipment: 9 inch (23 cm) nonstick or crêpe pan
thin, flexible spatula or palette knife
1/3 cup (80 ml) measure or small ladle
plate and clean tea towel for keeping pancakes warm

ingredients.item: unsalted butter, melted, plus more for the pan

ingredients.note: Cranberries work, with a little more sugar.

mise: Melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter for the batter and let it cool.
Measure flour, milk, eggs, sugar and salt.
Put a little extra butter in a small dish with a pastry brush or paper towel.
Measure the lingonberries, sugar and water for the compote.
Chill the bowl for the cream.
Set a plate and a folded tea towel by the stove.

timeline.do: Make the batter and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature.
Make the compote and let it cool.
Whip the cream to soft peaks; refrigerate.
Heat the pan; cook the pancakes one by one, about 90 seconds each.
Fill or fold the pancakes with compote and serve with cream.

steps.do: Whisk the flour, sugar and salt in the bowl. Pour in half the milk and whisk to a thick, completely smooth paste. Whisk in the eggs one at a time, then the rest of the milk gradually, then the cooled melted butter.
steps.look: A smooth, thin batter like single cream, with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Pouring all the milk in at once, which makes lumps that are hard to whisk out.
steps.fix: Make the thick paste first; if lumps remain, pour the batter through a sieve.

steps.do: Transfer to the jug, cover and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
steps.look: Any foam settles; the batter becomes slightly thicker and silkier.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, which gives tougher pancakes that tear.
steps.fix: Rest at least 20 minutes; overnight in the fridge is fine, whisked before use.

steps.do: For the compote, put the lingonberries, sugar and water in the small pan over medium heat. Bring to a simmer and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until some berries burst and the juice turns syrupy. Cool; it thickens as it cools.
steps.look: Glossy red berries, some whole, some broken, in a thick, bright syrup; a sharp, sweet taste.
steps.mistake: Cooking too long until it is a jam, which loses the fresh tartness.
steps.fix: Stop at 5 minutes; for a raw version, simply stir the berries with sugar and leave 30 minutes.

steps.do: Whip the cold cream in the chilled bowl to soft peaks, when the cream holds a shape that flops over at the tip. Refrigerate.
steps.look: Soft, billowy cream that just holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping into grainy butter.
steps.fix: Stop at soft peaks; if it goes grainy, fold in a spoonful of liquid cream.

steps.do: Heat the pan over medium high heat for 2 minutes. Brush it lightly with butter. Hold the pan off the heat, pour in about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of batter, and at once tilt and swirl the pan in a circle so the batter coats the base thinly and evenly.
steps.look: A thin, even layer covering the whole base, with a lacy edge that sizzles as it meets the pan.
steps.mistake: Pouring the batter and leaving it, so it sits in a thick puddle in the centre.
steps.fix: Pour and swirl in one movement; fill any holes with a drop of batter.

steps.do: Return the pan to the heat and cook for about 1 minute, until the surface looks dry and the edges turn golden and lift away from the pan.
steps.look: Matte surface, light golden lacy edges curling slightly.
steps.mistake: Trying to flip too early, so the pancake tears.
steps.fix: Wait until the edges lift on their own and you can slide a spatula under easily.

steps.do: Loosen the edge with the spatula, slide it under the centre and flip, or lift the edge with your fingertips and turn it quickly. Cook the second side 20 to 30 seconds. Slide onto the plate and cover with the tea towel. Repeat, buttering the pan lightly every two pancakes.
steps.look: A pale gold pancake with darker golden spots, thin and flexible.
steps.mistake: Too much butter in the pan, which fries the batter into greasy, crisp holes.
steps.fix: Brush on a thin film and wipe off any excess.

steps.do: To serve, spread a spoonful of compote over each pancake and roll it up or fold it into quarters. Serve two or three per person with whipped cream and more compote.
steps.look: Neat, thin rolls with a ribbon of red visible at each end, with a spoon of white cream beside them.
steps.mistake: The first pancake coming out uneven and blotchy.
steps.fix: That is normal: the first pancake seasons the pan. Eat it yourself and carry on.

science: With no baking soda or powder, this batter relies on eggs for structure. When the batter hits a hot pan, egg proteins set and starch from the flour gelatinises within seconds, turning a thin liquid film into a flexible sheet. Milk adds lactose and proteins that brown, giving the golden spots. Resting the batter lets the flour absorb liquid fully and lets air bubbles escape, so the pancake is smooth and tender rather than holey and tough. Swirling the pan spreads the batter thinly before it sets, which is why the pan is held off the heat at that moment. Lingonberries are high in acid and natural pectin, so a short simmer with sugar thickens them into a sharp compote that cuts the butter and cream.
plating: Roll three pancakes into neat cigars and lay them side by side at a slight angle on a plate. Spoon a line of compote across the middle, add a spoonful of whipped cream shaped with two spoons at one side, and finish with a few whole berries and a light dusting of icing sugar.

pairing.drink: A lingonberry spritz of lingonberry cordial, dry sparkling wine and soda: tart, fruity and light beside butter and cream.
pairing.brennans: Riviera: Lillet Blanc, sparkling wine and lemon, a light and fruity aperitif to drink with thin pancakes and tart berries.

variations: Fill with sliced strawberries and cream in early summer.
Make them savoury: fill with chopped ham and grated cheese and fold into quarters.
Bake the same batter in a hot buttered dish at 425°F (220°C) for 20 minutes for Swedish oven pancake (ugnspannkaka).
safety: Keep the hot pan handle turned in while swirling; your wrist will be close to the flame or element.
Pancakes are cooked through once set on both sides, well past 160°F (71°C) for the egg.

title: Syrniki
summary: Golden fritters made from drained farmer cheese bound with egg, a little sugar and as little flour as possible, fried in butter and served with sour cream and jam. They train the feel of a soft dough and the steady medium heat that browns without burning while the centre cooks.
equipment: sieve lined with muslin or a clean thin tea towel
fine sieve or potato ricer for smoothing the cheese
12 inch (30 cm) heavy nonstick or cast iron frying pan
baking tray and oven for finishing

ingredients.item: farmer cheese (tvorog) or dry cottage cheese
ingredients.note: If using wet cottage cheese or quark, drain it first (step 1).

ingredients.item: plain flour, plus more for dusting

ingredients.note: Stops the butter burning.
To serve.

ingredients.item: jam, such as sour cherry or apricot
ingredients.note: To serve.

mise: Drain the cheese in a lined sieve for 1 hour, or squeeze it in the cloth.
Push the cheese through a fine sieve or ricer for a smooth texture.
Spread flour on a plate for dusting.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Measure butter and oil.
Set out sour cream and jam in bowls.

timeline.do: Drain the cheese.
Smooth the cheese; mix in egg, sugar, vanilla, salt, flour.
Shape 8 to 10 thick patties and dust with flour.
Fry in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes a side.
Finish in the oven for 5 minutes if thick.
Serve warm with sour cream and jam.

steps.do: Line the sieve with muslin, add the cheese, set over a bowl and leave it to drain for 1 hour, or gather the cloth and squeeze firmly to remove excess liquid.
steps.look: The cheese feels dry and crumbly, like damp sand, and holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Using wet cheese, which needs so much flour to bind that the syrniki turn heavy and bready.
steps.fix: Drain the cheese, not the recipe: squeeze until barely any whey drips out.

steps.do: Press the drained cheese through a fine sieve or ricer into the bowl with the back of a spoon. This removes lumps and gives a smooth, light fritter.
steps.look: A fine, fluffy, even cheese with no large curds.
steps.mistake: Leaving large curds, which make syrniki crumble in the pan.
steps.fix: Sieve it, or mash it thoroughly with a fork for 2 minutes.

steps.do: Add the egg, sugar, vanilla and salt and mix well with a fork. Add 3 tbsp (25 g) flour and mix just until it forms a soft, slightly sticky dough.
steps.look: A soft dough that holds together in a ball when squeezed and only slightly sticks to your fingers.
steps.mistake: Adding lots of flour to make it easy to handle, which makes them dense and floury.
steps.fix: Use floured hands rather than more flour in the dough; add 1 tbsp (8 g) more only if it cannot hold a shape at all.

steps.do: With floured hands, take about 1/4 cup (60 g) of dough, roll it into a ball, then flatten into a thick patty about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) across and 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick. Roll the edge on the floured plate so the sides are straight, and dust both faces lightly.
steps.look: Even, neat pucks with smooth sides and a light coat of flour.
steps.mistake: Patties of different sizes, which cook unevenly.
steps.fix: Weigh or measure each portion; level the sides by rolling the edge like a coin on the floured plate.

steps.do: Heat the butter and oil in the pan over medium low heat until the butter foams. Add half the patties, leaving space between them, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is deep golden.
steps.look: A gentle, steady sizzle; when lifted, an even golden brown crust.
steps.mistake: Medium high heat, which burns the outside while the inside stays raw and pasty.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; syrniki want a patient, moderate fry.

steps.do: Turn them carefully with the spatula and fry the second side 3 to 4 minutes. Transfer to the baking tray and fry the second batch, adding more butter if the pan is dry.
steps.look: Both sides golden, the syrniki slightly puffed, the sides set.
steps.mistake: Turning too often, which breaks them before a crust forms.
steps.fix: Turn once only, when the first side is properly browned.

steps.do: If they are thick or feel soft in the middle, bake on the tray at 350°F (175°C) for 5 minutes to cook the centre through, to about 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: Puffed and springy when pressed in the centre.
steps.mistake: Serving with a raw, gluey middle.
steps.fix: Bake a few minutes more; check one by cutting it open.

steps.do: Serve warm with a spoonful of sour cream and jam.
steps.look: Golden outside, soft, creamy and slightly tangy inside like a light cheesecake.
steps.mistake: Letting them sit long, when they lose their crisp crust.
steps.fix: Serve within a few minutes; reheat in a dry pan if needed.

science: Farmer cheese is milk protein, casein, curdled and drained. Its moisture decides everything: water in the cheese turns to steam in the pan and must be held by a binder, so wet cheese needs more flour, and more flour makes the fritters dense. Draining removes whey, letting the egg do most of the binding: as it heats, egg proteins set around the cheese curds and hold them together. A small amount of flour absorbs remaining moisture and forms a light coating that browns. Moderate heat is essential because the dusting of flour and the sugar in the mix brown quickly through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, while the thick centre needs several minutes to heat through. A mix of butter and oil gives butter's flavour while the oil raises the temperature at which it burns.
plating: Arrange three syrniki slightly overlapping on a warm plate. Add a generous spoonful of sour cream beside them, swirled with the back of the spoon, and a smaller spoonful of jam on top of the cream so the colours marble. Dust lightly with icing sugar and add a few fresh berries.

pairing.drink: Black tea with lemon is traditional; for a brunch cocktail, a Kir Royale of crème de cassis and dry sparkling wine echoes the berry jam.

variations: Add 1/4 cup (35 g) of raisins soaked in hot water, drained, to the dough.
Replace the flour with fine semolina for a slightly crisper crust.
Savoury syrniki: leave out the sugar and vanilla and add chopped dill and spring onion.
safety: The centre should reach 160°F (71°C) because the dough contains raw egg; finish thick ones in the oven.
Butter spits when wet patties go in; lay them away from you.
Keep fresh cheese refrigerated until use.

title: Irish Soda Farls
summary: Ulster soda bread dough of flour, bicarbonate of soda, salt and buttermilk, patted into a round, cut into quarters and baked on a dry griddle until risen and golden. The quickest bread there is teaches that a soda dough wants as little handling as possible and no waiting.
skills: mixing only until it comes together
equipment: flat griddle or 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm) heavy cast iron pan

ingredients.item: plain flour, plus more for dusting

ingredients.note: Check it is fresh; old soda gives a flat, soapy farl.
You may not need it all.

mise: Put the griddle over medium low heat to warm for 5 to 10 minutes.
Weigh the flour, soda and salt.
Measure the buttermilk.
Flour the work surface lightly.
Set out the rack and tea towel.

timeline.do: Heat the griddle low; weigh and measure.
Mix the dough in under a minute and shape it.
Farls onto the dry, floured griddle; bake 6 to 8 minutes a side.
Stand the farls on their edges for 1 to 2 minutes to cook the sides.
Split, butter and serve warm.

steps.do: Heat the dry griddle or pan over medium low heat for 5 to 10 minutes. Test it by sprinkling a little flour on the surface: it should turn light beige in about 3 minutes, not brown in seconds.
steps.look: Flour browning gently and slowly; the pan evenly warm across its surface.
steps.mistake: A hot pan that burns the outside before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: If the flour darkens within a minute, take the pan off the heat for 2 minutes and lower the setting.

steps.do: Whisk the flour, bicarbonate of soda and salt together in the bowl for 30 seconds so the soda is spread perfectly evenly. Lumps of soda leave yellow, bitter spots.
steps.look: An even white mix with no specks or lumps.
steps.mistake: Not whisking, so pockets of soda make some bites soapy.
steps.fix: Sieve the soda into the flour if it is lumpy.

steps.do: Make a well in the centre and pour in most of the buttermilk. With one hand shaped like a claw, stir from the centre outwards in wide circles, bringing in the flour, for about 30 seconds, adding the rest of the buttermilk only if dry patches remain.
steps.look: A soft, shaggy, slightly sticky dough that comes together with no dry flour left in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Kneading the dough like yeast bread, which develops gluten and makes tough, dense farls.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it holds together; a rough dough is a good dough here.

steps.do: Turn the dough onto the floured surface, dust the top with flour and, with floured hands, pat it gently into a round about 8 inches (20 cm) across and 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick. Cut it into four quarters with the floured scraper.
steps.look: A soft, even round cut into four triangles (farls, from the old word for a fourth).
steps.mistake: Rolling with a pin and pressing hard, which knocks out the gas.
steps.fix: Pat lightly with your fingertips only, and work quickly: the gas is being made from the moment the buttermilk touches the soda.

steps.do: Dust the warm griddle lightly with flour and lay the farls on it with a little space between them. Bake for 6 to 8 minutes, until the underside is golden brown and the farls have risen to about 1 1/4 inches (3 cm).
steps.look: The farls puff noticeably; the underside is golden with darker freckles; the top looks dry at the edges.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, while the first side is pale and soft.
steps.fix: Wait for the rise and a proper golden underside; lift one corner to check.

steps.do: Turn the farls over and bake the second side 6 to 8 minutes. Then stand each one on its edges for 1 to 2 minutes on each side to cook the sides.
steps.look: Golden on both faces, the cut edges dry and firm to the touch; tapped underneath, the farl sounds hollow, and the centre reads about 200°F (93°C).
steps.mistake: A doughy, raw centre because the heat was too high and the outside finished first.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and cook longer; split one to check the crumb is dry and fluffy.

steps.do: Wrap the farls in the tea towel on the rack for 5 minutes, which softens the crust, then split them horizontally and spread with plenty of butter. Serve warm.
steps.look: A soft, floury crust and a light, fluffy crumb with a gentle tang.
steps.mistake: Cutting them while they are still very hot, so the crumb is gummy.
steps.fix: Rest 5 minutes in the towel.

steps.do: For an Ulster fry, split day-old farls and fry the cut sides in bacon fat or butter until crisp and golden.
steps.look: Crisp, golden cut faces, soft inside.
steps.mistake: Frying at too low a heat, so they soak up fat.
steps.fix: Use medium heat and a hot fat; fry 2 minutes a side.

science: Soda bread rises by a reaction, not by yeast. Bicarbonate of soda is an alkali; the lactic acid in buttermilk neutralises it, releasing carbon dioxide gas the moment they meet. That gas inflates small bubbles in the dough, and heat from the griddle expands them further before the starch and proteins set around them. Because the reaction starts on mixing, the dough must be shaped and cooked straight away, before the gas escapes. Plain flour forms some gluten when worked with liquid; soda bread is barely mixed so the crumb stays tender and cake-like rather than chewy. Too much soda, or soda without enough acid, leaves an alkaline, soapy taste and yellow colour. Low griddle heat lets the thick dough cook through before the crust burns.
plating: Stack the split farls on a wooden board, buttered sides up, with a dish of soft salted butter and a pot of marmalade or jam. As part of an Ulster fry, lay a fried farl at the edge of the plate beside bacon, sausage and egg.

pairing.drink: A Black Velvet of stout and dry sparkling wine, or simply strong tea with milk: something with body and bitterness for buttered bread.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Irish Coffee: Irish whiskey, coffee and cream are the natural companions of an Irish griddle bread.

variations: Wheaten farls: replace half the flour with wholemeal flour for a nuttier, brown farl.
Cheese and spring onion farls: add 1/2 cup (50 g) grated Cheddar and 2 sliced spring onions to the dry ingredients.
Bake a full soda loaf: double the recipe, shape into a round, cut a deep cross and bake at 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes, then 400°F (200°C) for 25.
safety: A heavy cast iron pan stays hot long after use; handle with a dry cloth and let it cool before washing.
Use fresh buttermilk well within its date.
