title: Buttermilk Biscuits with Sausage Gravy
summary: Flaky, tall buttermilk biscuits made with cold butter and folded for layers, split and covered with a peppery milk gravy thickened by a roux built in browned sausage fat. The Southern breakfast joins a quick bread built on cold fat with a first milk gravy, so the cook learns lamination and the roux in one morning.
skills: a roux gravy from sausage fat
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast iron or heavy frying pan
small saucepan to warm the milk

ingredients.item: plain flour, plus more for dusting
ingredients.note: A soft Southern flour gives the most tender biscuit.

ingredients.item: unsalted butter, very cold or frozen
ingredients.note: Plus 1 tbsp (14 g) melted to brush.
Out of its casing if in links.

ingredients.item: unsalted butter, for the gravy if needed
ingredients.note: Only if the sausage gives less than 3 tbsp (45 ml) of fat.
Sausage gravy is well peppered.
Sausage is already salty.

mise: Freeze the butter for 15 minutes; heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a rack in the upper middle.
Whisk flour, baking powder, soda, salt and sugar in the bowl.
Measure the buttermilk and keep it in the fridge.
Line the baking sheet; flour the work surface and the cutter.
Warm the milk for the gravy in the small saucepan until steaming, about 150°F (65°C).
Have pepper, sage and cayenne measured.

timeline.do: Butter in the freezer; oven to 450°F (230°C); mix dry ingredients.
Grate in the butter; add buttermilk; fold the dough three times.
Cut the biscuits; chill 10 minutes while the oven finishes heating.
Bake the biscuits 12 to 15 minutes; brown the sausage.
Make the roux in the sausage fat; whisk in the milk; simmer.
Split the hot biscuits and ladle gravy over.

steps.do: Grate the frozen butter on the large holes of the box grater straight into the bowl of dry ingredients, tossing the shreds in the flour every few strokes so they stay separate. Then rub briefly with your fingertips until the pieces are the size of peas and flat flakes.
steps.look: Flour with visible flakes and pea-sized pieces of cold butter scattered through it; the mixture feels cold.
steps.mistake: Warm butter rubbed in to fine crumbs, which gives a cakey, flat biscuit with no layers.
steps.fix: Keep everything cold; if the butter softens, put the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes.

steps.do: Pour in the cold buttermilk and stir with a fork for about 20 seconds, just until a shaggy dough forms with some dry bits remaining.
steps.look: A rough, lumpy dough that barely holds together.
steps.mistake: Mixing until smooth, which makes tough biscuits.
steps.fix: Stop early; the folding will bring the dough together.

steps.do: Tip onto the floured surface and pat into a rectangle about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick. Fold it in thirds like a letter, using the bench scraper to lift it. Turn it 90 degrees, pat out again and fold again. Repeat for three folds in total.
steps.look: After the third fold, a smoother dough with visible streaks of butter, which become the flaky layers.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard and over-flouring, which smears the butter and dries the dough.
steps.fix: Pat gently, brush off excess flour before folding, and work quickly.

steps.do: Pat the dough to 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick. Cut biscuits with the floured cutter, pushing straight down and lifting straight up without twisting. Place them on the lined sheet just touching each other. Gently press the scraps together and cut again. Chill the tray for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Clean, straight sides on each biscuit; biscuits standing shoulder to shoulder.
steps.mistake: Twisting the cutter, which seals the edges and stops the biscuits rising.
steps.fix: Press straight down and lift; flour the cutter between each cut.

steps.do: Brush the tops with melted butter and bake at 450°F (230°C) for 12 to 15 minutes, turning the tray halfway, until tall and deep golden.
steps.look: Biscuits doubled in height, with flaky layers visible on the sides and golden brown tops.
steps.mistake: A cool oven, in which the butter melts out before the biscuits set, leaving them flat and greasy.
steps.fix: Make sure the oven is fully heated; an oven thermometer tells you the truth.

steps.do: While the biscuits bake, cook the sausage in the cast iron pan over medium heat, breaking it into small pieces with a wooden spoon, for 8 to 10 minutes, until no pink remains and it has browned in places, at least 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: Browned, crumbly sausage with crusty bits stuck on the pan and clear fat pooling.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, so the sausage steams grey without browning.
steps.fix: Let it sit 1 to 2 minutes between stirs to build a crust; that crust is flavour for the gravy.

steps.do: Tilt the pan and check the fat: you need about 3 tbsp (45 ml). Add butter if there is less, or spoon some off if there is much more. Sprinkle the 1/3 cup (40 g) flour over the sausage and stir constantly for 2 minutes over medium heat.
steps.look: The flour disappears into the fat and coats the sausage; it smells toasty, like a biscuit, with no raw flour taste.
steps.mistake: Adding the milk before the flour has cooked, which leaves a pasty, raw flour taste.
steps.fix: Cook the roux a full 2 minutes, stirring so it does not scorch.

steps.do: Pour in the warm milk in a slow stream, whisking constantly and scraping the bottom of the pan. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring often, for 5 to 8 minutes until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
steps.look: A creamy gravy that thickens as it bubbles; a finger drawn across the coated spoon leaves a clear line.
steps.mistake: Adding cold milk all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Use warm milk, add it gradually and whisk; small lumps can be whisked out as it simmers.

steps.do: Season with plenty of black pepper, the sage, cayenne and salt to taste. Take it off the heat while still a little thinner than you want; it thickens as it stands. Loosen with a splash of milk if needed.
steps.look: A thick but pourable gravy, speckled all over with pepper and sausage.
steps.mistake: A stiff, pasty gravy.
steps.fix: Whisk in warm milk a few tablespoons at a time.

steps.do: Split two hot biscuits per person, lay them cut side up and ladle the gravy over. Serve at once with extra pepper.
steps.look: Flaky golden biscuits half hidden under a creamy, peppered gravy.
steps.mistake: Pouring gravy over biscuits long before eating, so they turn to mush.
steps.fix: Ladle at the table or the moment before serving.

science: Flaky biscuits depend on cold fat. Pieces of butter that stay solid in the dough melt in the hot oven and release steam, which pushes apart layers of dough to create flakes. Folding the dough three times stacks thin sheets of butter and dough into layers, a simple form of lamination. A very hot oven sets the dough quickly before the butter can run out. Baking powder and the reaction between soda and buttermilk provide gas for lift. The gravy is thickened by a roux: flour cooked in fat coats each starch granule so it disperses without lumping, and cooking removes the raw taste. When hot milk is added and simmered, the starch granules absorb liquid and swell, thickening the gravy, and they continue to thicken as it cools.
plating: Use a warm, wide shallow bowl. Set the bottom halves of two biscuits cut side up, lean the tops against them at an angle so the flaky layers show, and ladle the gravy over the bottoms only. Finish with a heavy grind of black pepper and a few snipped chives for colour.

pairing.drink: A Bloody Mary with a celery stalk, salty and peppery against the rich gravy, or a pot of strong black coffee.
pairing.brennans: Buttermilk Biscuit: Brennan's own breakfast biscuit, made on the same cold butter and buttermilk principle.

variations: Chicken and biscuits: top split biscuits with fried chicken and the same gravy.
Herb biscuits: add 2 tbsp (6 g) chopped chives and 1/2 cup (50 g) grated sharp Cheddar to the dry mix.
Vegetarian mushroom gravy: brown 8 oz (225 g) chopped mushrooms in 3 tbsp (42 g) butter and build the roux in that.
safety: Pork sausage must reach at least 160°F (71°C), with no pink remaining.
Wash hands after handling raw sausage and before touching the biscuits.
Hot fat and roux can cause serious burns; stir with a long wooden spoon and add milk slowly to avoid splattering.
Use the grater carefully on frozen butter; stop before your knuckles reach the blade and use the last piece in the dough by hand.

title: Horiatiki (Greek Village Salad)
summary: The Greek village salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, green pepper, red onion and olives, dressed with olive oil, red wine vinegar and oregano and crowned with a whole slab of feta. A salad with no lettuce and nowhere to hide puts the knife first, which is where every cook begins.
skills: cutting tomato, cucumber and onion cleanly
dressing with oil, vinegar and oregano
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) chef's knife, freshly sharpened
serrated tomato knife (useful for soft tomatoes)
large chopping board with a damp cloth underneath
small bowl of iced water for the onion
small jar or bowl for the dressing

ingredients.note: Never refrigerated; cold kills tomato flavour.
Partly peeled in stripes if the skin is thick.

ingredients.item: green pepper, preferably a long Greek or Italian frying pepper
Greek feta in brine, in one slab

ingredients.note: Rubbed between the palms.

ingredients.item: extra virgin olive oil, Greek if possible

ingredients.note: Feta is salty; season the vegetables lightly.
Optional, as on the islands.
For the juices at the bottom of the bowl.

mise: Sharpen the knife and set the board on a damp cloth.
Wash and dry the tomatoes, cucumber and pepper.
Fill a small bowl with iced water.
Drain the feta and pat it dry.
Measure oil, vinegar, oregano and salt.

timeline.do: Slice the onion and soak it in iced water for 10 minutes.
Cut the tomatoes, salt them in the bowl and let them weep.
Cut the cucumber and pepper; drain the onion.
Combine, dress, lay the feta slab on top.
Oregano and a last thread of oil; serve with bread.

steps.do: Set up the claw grip: the hand holding the food curls its fingertips under, so the knuckles face the blade and guide it. Keep the knife tip in contact with the board and slice by pushing the blade forward and down, not by chopping straight down.
steps.look: Fingertips tucked out of sight behind the knuckles; the flat of the blade glides against them.
steps.mistake: Flat fingers on the vegetable, fingertips under the edge of the knife.
steps.fix: Stop and reset the grip each time you move your hand. Slow, safe and even beats fast.

steps.do: Halve the red onion through the root, peel it and lay it flat. Slice it from top to root into thin half-moons about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Drop the slices into the iced water and leave for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Thin, even crescents that separate into curls; after soaking they are crisp and their sharpness has softened.
steps.mistake: Thick chunks of raw onion that dominate every bite.
steps.fix: Slice thinner, and always soak raw onion for salads; it removes harsh sulphur compounds while keeping the crunch.

steps.do: Core each tomato with the tip of the knife. Cut it into wedges: halve, then cut each half into 3 or 4 wedges, then cut longer wedges in half crosswise into rough bite sized chunks. Put them in the serving bowl, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and leave for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Clean cut faces with the seeds still in place; after salting, a pool of pink juice gathers in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Crushing the tomatoes with a blunt knife so they leak and look ragged.
steps.fix: Use a sharp blade or the serrated knife, with a gentle sawing motion and no downward pressure.

steps.do: Trim the cucumber ends, peel away strips of skin lengthways if it is thick, halve it lengthways and cut into thick half-moons about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick.
steps.look: Even half-moons of the same thickness, with clean edges.
steps.mistake: Pieces of very different sizes, some wafer thin, some chunky.
steps.fix: Keep your guiding knuckles moving back by the same distance each cut.

steps.do: Cut the stalk end off the pepper, scrape out the seeds and pale ribs and slice it into thin rings about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: Neat green rings without seeds.
steps.mistake: Leaving seeds and white pith, which are bitter.
steps.fix: Tap the pepper upside down to release seeds, and trim the ribs with the knife tip.

steps.do: Drain the onion and pat it dry. Add the cucumber, pepper, onion, olives and capers to the tomatoes and their juice. Toss gently with your hands once.
steps.look: Colourful chunks evenly mixed, glistening with tomato juice.
steps.mistake: Tossing hard, which breaks the tomatoes.
steps.fix: Lift and turn gently with your hands, once or twice only.

steps.do: Sprinkle the vinegar over the vegetables, then pour over the olive oil generously. Do not toss again.
steps.look: Oil and vinegar pooling with the tomato juice at the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Being shy with the oil; the oil and juices are the sauce.
steps.fix: Use the full 1/4 cup (60 ml); Greeks pour freely.

steps.do: Lay the whole slab of feta on top. Rub the oregano between your palms over the salad so it falls on the feta and vegetables. Add a final thread of oil over the feta and serve with bread for mopping up the juices.
steps.look: A white slab of feta on a colourful mound, speckled green with oregano, a golden pool of dressing below.
steps.mistake: Crumbling the feta through the salad, which makes it cloudy and loses the look of the dish.
steps.fix: Keep it whole; each person breaks off their own piece at the table.

science: Salting tomatoes before dressing them draws out juice by osmosis: salt on the cut surface pulls water from inside the cells, and that juice, rich in sugar, acid and glutamates, mixes with oil and vinegar into the pool of dressing at the bottom of the bowl. Refrigerating tomatoes below about 50°F (10°C) damages the enzymes that produce their aroma, which is why they are kept at room temperature. Raw onion tastes harsh because cutting it releases sulphur compounds; soaking the slices in iced water rinses those compounds away while keeping the cells crisp. A sharp knife slices through cells cleanly rather than crushing them, so tomatoes leak less and cut vegetables stay firm and bright.
plating: Use a wide, shallow bowl so the juices can pool. Pile the vegetables loosely with the tomatoes showing, set the feta slab at a slight angle on the top, scatter the oregano over everything and finish with a thread of olive oil on the cheese. Serve the bread alongside, never on the plate.

pairing.drink: A crisp, salty Assyrtiko from Santorini: high acidity for the tomato and vinegar and a mineral edge for the feta and olives.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: the Santorini white on the Brennan's list is exactly the wine this salad calls for.

variations: Add a handful of purslane or rocket leaves for a peppery green note.
Make a dakos version: spoon the dressed vegetables over a barley rusk softened with a splash of water, and crumble the feta over the top.
Add thin slices of caper leaves or sliced pickled pepper for sharpness.
safety: Sharpen your knife before you start: a blunt knife needs force and slips.
Keep the board on a damp cloth so it cannot slide.
Wash vegetables under running water before cutting.

title: Tabbouleh
summary: The Lebanese parsley salad: a great deal of finely sliced flat leaf parsley and mint with a little fine bulgur, tomato and spring onion, dressed sharply with lemon and olive oil. A salad that is mostly parsley demands a sharp knife and a clean, slicing cut rather than a crush, and that the herbs be bone dry.
equipment: very sharp 8 inch (20 cm) chef's knife
large chopping board on a damp cloth

ingredients.note: Fine, not coarse.
From about 2 lemons.

ingredients.item: ground allspice or Lebanese seven spice
Little Gem or Cos lettuce leaves
ingredients.note: For scooping.

mise: Pick the parsley leaves and the thinnest stems from the thick stalks.
Wash parsley and mint in cold water, spin dry, then roll in tea towels and leave 15 minutes.
Rinse the bulgur in the sieve and drain.
Squeeze the lemons.
Separate the lettuce leaves, wash and dry.

timeline.do: Wash, spin and towel dry the herbs.
Dice the tomatoes; soak the bulgur in their juice and the lemon.
Slice the spring onions; slice the parsley and mint.
Combine and dress.
Serve at once with lettuce leaves.

steps.do: Wash the picked parsley and mint in a large bowl of cold water, lifting them out so grit stays behind. Spin dry in the salad spinner, then spread on a clean tea towel, roll it up loosely and leave for 15 minutes.
steps.look: Leaves completely dry to the touch with no droplets clinging; the towel damp.
steps.mistake: Chopping damp parsley, which bruises into a dark green paste and makes the salad soggy.
steps.fix: Dry thoroughly; if still damp, spread the leaves on a fresh towel for another 10 minutes.

steps.do: Dice the tomatoes: core them, cut into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, then strips, then across into small dice. Keep all the juice. Put the dice and juice in the mixing bowl.
steps.look: Small, even red cubes and a puddle of juice on the board, scraped into the bowl.
steps.mistake: Pressing down hard, which squashes the tomato rather than slicing it.
steps.fix: Let the sharp blade do the work with a gentle forward stroke.

steps.do: Scatter the rinsed bulgur over the tomatoes and pour over half the lemon juice. Leave to soak for 15 to 20 minutes without cooking.
steps.look: The grains swell and soften but stay distinct and slightly chewy.
steps.mistake: Boiling the bulgur, or using coarse bulgur, which makes a heavy, grain-forward salad.
steps.fix: Fine bulgur needs only tomato juice and lemon to soften; it should be a minor presence.

steps.do: Trim the spring onions and slice them very thinly into rings, white and green parts.
steps.look: Fine rings, no thicker than 1/16 inch (2 mm).
steps.mistake: Thick rings that dominate the herbs.
steps.fix: Slice thinner, holding several onions together under the claw grip.

steps.do: Gather a handful of dry parsley into a tight bundle on the board, hold it with the claw grip and slice across it as thinly as you can in one pass, using long forward strokes of the knife. Do not go back and forth over the pile. Repeat until all the parsley and mint are sliced.
steps.look: Fine, bright green, separate shreds that look fresh and feathery, with no dark green juice on the board.
steps.mistake: Chopping repeatedly with a rocking motion, which crushes the parsley into a wet, dark mass that tastes like grass clippings.
steps.fix: Slice once through a tight bundle; if the knife is dragging, stop and sharpen it.

steps.do: Add the parsley, mint and spring onion to the bowl of tomatoes and bulgur. Add the salt, allspice, pepper, the remaining lemon juice and the olive oil. Toss gently with your hands until evenly mixed.
steps.look: A bright green salad flecked with red tomato and pale bulgur, glistening with oil.
steps.mistake: Dressing too early, so the parsley wilts and weeps.
steps.fix: Dress just before serving.

steps.do: Taste and adjust. It should be sharp, fresh and clearly lemony, balanced with salt and oil.
steps.look: A taste that makes the mouth water, bright first and rich second.
steps.mistake: A timid dressing; tabbouleh is meant to be the sharp note on a rich table.
steps.fix: Add more lemon and salt in small amounts until it tastes vivid.

steps.do: Serve at once in a shallow bowl with lettuce leaves arranged around it for scooping.
steps.look: A mound of green salad framed by pale green lettuce leaves.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit for an hour, by which time it turns limp and watery.
steps.fix: Make it close to serving; store only the undressed chopped herbs, covered, in the fridge.

science: Parsley's flavour lives in volatile oils inside its cells. A sharp knife slices through cells cleanly, releasing a little of that aroma at the cut. A blunt knife or repeated chopping crushes cells across the whole leaf, letting enzymes and air oxidise the chlorophyll and leaf compounds into a dark, grassy, bitter mash. Water on the leaves makes this worse, because wet leaves slide and bruise under the blade and the water dilutes the dressing. Fine bulgur has been parboiled and dried, so it only needs to absorb liquid to soften; soaking it in tomato juice and lemon flavours each grain without making it mushy. Salt and lemon draw juice from the tomatoes and wilt the herbs over time, which is why tabbouleh is dressed at the last moment.
plating: Mound the tabbouleh in the centre of a wide, shallow dish and press it lightly into a neat dome. Tuck crisp lettuce leaves around the edge like petals, cupped side up, add a lemon wedge and finish with a thread of olive oil over the top.

pairing.drink: Arak diluted with iced water until cloudy, the Lebanese way, or a crisp, high acid white such as Albariño.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: a bright, citrusy white from the Brennan's list to stand up to lemon and herbs.

variations: Add finely diced cucumber for extra freshness in summer.
Gluten free tabbouleh: replace the bulgur with an equal weight of cooked quinoa, cooled.
Add a pinch of sumac and some pomegranate seeds for a sweet-sour finish.
safety: Wash herbs thoroughly in plenty of water; soil and grit hide in the stems.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one; keep fingers curled under.
Keep the salad cold and eat within a few hours of dressing.

title: Salade Niçoise
summary: A composed salad from Nice of separately cooked new potatoes, green beans and eggs with ripe tomatoes, olives, anchovies and good olive oil tuna, dressed with a mustard vinaigrette. It introduces blanching and shocking, the oil and vinegar emulsion, and timing several components to finish together.
skills: boiling eggs and potatoes to time
equipment: large pot, about 5 quart (4.7 litre), for beans
small bowl and whisk, or a jar with a lid, for the vinaigrette

ingredients.note: Cut into wedges.

ingredients.item: good tuna in olive oil, drained
small black olives, Niçoise or Kalamata

ingredients.note: Optional; Nice purists leave it out.
For 4 quarts (3.8 litres) of water.

ingredients.us: 1/2 tsp salt, a few turns of pepper
ingredients.metric: 3 g salt, a few turns of pepper

mise: Put the large pot of salted water on to boil for the beans.
Fill the large bowl with iced water.
Scrub the potatoes; put them in the medium saucepan with cold salted water.
Trim the stem ends of the beans.
Mince the shallot; cut tomatoes into wedges.
Drain the tuna and anchovies; wash and dry the lettuce.

timeline.do: Potatoes on in cold salted water; bean water on to boil.
Make the vinaigrette and let the shallot soften in it.
Eggs into boiling water for 8 minutes, then into iced water.
Blanch the beans 3 to 4 minutes; shock in iced water.
Drain the potatoes, halve and dress them while warm.
Compose the platter.
Spoon over the last of the dressing and serve.

steps.do: Cover the potatoes with cold water by 1 inch (2.5 cm), add 1 tsp (6 g) salt, bring to the boil, then simmer for 15 to 18 minutes, until a knife slides into the largest one with no resistance.
steps.look: Tender potatoes with skins intact, not cracked open.
steps.mistake: Starting potatoes in boiling water, so the outsides fall apart before the centres cook.
steps.fix: Always start potatoes in cold water so they heat evenly through.

steps.do: Make the vinaigrette: whisk the shallot, mustard, vinegar, 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and some pepper in the small bowl and leave 5 minutes. Then add the olive oil in a thin stream, whisking constantly, or shake everything hard in the jar for 30 seconds.
steps.look: A thick, creamy, pale dressing that holds together without separating for several minutes.
steps.mistake: Pouring in all the oil at once, which leaves it oily and separated.
steps.fix: Whisk in a teaspoon of warm water and keep whisking; the mustard will pull it back together.

steps.do: Lower the eggs into a pan of boiling water, simmer for 8 minutes, then transfer to the iced water for 5 minutes. Peel them under the water and cut into quarters.
steps.look: Firm whites and yolks set but still soft and deep yellow in the very centre.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, giving grey ringed, chalky yolks.
steps.fix: Eight minutes then iced water, every time.

steps.do: When the bean water is at a full rolling boil, drop in the beans and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until bright green and tender with a slight snap. Lift them out with the spider straight into the iced water for 2 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
steps.look: Vivid green beans that bend slightly but still snap when bitten.
steps.mistake: Cooking them in a small amount of water that stops boiling, or leaving them warm, so they turn dull olive green.
steps.fix: Use plenty of well salted water at a full boil and shock immediately.

steps.do: Drain the potatoes, halve them while still warm and toss with 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the vinaigrette. Leave them to absorb it for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Glossy potatoes that look as though they have drunk the dressing.
steps.mistake: Dressing cold potatoes, which stay bland and greasy.
steps.fix: Dress them warm; this is the lesson for every potato salad.

steps.do: Compose the platter: lay the lettuce leaves, if using, as a bed. Arrange the potatoes, beans, tomato wedges and egg quarters in separate groups around the platter. Break the tuna into large flakes and pile it in the centre. Scatter the olives and lay the anchovies over the eggs.
steps.look: Distinct groups of colour and texture, each element visible.
steps.mistake: Tossing everything together into a muddle.
steps.fix: Niçoise is composed, never tossed: each part keeps its own texture and temperature.

steps.do: Spoon the remaining vinaigrette over everything, season the tomatoes and eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper, scatter torn basil and serve.
steps.look: A glistening, colourful platter.
steps.mistake: Drowning the salad in dressing so it pools.
steps.fix: Spoon it over sparingly and serve the rest on the side.

science: Blanching cooks green vegetables fast in plenty of boiling salted water, softening their cell walls while their colour brightens as air trapped between cells is driven out. Cooking too long, or in water that stops boiling, lets acids from the vegetable convert green chlorophyll to olive coloured pheophytin; shocking in iced water stops the cooking and fixes the colour. Warm potatoes absorb dressing because their gelatinised starch and loosened cell walls take up liquid as they cool. A vinaigrette is an emulsion: oil broken into tiny droplets suspended in vinegar. Mustard contains compounds that coat the droplets and keep them apart, which is why a mustard vinaigrette stays creamy while plain oil and vinegar separate within seconds.
plating: Use a large, white oval platter. Set the tuna as the centrepiece, then arrange each element in its own wedge-shaped group around it like the spokes of a wheel: potatoes, beans, tomatoes, eggs. Criss-cross the anchovies over the egg quarters, dot olives between the groups, and finish with torn basil and a spoon of dressing on top.

pairing.drink: A dry Provence or Bandol rosé, the wine of Nice: red fruit, salinity and acidity that suit tuna, anchovy and tomato.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Tempier Bandol Rosé 2024: a celebrated Provençal rosé on the Brennan's list, a natural match for the food of Nice.

variations: Use seared fresh tuna steak, cooked rare and sliced, instead of canned tuna.
Pan bagnat: pile the salad into a split round loaf brushed with olive oil, wrap and press for an hour.
Add blanched broad beans or artichoke hearts in spring.
safety: Drain boiling water away from you, tilting the pan slowly.
Keep the composed salad cool if it waits; refrigerate within 2 hours.
Eggs cooked for 8 minutes are set and safe for everyone.

title: Gazpacho Andaluz
summary: The chilled Andalusian soup of very ripe tomatoes, cucumber, green pepper, garlic and stale bread, blended with sherry vinegar and emulsified with olive oil until pale coral and creamy, then passed through a sieve. It shows how olive oil emulsifies into vegetables and why cold food needs more salt.
skills: blending oil into a vegetable base

ingredients.note: The ripest you can find; this is the whole flavour.

ingredients.item: green pepper, preferably an Italian frying pepper

ingredients.note: Soaked in water for 5 minutes, then squeezed.
Taste again once chilled.
Only if needed to loosen.

ingredients.item: garnish: cucumber, green pepper and red onion in fine dice

mise: Core and roughly chop the tomatoes.
Chop the cucumber, pepper and garlic.
Soak the bread in water, then squeeze it out.
Measure the vinegar, oil and salt.
Cut the garnish into a fine brunoise of 1/8 inch (3 mm).
Chill four bowls or glasses in the fridge.

timeline.do: Chop the vegetables, soak the bread.
Blend for 2 minutes; stream in the oil; pass through the sieve.
Chill at least 2 hours.
Cut the garnish brunoise; make croutons.
Taste cold; adjust salt and vinegar.
Pour into chilled bowls or glasses and garnish.

steps.do: Put the tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, garlic, squeezed bread, vinegar and salt in the blender, tomatoes at the bottom so their juice gets the blades going. Blend on high for a full 2 minutes.
steps.look: A completely smooth, bright red purée with no visible pieces.
steps.mistake: Blending for a few seconds only, leaving a coarse salsa that separates.
steps.fix: Keep blending for minutes, not seconds; a powerful blender makes a silkier soup.

steps.do: With the blender running on medium, pour the olive oil in through the lid in a slow, thin stream over about 1 minute.
steps.look: The colour changes from bright red to a pale coral orange, and the texture turns creamy and thick.
steps.mistake: Pouring the oil in all at once, which leaves an oily slick that floats on top.
steps.fix: Stream slowly; if it separates, blend again on high for 30 seconds.

steps.do: Set the sieve over a large bowl and pour the soup through, pressing with the back of a ladle and scraping the underside of the sieve. Discard the seeds and skin left behind.
steps.look: A smooth, velvety soup in the bowl; a small amount of dry pulp and seeds in the sieve.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, which leaves bits of skin and seed in a soup meant to be silky.
steps.fix: Pass it; work in batches and press firmly.

steps.do: Taste and check the texture: it should coat a spoon but be pourable, like single cream. Loosen with a little cold water if needed. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
steps.look: A creamy soup that runs slowly from the spoon.
steps.mistake: Serving it straight away, warm and thin.
steps.fix: Chill thoroughly; gazpacho tastes and feels best ice cold.

steps.do: While it chills, cut the garnish: slice cucumber, pepper and onion into thin planks, then strips 1/8 inch (3 mm) wide, then across into tiny cubes. Toast small cubes of bread in a pan with a little olive oil over medium heat until golden.
steps.look: Tiny, even cubes of vegetable and crisp, golden croutons.
steps.mistake: Large, uneven garnish that overwhelms the smooth soup.
steps.fix: Practise the brunoise: even planks first, then even strips, then cubes.

steps.do: Taste the chilled soup again and adjust: it will need more salt and probably a splash more vinegar, because cold dulls both.
steps.look: A soup that tastes bright, fresh and fully seasoned when ice cold.
steps.mistake: Seasoning only while warm, so it tastes flat from the fridge.
steps.fix: Always season cold food at the temperature it will be eaten.

steps.do: Pour into the chilled bowls or glasses, scatter a little of each garnish and the croutons over the top and finish with a few drops of olive oil.
steps.look: A pale coral soup, glossy, topped with green, white and red cubes and golden croutons.
steps.mistake: Adding croutons long before serving, so they go soggy.
steps.fix: Add at the very last moment.

science: Gazpacho is an emulsion as well as a soup. A blender breaks olive oil into tiny droplets, and the soaked bread and the pectin and fibre from the vegetables surround those droplets and stop them merging again. The droplets scatter light, which is why the colour shifts from red to pale coral and the soup turns creamy without any dairy. Streaming the oil slowly gives the blades time to break it into droplets rather than overwhelming the mixture. Passing through a sieve removes skin and seed fragments for a smooth texture. Cold food needs more seasoning because our taste receptors and sense of smell are less responsive at low temperatures, so a soup seasoned at room temperature tastes muted when chilled to 40°F (4°C).
plating: Pour the gazpacho into chilled shallow bowls or short glasses. In a bowl, arrange the garnish in three small neat lines or a cluster in the centre with the croutons beside it, then add a few drops of olive oil so they sit as golden beads on the surface.

pairing.drink: A chilled glass of fino or manzanilla sherry: dry, salty and nutty, it matches the sherry vinegar and the oil.
pairing.brennans: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml): the dry manzanilla on the Brennan's list is the Andalusian partner for an Andalusian soup.

variations: Salmorejo: use more bread and only tomato and garlic for a thicker Córdoba soup, topped with chopped egg and ham.
Watermelon gazpacho: replace a third of the tomatoes with watermelon.
Ajo blanco: blend almonds, bread, garlic, oil and vinegar for the white cold soup of Málaga.
safety: Raw garlic and vegetables should be washed; keep gazpacho refrigerated and eat within 2 days.
Keep fingers and spoons out of a running blender; stop it before scraping down.
Cut the brunoise slowly with the claw grip; tiny cuts mean fingers close to the blade.

title: Gỏi Cuốn (Fresh Spring Rolls)
summary: Vietnamese fresh rolls of rice paper wrapped around poached prawns, rice vermicelli, lettuce, herbs and julienned vegetables, served with a hoisin and peanut dipping sauce. Julienne and neat, tight rolling are knife and hand skills that every later dumpling and roll relies on.
equipment: saucepan or kettle for the noodles
wide shallow dish of warm water for dipping rice paper
damp, clean tea towel or a wooden board to roll on
plate covered with a damp towel for finished rolls

ingredients.note: Buy a few extra; some will tear while you learn.

ingredients.item: soft lettuce leaves, such as butterhead
ingredients.note: Ribs trimmed.
Julienned.
Seeded and julienned.

ingredients.item: mint, coriander and Thai basil leaves
garlic chives or spring onion greens
ingredients.note: Optional, poking out of each roll.

mise: Julienne the carrot and cucumber into matchsticks 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and 3 inches (7.5 cm) long.
Pick the herbs; wash and dry the lettuce and herbs.
Cook the vermicelli, rinse in cold water and drain well.
Poach, chill, peel and halve the prawns lengthways.
Make the dipping sauce.
Arrange all fillings in order around the rolling board, with the dish of warm water.

timeline.do: Julienne the vegetables; pick herbs.
Poach and chill the prawns; peel and halve them.
Cook and drain the noodles; make the sauce.
Set up the rolling station; roll one at a time.
Serve the rolls seam side down with the sauce.

steps.do: Julienne the carrot: cut it into 3 inch (7.5 cm) lengths, slice a thin strip off one side so it lies flat, then cut into planks 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Stack two or three planks and cut into matchsticks 1/8 inch (3 mm) wide. Repeat with the seeded cucumber.
steps.look: Thin, even matchsticks of the same length and thickness, like a pile of straight pins.
steps.mistake: Rolling vegetables that wobble on the board, which is how fingers get cut.
steps.fix: Always cut a flat base first so the vegetable sits still.

steps.do: Bring a saucepan of water with 1 tsp (6 g) salt to the boil, drop in the prawns, and cook 2 to 3 minutes, until they curl into a loose C, turn pink and opaque right through. Lift into the iced water to stop the cooking.
steps.look: Pink, opaque prawns, firm but springy; cut one at the thickest part and it is pearly white throughout.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until they curl into tight O shapes, which makes them rubbery.
steps.fix: Take them out as soon as they are opaque; a C means cooked, an O means overcooked.

steps.do: Peel the prawns, remove the dark vein along the back with the knife tip, and slice each one in half lengthways through its thickness.
steps.look: Flat, half moon halves with the pink, striped outer side visible.
steps.mistake: Leaving the vein, which is gritty.
steps.fix: Run the knife tip along the back and lift it out.

steps.do: Cook the vermicelli according to the packet, usually 3 to 4 minutes in boiling water, then drain, rinse under cold water and drain very well, shaking the colander.
steps.look: Soft, white, separate noodles with no water dripping from them.
steps.mistake: Wet noodles, which make the rice paper soggy so it tears.
steps.fix: Drain thoroughly and pat with paper towel.

steps.do: Make the sauce: warm the hoisin, peanut butter and water in the small saucepan over low heat, whisking until smooth, about 2 minutes. Stir in the vinegar and chilli sauce. Cool and top with crushed peanuts.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth, pourable brown sauce.
steps.mistake: Sauce too thick to dip.
steps.fix: Whisk in more water a teaspoon at a time.

steps.do: Dip one rice paper in the warm water for 2 to 3 seconds, turning it so it is all wet, and lay it flat on the damp towel or board. It will still feel slightly stiff; it softens as you fill it.
steps.look: A sheet that is pliable but still holds some texture.
steps.mistake: Soaking until floppy, so it tears and sticks to itself.
steps.fix: Under-soak; count two seconds. If it tears, start a new sheet.

steps.do: On the third of the sheet nearest you, lay a lettuce leaf, a small bundle of noodles, some carrot and cucumber and a few herbs, in a log about 4 inches (10 cm) long. Above that, in the middle of the sheet, lay 3 or 4 prawn halves in a row, pink side down.
steps.look: A neat log of filling and a row of prawns, leaving 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) of bare paper on each side.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, which stops the roll closing and tears the sheet.
steps.fix: Use less filling than you think; a slim roll is a tidy roll.

steps.do: Lift the edge nearest you over the filling and tuck it under firmly. Fold in both sides. Then roll forward, keeping it tight, over the prawns, laying in a chive stalk so it pokes out of one end if using. Place seam side down on the plate under a damp towel.
steps.look: A firm, tight, translucent roll with the prawns showing pink through the paper.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely so the filling slides out.
steps.fix: Pull the filling back towards you with your fingertips as you roll, like a burrito.

steps.do: Repeat with the remaining sheets. Serve within an hour, whole or cut in half on the diagonal, with the dipping sauce.
steps.look: A row of neat, identical rolls.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating the rolls, which hardens the rice paper.
steps.fix: Keep them covered with a damp towel at cool room temperature and eat within 1 hour.

science: Rice paper is a thin sheet of dried rice starch. Dipped in warm water, the starch absorbs moisture and gelatinises, turning from brittle to flexible, and it keeps absorbing water from its own surface after it leaves the dish, which is why a brief dip is enough and a long soak leaves it weak and sticky. Gelatinised rice starch is sticky, so the roll seals itself. Refrigerated, the starch firms as it retrogrades, so the paper turns hard and chewy. Prawns cook quickly because their muscle proteins set between about 120°F and 140°F (49°C and 60°C); overcooking contracts the fibres and squeezes out moisture, making them rubbery. Even julienne means every bite has the same texture and the roll stays smooth.
plating: Cut each roll in half on a sharp diagonal and stand the halves upright on a long plate, cut faces up, so the colourful filling shows. Arrange them in a neat row, put the dipping sauce in a small bowl at one end and scatter a few herbs and crushed peanuts over the sauce.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling Kabinett: lime and peach fruit, a touch of sweetness for the hoisin and chilli, and lively acidity for the herbs.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: a dry, citrusy Alsace Riesling on the Brennan's list, crisp against herbs and prawn.

variations: Add thin slices of poached pork belly beside the prawns, the traditional pairing.
Vegetarian rolls: replace the prawns with strips of fried tofu and add mango.
Serve with nước chấm, a dipping sauce of fish sauce, lime, sugar, garlic and chilli.
safety: Cook prawns until opaque throughout, at least 145°F (63°C), and chill them quickly in iced water.
Keep raw prawns and their board separate from the herbs and vegetables; wash hands and utensils after handling raw seafood.

title: Gado-Gado
summary: Indonesia's warm salad of blanched vegetables, boiled potatoes and eggs, fried tofu and tempeh and raw cucumber, all covered in a thick, sweet, sour and hot peanut sauce and crowned with crackers and fried shallots. Blanching a whole market of vegetables in sequence and binding them with a cooked sauce builds timing.
equipment: large pot, about 5 quart (4.7 litre), for blanching
medium saucepan for potatoes and eggs

ingredients.item: green beans, trimmed and cut into 2 inch (5 cm) lengths
white or green cabbage, cut into 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces

ingredients.note: Raw.

ingredients.item: firm tofu, pressed and cut into 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) slabs
tempeh, cut into 1/4 inch (6 mm) slices

ingredients.note: For 4 quarts (3.8 litres) water.

ingredients.item: red chillies, seeded for less heat
palm sugar or dark brown sugar

ingredients.note: Or 1 1/2 tbsp (22 ml) lime juice.
Optional.

ingredients.item: prawn crackers (krupuk) and crispy fried shallots
ingredients.note: For the crunch on top.

mise: Press the tofu between paper towels under a weighted plate for 15 minutes.
Prepare all the vegetables, keeping each kind separate, in the order they will be blanched.
Fill the large pot with salted water and bring to the boil; fill the iced water bowl.
Scrub the potatoes.
Measure the sauce ingredients.
Slice the cucumber; set out the crackers and shallots.

timeline.do: Press the tofu; potatoes on in cold salted water; blanching water on.
Eggs into boiling water for 10 minutes, then into iced water.
Blanch the vegetables in sequence, shocking each.
Fry the tofu and tempeh.
Make and simmer the peanut sauce.
Arrange everything on the platter.
Pour over the warm sauce; scatter crackers and shallots.

steps.do: Cover the potatoes with cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer 15 to 18 minutes until tender. In another pan, boil the eggs for 10 minutes, then cool them in iced water and peel. Halve the potatoes and the eggs.
steps.look: Potatoes yielding to a knife; eggs with fully set yolks and no grey ring.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the potatoes while concentrating on the vegetables.
steps.fix: Start them first and set a timer; they are the longest job.

steps.do: With the large pot at a full rolling boil, blanch the vegetables one kind at a time, mildest first so the water stays clean: bean sprouts 20 seconds, spinach 30 seconds, cabbage 1 1/2 minutes, green beans 3 minutes. Lift each batch out with the spider straight into the iced water, then into the colander.
steps.look: Each batch bright in colour and tender-crisp; the water returns to the boil before each new batch.
steps.mistake: Throwing everything in at once, so the delicate sprouts and spinach turn to mush while the beans stay raw.
steps.fix: Work in sequence, waiting for the boil to return each time; refresh the ice if it melts.

steps.do: Squeeze the spinach gently into a ball to remove water, and let all the vegetables drain well on a towel.
steps.look: Dry, bright vegetables with no water pooling beneath them.
steps.mistake: Wet vegetables that dilute the sauce into a thin puddle.
steps.fix: Drain thoroughly; pat dry with a clean towel.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium high heat until it shimmers, about 350°F (175°C). Fry the tofu slabs for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, then the tempeh slices for 2 minutes per side. Drain on paper towel and cut the tofu into bite sized triangles.
steps.look: Tofu golden with a crisp skin and soft centre; tempeh deep golden and nutty smelling.
steps.mistake: Adding wet tofu to oil that is not hot, so it sticks and spits.
steps.fix: Press and pat the tofu dry, heat the oil properly and lower it in away from you.

steps.do: For the sauce, pour off all but 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the frying oil. Fry the garlic and chillies in it over medium heat for 1 minute until fragrant. Put them in the blender with the peanuts, sugar, tamarind, kecap manis, salt and 1 cup (240 ml) warm water. Blend to a thick, slightly coarse paste.
steps.look: A thick, rough brown paste flecked with red chilli.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic in the hot oil, which makes the sauce bitter.
steps.fix: Let the oil cool slightly first and stir the garlic constantly; pull it at pale gold.

steps.do: Pour the sauce into the small saucepan and simmer over medium low heat, stirring, for 3 to 5 minutes until it thickens and darkens slightly. Loosen with warm water a tablespoon at a time until it pours slowly from a spoon. Taste: it should be sweet first, then sour, then hot, then salty.
steps.look: A thick sauce, glossy with a little peanut oil, that coats the back of a spoon heavily.
steps.mistake: A thin, watery sauce that slides off the vegetables.
steps.fix: Simmer longer or blend in more peanuts; a thin gado-gado sauce is the classic failing.

steps.do: Arrange the potatoes, blanched vegetables, cucumber, tofu, tempeh and eggs in generous separate piles on the platter.
steps.look: A colourful platter of distinct piles, each vegetable visible.
steps.mistake: Piling everything into one heap, so the colours disappear under sauce.
steps.fix: Arrange in sections around the platter.

steps.do: Pour the warm sauce over the middle of the platter, leaving some colour showing, and serve more on the side. Scatter the prawn crackers and fried shallots on top and mix at the table.
steps.look: Warm sauce flooding the centre, crunchy crackers and shallots on top.
steps.mistake: Adding crackers early so they go soft in the sauce.
steps.fix: Add them at the table.

science: Blanching vegetables in sequence uses one pot of water for several jobs. Mild, quick vegetables go first so they are not flavoured by stronger ones such as cabbage. Each batch cooks fast in plenty of water at a full boil, which softens cell walls and drives trapped air out of green leaves so they turn vivid; plunging them into iced water stops the cooking before acids dull the chlorophyll. Roasted peanuts are about half fat; blending breaks the cells and releases their oil, and simmering the paste with water swells the remaining starch and proteins into a thick, stable sauce. Sugar, tamarind's tartaric acid, chilli and salt hit different taste receptors, so a balanced sauce tastes rounded rather than simply sweet.
plating: Use a large platter or wide shallow bowls. Arrange the potatoes and vegetables in neat piles like the segments of a clock, set the egg halves and tofu triangles on top, pour the sauce across the centre in a broad ribbon, then scatter fried shallots over the sauce and stand the crackers at the edge.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or a cold, light lager: a touch of sweetness for the peanut sauce and refreshment against chilli.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: an off-dry Riesling on the Brennan's list that meets sweet, sour and hot head on.

variations: Add boiled corn on the cob, cut into rounds, and blanched carrot slices.
Ketoprak: serve the vegetables and tofu with rice noodles and rice cake under the same sauce.
Use crunchy peanut butter loosened with water and seasoned with the same flavourings for a quick sauce.
safety: Lower tofu into hot oil away from you; wet tofu spits.
Keep the platter cool if it waits, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.
Peanut sauce scorches easily; stir while it simmers.

title: Smørrebrød
summary: Danish open sandwiches on dense rye bread buttered to the edges and topped with carefully sliced, balanced toppings: egg and prawn with dill and lemon, and new potato with radish, chives and mayonnaise. The Danish open sandwich is knife work and composition on a slice of rye.
skills: balancing toppings on an open sandwich
equipment: sharp paring knife or small chef's knife
small saucepan for eggs and one for potatoes

ingredients.item: Danish rye bread (rugbrød), sliced 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick
ingredients.note: Dense, seeded, sour rye.

ingredients.item: small cooked peeled prawns, such as cold water prawns
ingredients.note: Drained and patted dry.
Divided between toppings.
Thin slices and juice.
Shop bought; for the potato topping.
Thinly sliced.

mise: Boil the potatoes in salted water until just tender, 12 to 15 minutes; cool completely.
Boil the eggs for 10 minutes, cool in iced water and peel.
Bring the butter to room temperature.
Pick the dill into small sprigs; snip the chives.
Wash the radishes; cut the lemon into thin slices and a wedge.

timeline.do: Boil potatoes and eggs; cool them.
Slice the potatoes, eggs, radishes, cucumber and lemon.
Butter the bread to the edges.
Build both toppings and garnish.
Serve at once with knife and fork.

steps.do: Spread each slice of rye with butter right to the edges and corners in an even layer about 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick, using the butter knife in long strokes.
steps.look: Every bit of the surface glossy with butter, no bare patches at the crust.
steps.mistake: A dab in the middle, which lets the toppings soak into the bread and makes it soggy.
steps.fix: Spread to the very edge: the butter is a waterproof layer, not a garnish.

steps.do: Slice the eggs into even rounds about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick with a wet knife or the egg slicer.
steps.look: Clean rounds with neat yolks, not crumbled.
steps.mistake: A dry knife dragging the yolk into crumbs.
steps.fix: Dip the knife in water between slices and use a single smooth stroke.

steps.do: Slice the cooled potatoes into rounds 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Slice the radishes into paper thin coins, holding them with the claw grip, and slice the cucumber thinly. Cut thin lemon slices and then cut each slice from the centre to the edge so it can twist.
steps.look: Thin, even slices with clean edges, the radishes translucent at their edges.
steps.mistake: Thick, uneven slices that stack clumsily and fall off.
steps.fix: Cut a flat edge on round vegetables first so they sit still, and slow down.

steps.do: Egg and prawn: lay the egg slices in overlapping rows across two buttered slices, covering the bread. Pile the prawns generously on top, add a small spoon of mayonnaise in the centre, a squeeze of lemon, a lemon twist and sprigs of dill.
steps.look: Bread hidden beneath a neat row of egg and a tall pile of pink prawns, finished with yellow and green.
steps.mistake: A sparse topping that leaves bread showing.
steps.fix: Danish rule: the topping should cover the bread; add more prawns.

steps.do: Potato: spread a thin layer of mayonnaise over the other two slices. Arrange the potato slices in neat, overlapping rows like roof tiles. Season with flaky salt and pepper, then add radish coins, a few cucumber slices, a generous sprinkle of chives and the fried onions.
steps.look: Shingled potato, pink and white radish coins, bright green chives and golden onions.
steps.mistake: Seasoning only the mayonnaise, so the potatoes taste bland.
steps.fix: Salt and pepper the potatoes directly once arranged.

steps.do: Check the balance of each sandwich: something soft, something sharp, something crunchy and something fresh and green. Adjust with lemon, salt, chives or onions.
steps.look: Each slice tells a complete story in every bite.
steps.mistake: Every element soft, so the sandwich tastes flat.
steps.fix: Add the crunch and the acid last; they are what make smørrebrød lively.

steps.do: Serve straight away on flat plates, eaten with a knife and fork. In Denmark the fish slices are eaten before the meat or potato.
steps.look: Two contrasting open sandwiches on each plate, neat and upright.
steps.mistake: Making them far ahead, so the bread softens and the herbs wilt.
steps.fix: Prepare the parts ahead; assemble just before eating.

science: Butter is mostly fat, and fat repels water, so an even layer across rye bread stops moist toppings such as egg, prawns and mayonnaise from soaking in and turning the bread soggy. Dense sourdough rye holds up well because its crumb has less open structure than wheat bread, and its acidity balances rich toppings. Thin slicing changes texture and how flavour reaches the tongue: a paper thin radish is crisp and peppery without being harsh, and thin potato slices make a tender layer. Composition matters because contrast keeps the palate interested: the acid of lemon and the crunch of fried onion stop rich, soft ingredients from tasting heavy. Cooled potatoes slice cleanly because their starch has firmed.
plating: Place one egg and prawn and one potato smørrebrød side by side on a flat white plate with a little space between them. Make sure every topping is visible from above, the lemon twist and dill standing up on the prawns, and set a knife and fork beside them.

pairing.drink: A small glass of chilled aquavit with a cold Danish pilsner, the Copenhagen lunch tradition, or a crisp, briny Muscadet.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de la Pépière ‘Monnières-Saint Fiacre’ Muscadet 2020: a mineral, saline white from the Brennan's list, made for prawns and eggs.

variations: Roast beef: rare roast beef slices with remoulade, grated horseradish, pickled cucumber and crisp onions.
Pickled herring with sliced egg, red onion rings and dill, the first course of a traditional lunch.
Smoked salmon with scrambled egg, chives and lemon.
safety: Keep prawns and mayonnaise refrigerated until assembly and eat within 2 hours of making.
Use the claw grip for small round vegetables like radishes; cut a flat base first.
Hard-boiled eggs should be cooled quickly and kept cold.

title: Miso Soup with Tofu and Wakame
summary: A clear, smoky dashi made from kombu and katsuobushi, seasoned with miso dissolved off the boil, with cubes of silken tofu, wakame and spring onion. Dashi is the shortest stock in the world and the gateway to Japanese cooking, and miso teaches that some seasonings must never boil.
skills: making dashi from kombu and katsuobushi
equipment: fine mesh sieve lined with paper towel or muslin
small fine sieve or ladle for the miso

ingredients.note: Soft or filtered water is best.
Wipe with a damp cloth; do not wash off the white powder, which is flavour.
For a vegan dashi, use 4 dried shiitake instead.
It swells about ten times.

mise: Wipe the kombu and soak it in the cold water in the saucepan for 30 minutes.
Soak the wakame in a small bowl of cold water for 5 minutes, then drain and squeeze.
Line the sieve with paper towel and set it over a bowl.
Slice the spring onions.
Measure the miso into a small bowl.
Warm the soup bowls.

timeline.do: Kombu soaking in cold water.
Heat slowly; lift out the kombu just before the boil.
Add katsuobushi; off the heat; steep and strain.
Return dashi to the pan with tofu and wakame; warm gently.
Off the heat; dissolve the miso through the sieve.
Ladle into bowls, add spring onion, serve.

steps.do: Soak the wiped kombu in the 4 1/4 cups (1 litre) of cold water for 30 minutes. Then set the pan over medium low heat and warm slowly for about 10 minutes.
steps.look: The kombu softens and swells; tiny bubbles start to form on its surface and at the edge of the pan.
steps.mistake: Heating fast over high heat, which gives less flavour from the kombu.
steps.fix: Keep it gentle; slow heating extracts more savouriness.

steps.do: Just before the water boils, when small bubbles rise steadily from the base, around 175°F to 185°F (80°C to 85°C), lift out the kombu with tongs.
steps.look: Water barely moving, with small bubbles but no rolling boil; it smells faintly of the sea.
steps.mistake: Boiling the kombu, which releases slimy, bitter compounds.
steps.fix: If it boils, take it out at once; a few seconds will not ruin it, minutes will.

steps.do: Bring the water to the boil, add the katsuobushi all at once, and immediately turn off the heat. Let the flakes steep without stirring for 2 to 3 minutes, until they sink to the bottom.
steps.look: The flakes float, darken and sink; the liquid turns pale golden and smells smoky and savoury.
steps.mistake: Simmering or squeezing the flakes, which makes a cloudy, fishy, bitter dashi.
steps.fix: Steep off the heat and strain without pressing.

steps.do: Pour the dashi gently through the lined sieve into the bowl and let it drip through. Do not squeeze the flakes. You should have about 3 3/4 cups (900 ml).
steps.look: A clear, pale gold liquid that tastes clean, lightly smoky and savoury even without salt.
steps.mistake: Pressing the flakes for every last drop.
steps.fix: Let gravity do it; the squeezed flakes can be kept for a second, stronger dashi.

steps.do: Drain the tofu and slide it onto your palm or the board. Cut it into 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) cubes: slice horizontally once or twice, then cut lengthways and across. If cutting in your palm, cut gently down onto the hand without sawing, as Japanese cooks do, only if you are confident; otherwise use the board.
steps.look: Neat, even cubes with sharp edges, unbroken.
steps.mistake: Tipping the cubes from a height, which breaks silken tofu.
steps.fix: Slide them gently into the pan from the board or your palm, close to the surface.

steps.do: Return the dashi to the cleaned pan over low heat. Add the tofu and wakame and warm through for 2 to 3 minutes, without boiling.
steps.look: Steam rising, tofu warmed, wakame bright green and glossy.
steps.mistake: Boiling the tofu, which makes it pitted and spongy.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle steaming heat.

steps.do: Turn off the heat. Put the miso in the small sieve or ladle, lower it into the dashi and press and stir it through with chopsticks or a spoon until dissolved. Start with 3 tbsp (50 g), taste, and add more if needed.
steps.look: The soup clouds softly as the miso disperses in drifting clouds; it smells fragrant and savoury.
steps.mistake: Boiling the soup after adding miso, which dulls its aroma and makes it grainy.
steps.fix: Always add miso last, off the heat; reheat leftovers gently and never boil them.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls, making sure each has tofu and wakame, and scatter with spring onion. Serve at once.
steps.look: A cloudy, golden soup with white cubes, green seaweed and bright onion rings.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit, as the miso settles to the bottom.
steps.fix: Stir before ladling; it is normal for miso to settle into soft clouds.

science: Dashi is the clearest demonstration of umami synergy. Kombu is rich in glutamate, and katsuobushi, fermented and smoked skipjack tuna, is rich in inosinate. Together they enhance each other many times beyond either alone, so a ten minute stock tastes deeply savoury. Kombu releases glutamate best below the boil; at a full boil it also releases slippery alginates and bitter compounds, hence lifting it out first. Katsuobushi needs only a brief steep, since the shaved flakes give up their flavour fast and longer contact extracts fishy, bitter notes. Miso is fermented soybean paste carrying volatile aroma compounds that boiling drives off, and its proteins can turn grainy, so it is dissolved last, off the heat.
plating: Serve in small lacquer or ceramic bowls, ideally with lids. Ladle the soup so a few cubes of tofu and a little wakame sit in the centre, scatter the spring onion over them, and serve with chopsticks; the soup is sipped from the bowl.

pairing.drink: A gently warmed junmai sake or a cup of roasted green tea (hojicha): both are savoury and soft enough to sit with dashi.

variations: Clam miso soup: steam open small clams in the dashi, then add red miso.
Mushroom and spinach miso soup with shimeji and wilted spinach.
Tonjiru: simmer pork belly, daikon, carrot and burdock in the dashi before adding miso for a hearty soup.
safety: Do not boil the kombu or the finished soup; this is about flavour, but also prevents boil-overs of a liquid you are watching closely.
Cut silken tofu on a board until you are confident; cutting on the palm is a skill learned slowly.
Keep leftover soup refrigerated and use within 2 days, reheating gently.

title: Potato and Leek Soup
summary: Leeks sweated slowly in butter without colour, simmered with floury potato and stock, then blended smooth and finished with cream and chives. Sweating leeks gently teaches flavour without browning, and the blender finishes the lesson with the safe handling of hot liquids.
equipment: heavy 4 quart (3.8 litre) pot with a lid
large bowl of cold water for washing leeks
circle of baking parchment the size of the pot (a cartouche)

ingredients.item: leeks, white and pale green parts only
ingredients.note: Keep the dark green tops for stock.

ingredients.item: floury potatoes, such as Russet or Maris Piper, peeled
ingredients.note: Cut into 3/4 inch (2 cm) dice.
Low salt if shop bought.

ingredients.item: bay leaf and a few thyme sprigs

mise: Trim, split and wash the leeks (step 1), then slice them.
Peel and dice the potatoes into even 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes; keep them in cold water.
Cut a parchment circle to fit inside the pot.
Warm the stock.
Snip the chives; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Clean and slice the leeks; dice the potatoes.
Sweat the leeks under parchment for 12 to 15 minutes.
Add potatoes, stock and herbs; simmer 15 to 20 minutes.
Remove herbs; blend until smooth; add cream.
Season, ladle into warm bowls, add chives.

steps.do: Cut off the root and the dark green tops of the leeks. Slice each leek in half lengthways. Hold each half under cold running water, root end up, and fan the layers apart with your thumb so the water washes out the grit between them. Then slice into half moons 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and swish them in the bowl of cold water; lift them out, leaving the grit at the bottom.
steps.look: Clean, pale green and white half moons; a little sand at the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Slicing unwashed leeks, so grit crunches in the finished soup.
steps.fix: Wash twice: once split, once sliced; lift them out of the water rather than pouring through a colander.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the pot over medium low heat. Add the drained leeks and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and stir to coat. Lay the parchment circle directly on the leeks, turn the heat to low and sweat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes.
steps.look: Leeks collapsing, soft and silky, glossy and still pale, smelling sweet; a quiet sizzle at most.
steps.mistake: Browning the leeks, which gives a bitter edge and a brown, muddy soup.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add 2 tbsp (30 ml) of water if anything starts to colour. Sweating is about softness without colour.

steps.do: Add the drained potatoes, the warm stock, bay and thyme. Bring to the boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 15 to 20 minutes, until the potatoes are completely soft.
steps.look: A potato cube crushes easily against the side of the pot with a spoon.
steps.mistake: Uneven potato pieces, some soft and some still hard when you blend.
steps.fix: Cut even cubes; test the largest piece before blending.

steps.do: Take out the bay leaf and thyme stalks. Blend the soup with a stick blender in the pot, keeping the blade fully submerged, for about 1 minute until smooth. If using an upright blender, fill it no more than half full, remove the centre cap of the lid, cover the hole with a folded towel and start on low.
steps.look: A smooth, pale, velvety soup with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Filling an upright blender to the top with hot soup and sealing the lid; steam pressure can blow it off and scald you.
steps.fix: Half full, vent the lid, towel over the top, start slow.

steps.do: Do not over-blend: as soon as it is smooth, stop. For a restaurant finish, push the soup through a fine sieve with the back of the ladle.
steps.look: Silky, flowing texture.
steps.mistake: Blending potato for minutes on high, which can make it gluey and elastic.
steps.fix: Blend briefly; if it has gone gluey, thin with a little hot stock and do not blend again.

steps.do: Return to low heat, stir in the cream and warm through without boiling. Thin with a little hot stock or water if needed; it should coat a spoon but pour easily. Season with the remaining salt and white pepper.
steps.look: A creamy, pale green-ivory soup that coats the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Under-salting; potato soaks up seasoning.
steps.fix: Taste and add salt a pinch at a time until the leek flavour comes forward.

steps.do: Ladle into the warm bowls, finish with a swirl of cream and a scattering of chives, and serve with crusty bread.
steps.look: A smooth surface with a white swirl and bright green chives.
steps.mistake: Serving in cold bowls so the soup cools fast and forms a skin.
steps.fix: Warm the bowls with hot water and dry them.

science: Sweating cooks vegetables gently in fat at a temperature low enough that their water evaporates slowly and they never reach the 300°F (150°C) or so needed for strong browning. Heat breaks down the leeks' cell walls and converts their sharp sulphur compounds into milder, sweet ones; covering them with parchment traps steam, which keeps the temperature down and softens them evenly. Floury potatoes have large starch granules that swell and burst when simmered, thickening the soup naturally. Blending breaks the cooked cells into a smooth suspension, but too much shearing ruptures the swollen starch granules, releasing sticky starch that makes the soup gluey, which is why potato soups are blended briefly. Cream adds fat that smooths the texture and carries flavour.
plating: Ladle the soup into warm, wide bowls. Drizzle a spoonful of cream in a spiral from the centre outwards and drag the tip of a knife through it once, then scatter chives over one side and add a turn of white pepper. Serve bread on a side plate.

pairing.drink: A dry, unoaked Chablis: crisp Chardonnay with enough body for cream and enough acidity to keep the soup bright.
pairing.brennans: Louis Michel Chablis 2022: an unoaked Chablis on the Brennan's list, clean and mineral beside a creamy soup.

variations: Vichyssoise: chill the soup thoroughly, adjust the seasoning cold and serve with chives.
Add a handful of watercress at the end before blending for a peppery green soup.
Top with crisp bacon pieces and a little grated Cheddar for a heartier bowl.
safety: Hot soup in a sealed blender can explode the lid: fill half full, vent and cover with a towel.
Keep the stick blender blade submerged to avoid splashing hot soup.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

title: Mercimek Çorbası (Red Lentil Soup)
summary: The red lentil soup of Turkish lunch counters: red lentils simmered with onion, carrot and pepper paste until they collapse, blended smooth and finished with a sizzling butter of paprika and mint and a squeeze of lemon. It adds pulses and a spiced butter to the puréed soup lesson.
skills: simmering red lentils until they collapse

ingredients.note: Split red lentils, which collapse when cooked.

ingredients.item: floury potato, peeled and diced (optional, for body)
Turkish red pepper paste (biber salçası) or tomato paste
light chicken or vegetable stock, or water

ingredients.note: Less if the stock is salted.

ingredients.item: Aleppo pepper (pul biber) or sweet paprika

mise: Rinse the lentils in the sieve until the water runs mostly clear; pick out any stones.
Chop the onion, carrot and potato into rough 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) pieces.
Warm the stock.
Measure the butter, Aleppo pepper and mint by the small saucepan.
Cut the lemon into wedges; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Rinse lentils; chop vegetables.
Sweat the onion and carrot for 8 to 10 minutes; add paste and cumin.
Add lentils, potato and stock; simmer 25 minutes until collapsed.
Blend smooth and season.
Make the paprika butter.
Ladle, drizzle the butter, serve with lemon.

steps.do: Rinse the lentils in the sieve under cold water, rubbing them with your fingers, until the water runs nearly clear. Pick out any small stones.
steps.look: Bright orange lentils; the water changing from cloudy to nearly clear.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rinse, which gives a scummy, dusty tasting soup.
steps.fix: Rinse thoroughly, and skim any foam during simmering.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the pot over medium low heat. Add the onion and carrot with a pinch of salt and sweat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until soft and sweet without browning.
steps.look: Onion translucent, carrot softened, everything glossy.
steps.mistake: Browning the onion, which darkens the soup and makes it bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; add a splash of water if anything sticks.

steps.do: Stir in the pepper paste and cumin and cook for 1 minute, stirring, until the paste darkens slightly and smells sweet and toasted.
steps.look: The oil turns red; a warm, spiced smell.
steps.mistake: Scorching the paste on the base of the pan.
steps.fix: Keep stirring and move on to the lentils within a minute.

steps.do: Add the lentils, potato and warm stock. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then lower the heat and simmer partly covered for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have completely collapsed.
steps.look: The lentils lose their shape and turn pale yellow-orange; the soup is thick and the potato soft.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so lentils settle and stick to the base.
steps.fix: Stir every 5 minutes and scrape the bottom; add hot water if it thickens too much.

steps.do: Blend the soup until completely smooth with the stick blender, blade submerged, or in batches in an upright blender filled no more than half full with the lid vented and covered with a towel.
steps.look: A velvety, golden orange soup.
steps.mistake: Over-thick soup that sits like porridge.
steps.fix: Thin with hot water or stock until it pours from the ladle like single cream.

steps.do: Season with salt, tasting as you go. Keep warm on low heat.
steps.look: A soup that tastes rounded, earthy and well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning; lentils need generous salt.
steps.fix: Add salt a pinch at a time and taste with a squeeze of lemon, which also brightens it.

steps.do: Just before serving, melt the butter in the small saucepan over medium heat until it foams. Take it off the heat and stir in the Aleppo pepper and mint; let them sizzle for 10 seconds until the butter turns brick red.
steps.look: Red, fragrant butter with the mint flakes floating in it.
steps.mistake: Adding the spices over the flame so they burn.
steps.fix: Always off the heat; the hot butter is enough to bloom them.

steps.do: Ladle the soup into warm bowls, drizzle the red butter over the surface and serve with lemon wedges and warm bread.
steps.look: A golden soup with streaks of glossy red butter and a scent of mint.
steps.mistake: Stirring the butter in, which hides it.
steps.fix: Drizzle it on top so each spoonful catches some.

science: Split red lentils have had their seed coats removed, so water reaches the starch directly and they cook quickly. As they simmer, starch granules swell and burst and the thin cell walls break down, so the lentils collapse into a purée even before blending, thickening the soup without flour or cream. Foam forms because proteins and saponins from the lentils trap air bubbles as they boil; skimming keeps the soup clean tasting. Blending finishes what simmering began, producing a smooth suspension. The finishing butter uses fat to carry flavour: the compounds that give paprika its colour and mint its scent dissolve in fat rather than water, so blooming them in butter and drizzling it over the top delivers a burst of aroma with each spoonful.
plating: Ladle the soup into warm bowls so the surface is smooth. Drizzle the red butter in a thin spiral or a few lines across the top, add a pinch of dried mint, set a lemon wedge on the rim, and serve warm flatbread alongside.

pairing.drink: Cold, salted ayran (a yoghurt drink) is the Turkish companion; for wine, a light, dry rosé with gentle fruit.

variations: Ezogelin soup: add a little bulgur and rice and leave it unblended, with more mint.
Add a pinch of chilli flakes and a spoon of tomato paste for a spicier, redder soup.
Serve with toasted cubes of bread fried in olive oil.
safety: Hot soup in a sealed blender can blow the lid off: fill half full, vent and cover with a towel.
Lentils stick and scorch; stir and scrape the base as they simmer.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; the soup thickens in the fridge, so thin it when reheating.
