title: Tomato Soup and Grilled Cheese
summary: A tomato soup with real depth from tomatoes, onion and garlic roasted until caramelised, blended smooth, served with a grilled cheese sandwich browned slowly in butter until the cheese melts completely. Two plain things done well teach roasting for flavour and the patient medium heat that browns bread evenly without burning.
skills: even browning of a sandwich over medium heat
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan or griddle
lid or a second pan to cover the sandwiches

ingredients.note: Out of season, use two 28 oz (794 g) cans of whole tomatoes, drained, roasted the same way.
Only if the tomatoes are tart.
Optional.

ingredients.item: white sandwich bread or sourdough, 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) slices

ingredients.note: For extra melt.

mise: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Halve the tomatoes, cut the onion into wedges, keep garlic unpeeled.
Grate both cheeses and toss them together.
Leave the butter out to soften fully.
Warm the stock; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Oven to 425°F (220°C); prepare the vegetables.
Roast the tomatoes, onion and garlic 35 to 45 minutes.
Simmer the roasted vegetables with stock for 10 minutes.
Blend the soup; build the sandwiches.
Cook the sandwiches on medium low, 3 to 4 minutes a side.
Ladle soup, cut sandwiches, serve together.

steps.do: Toss the tomatoes, onion and garlic with the olive oil and 3/4 tsp (4.5 g) salt on the baking sheet. Turn the tomatoes cut side up and spread everything in a single layer with space between pieces.
steps.look: An uncrowded single layer with the cut faces of the tomatoes glistening.
steps.mistake: Piling the tomatoes on top of each other, which makes them steam rather than roast.
steps.fix: Use two sheets if needed; space is what lets moisture escape and browning begin.

steps.do: Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 35 to 45 minutes, until the tomatoes have collapsed and their edges and the onion tips are charred and caramelised.
steps.look: Shrunken, wrinkled tomatoes with dark brown edges, sticky juices bubbling and darkening on the tray; a sweet, roasted smell.
steps.mistake: Taking them out pale and wet, which gives a soup that tastes like canned tomato.
steps.fix: Leave them until you see real colour at the edges; that colour is the depth of the soup.

steps.do: Squeeze the soft garlic from its skins. Scrape everything from the tray, juices and browned bits included, into the pot. Pour a splash of stock onto the hot tray, scrape up the remaining sticky bits and add them too. Add the rest of the stock and simmer 10 minutes.
steps.look: A thick red mixture with the browned juices dissolved in.
steps.mistake: Leaving the dark sticky juices on the tray.
steps.fix: Deglaze the tray with stock; those juices are concentrated flavour.

steps.do: Blend until smooth with the stick blender, or in an upright blender filled no more than half full with the lid vented and covered with a towel. Stir in the cream if using, taste and season with the remaining salt, pepper, and the sugar only if it is sharp. Tear in the basil.
steps.look: A smooth, brick red soup that coats a spoon and smells of roasted tomato and basil.
steps.mistake: A thin, watery soup.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered for a few minutes to reduce, or add less stock next time.

steps.do: Butter one side of every slice of bread right to the edges. On the board, lay four slices butter side down, pile the mixed cheese evenly over them to within 1/4 inch (6 mm) of the edge, and top with the other slices, butter side up.
steps.look: Even butter to the crust; cheese evenly spread, not heaped in the middle.
steps.mistake: Thick slices of cold cheese, which do not melt before the bread burns.
steps.fix: Grate the cheese; it melts quickly and evenly.

steps.do: Heat the frying pan over medium low heat for 2 minutes. Lay in the sandwiches, cover with a lid and cook 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is deep golden.
steps.look: A steady, quiet sizzle; when lifted, an even golden brown underside with no black patches.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the bread while the cheese inside stays cold and solid.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; patience gives even browning and fully melted cheese.

steps.do: Flip the sandwiches with the spatula, press very lightly once, cover again and cook another 3 minutes until the second side is golden and cheese is oozing at the edges.
steps.look: Both sides even golden brown, cheese melted and stretching when you lift a corner.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard and repeatedly, squashing the bread flat and squeezing out the cheese.
steps.fix: One light press only; the lid does the melting.

steps.do: Rest the sandwiches for 1 minute, then cut them diagonally with the bread knife. Serve with the hot soup in warm bowls.
steps.look: Crisp triangles with molten cheese at the cut, beside a bowl of deep red soup.
steps.mistake: Cutting immediately, so the cheese floods out.
steps.fix: One minute's rest lets the cheese set slightly.

science: Roasting at 425°F (220°C) evaporates the tomatoes' water and concentrates their sugars and acids, and once the surface dries it rises above the boiling point of water, where caramelisation and the Maillard reaction create new roasted, savoury flavours that simmering alone cannot. Deglazing the tray dissolves those browned compounds into the soup. A grilled cheese is a race between two processes: the bread's surface browning and the cheese's fat melting. Medium low heat and a lid slow the browning and trap heat so the cheese reaches its melting point, roughly 130°F to 150°F (54°C to 66°C) for Cheddar, before the bread burns. Grated cheese has more surface area, so it melts faster and more evenly. Butter spread on the outside browns the bread through its milk proteins and sugars.
plating: Serve the soup in a wide, warm bowl with a swirl of cream and a torn basil leaf. Cut the sandwich corner to corner and stand the triangles against each other on a side plate or the rim of a large plate, cut faces towards the guest so the melted cheese shows.

pairing.drink: A chilled, juicy Morgon from Beaujolais: red fruit for the tomato and soft tannin that does not fight the cheese.
pairing.brennans: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with Brabant Potatoes: the grilled cheese on Brennan's breakfast menu, a reminder that the simplest plate still deserves careful browning.

variations: Add a pinch of smoked paprika and a roasted red pepper to the tray for a smoky soup.
Grilled cheese with caramelised onions and Gruyère for a French onion style sandwich.
Use mayonnaise on the outside of the bread instead of butter for an even, crisp crust.
safety: Hot soup in a sealed blender can blow the lid: fill half full and vent.
Use oven gloves for the hot baking sheet; the juices on it can spit when stock is poured on.
Keep the pan handle turned inward and the heat moderate.

title: Welsh Rarebit
summary: A rich sauce of mature Cheddar melted into ale thickened with a little roux and seasoned with mustard and Worcestershire sauce, spread on toast and grilled until blistered and bubbling. A cheese sauce that must not split, finished under the overhead grill (broiler), is a first look at a sauce under heat.

ingredients.item: dark ale, stout or whole milk
ingredients.note: Ale gives a deeper, more bitter flavour.

ingredients.item: English mustard powder, or Dijon mustard

ingredients.note: Plus more to splash on top.
A strong, crumbly farmhouse Cheddar is best.
Optional, for a richer, puffier top.

ingredients.item: thick slices of sourdough or farmhouse bread

mise: Grate the cheese finely.
Separate the egg if using.
Measure the ale, mustard and Worcestershire.
Position the oven rack so the bread will sit 3 to 4 inches (7.5 to 10 cm) below the overhead grill.
Line the baking sheet with foil.

timeline.do: Grate cheese; prepare the grill rack.
Make the roux and whisk in the ale.
Melt in the cheese off the boil; season; add the yolk.
Toast the bread on both sides; heat the grill to high.
Spread the cheese to the edges; grill 2 to 4 minutes.
Splash with Worcestershire and serve.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the small saucepan over medium low heat. Add the flour and stir constantly with the wooden spoon for 2 minutes, without letting it colour.
steps.look: A smooth, bubbling paste that smells like baking biscuits, pale gold at most.
steps.mistake: Rushing this step, which leaves a raw flour taste.
steps.fix: Cook a full 2 minutes; turn the heat down if it starts to darken.

steps.do: Pour in the ale gradually, whisking constantly, and keep whisking until smooth and thickened, about 2 minutes. It will foam at first.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, glossy base that coats the whisk.
steps.mistake: Pouring the liquid in all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Add it in three goes, whisking each until smooth.

steps.do: Whisk in the mustard and Worcestershire. Turn the heat to its lowest. Add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring with the spoon until each melts before adding the next.
steps.look: The cheese melting into a thick, glossy, smooth sauce like warm paste.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil or adding the cheese over high heat, which makes the fat separate and the proteins seize into stringy, oily lumps.
steps.fix: Keep it barely warm. If it splits, take it off the heat and whisk in a tablespoon of cold ale or milk vigorously.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Season with cayenne and black pepper, then beat in the egg yolk if using. The mixture should be thick enough to spread without running.
steps.look: A thick, spreadable, smooth paste that holds peaks when lifted on a spoon.
steps.mistake: A loose sauce that runs off the toast under the grill.
steps.fix: Let it cool for 5 minutes; it firms up as it cools.

steps.do: Heat the overhead grill to high. Toast the bread lightly on both sides under the grill or in the toaster, then place the slices on the foil lined sheet.
steps.look: Crisp, golden toast that will support the heavy topping.
steps.mistake: Untoasted bread that goes soggy under the cheese.
steps.fix: Toast both sides first; the topping goes on firm, crisp bread.

steps.do: Spread the cheese mixture thickly over each slice, right to the edges and corners, so no bread is exposed to burn.
steps.look: An even layer about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick covering the whole surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving the edges bare, which char black under the grill.
steps.fix: Spread right to the crust.

steps.do: Grill 3 to 4 inches (7.5 to 10 cm) from the element for 2 to 4 minutes, watching constantly, until the top is bubbling, puffed and blistered with dark brown patches.
steps.look: A bubbling, golden surface with brown blisters and a smell of toasted cheese.
steps.mistake: Walking away; overhead grills burn food in seconds.
steps.fix: Stay at the oven door and turn the tray if one side browns faster.

steps.do: Lift out with oven gloves, splash a few drops of Worcestershire over each, cut in half and serve at once.
steps.look: Dark, glossy drops on a blistered golden surface, molten beneath.
steps.mistake: Serving straight onto a plate scalding hot to the mouth.
steps.fix: Let it stand 1 minute; molten cheese holds intense heat.

science: Cheese is a network of milk proteins holding fat and water. Heated gently, the network loosens and the cheese flows; overheated, the proteins tighten, squeezing out fat, and the sauce splits into stringy curds and oil. The roux helps: starch from the cooked flour swells in the ale and coats the fat droplets and proteins, keeping them apart, so the sauce stays smooth. Mustard adds its own emulsifying compounds and a sharpness that cuts the richness, while Worcestershire brings salt, acid and savoury depth. An egg yolk adds lecithin, another emulsifier, and protein that sets and puffs under the grill. The overhead grill works by radiant heat, browning the surface through the Maillard reaction within minutes without heating the toast through from below.
plating: Serve each rarebit on a warm plate, cut once on the diagonal and slightly separated so the molten centre shows. Add a small handful of dressed watercress or a few slices of tomato at the side, and a pot of mustard for those who want more.

pairing.drink: A malty English bitter or brown ale, the same beer used in the sauce, or a glass of tawny port.
pairing.brennans: Shells & Cheese: Brennan's side of Mimolette fondue, Grana Padano and Abita Amber is the same idea of cheese melted with beer.

variations: Buck rarebit: top each slice with a poached egg.
Add a spoonful of chutney beneath the cheese for sweetness.
Use half Lancashire and half Cheddar for a creamier, more crumbly flavour.
safety: The overhead grill is very hot: use oven gloves and keep your face back when opening the door.
Molten cheese holds heat and can burn the mouth; rest it for a minute.
The egg yolk cooks through under the grill; for vulnerable guests, leave it out.

title: Pasta e Fagioli
summary: The Italian bean and pasta soup built on a slowly sweated soffritto of onion, carrot and celery, simmered with beans, rosemary and a Parmigiano rind, part blended for body, with small pasta cooked directly in the pot. The soffritto is the Italian base of everything, and the pasta's starch finishes the soup.
skills: cooking pasta in the soup to thicken it
equipment: heavy 5 quart (4.7 litre) pot or casserole

ingredients.item: extra virgin olive oil, plus more to finish

ingredients.note: 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice.

ingredients.item: borlotti or cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
ingredients.note: Or 1 cup (200 g) dried, soaked and simmered until tender.
Plus hot water to adjust.
Optional, deeply savoury.

ingredients.us: 1 tsp salt, a few turns of pepper
ingredients.metric: 6 g salt, a few turns of pepper
ingredients.note: Adjust to the stock.
To serve.

mise: Dice the onion, carrot and celery into even 1/4 inch (6 mm) cubes.
Slice the garlic.
Drain and rinse the beans.
Warm the stock.
Grate the cheese; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Dice the soffritto vegetables.
Sweat the soffritto for 12 to 15 minutes.
Garlic, rosemary, chilli, tomato paste; then beans, stock and rind; simmer 20 minutes.
Blend a third; add the pasta and cook in the soup.
Season, finish with oil and cheese, serve at once.

steps.do: Dice the onion, carrot and celery into even 1/4 inch (6 mm) cubes: slice into planks, then sticks, then across into dice. Even sizes cook at the same rate.
steps.look: A neat pile of small cubes, all much the same size.
steps.mistake: Large, uneven chunks that stay crunchy while smaller pieces burn.
steps.fix: Take the time on the dice; it is the base of every Italian soup and sauce.

steps.do: Warm the olive oil in the pot over medium low heat. Add the soffritto with a pinch of salt and cook gently, stirring every couple of minutes, for 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: Vegetables soft, sweet smelling and translucent, the onion slumped, the carrot tender, the oil tinted gold; little or no browning.
steps.mistake: Cooking it fast on high heat for 3 minutes, which gives harsh, raw vegetables and little flavour.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and give it the full time; this slow base is what makes the soup taste of more than beans.

steps.do: Add the garlic, rosemary sprig and chilli and cook 1 minute. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until it darkens slightly.
steps.look: Fragrant garlic, rosemary sizzling, the paste turning from bright red to brick red.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and move on to the next step quickly.

steps.do: Add the beans, the warm stock and the Parmigiano rind. Bring to the boil, then lower the heat and simmer gently, partly covered, for 20 minutes.
steps.look: A gentle simmer, the beans softening further, the broth taking on colour and body.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which breaks up the beans into mush before the soup develops flavour.
steps.fix: Keep it at a lazy simmer.

steps.do: Remove the rosemary stalk and the rind. Scoop out about a third of the soup and blend it smooth, or blend briefly in the pot with the stick blender just to thicken, leaving most of the beans whole. Return it to the pot.
steps.look: A creamier, thicker broth with plenty of whole beans.
steps.mistake: Blending the whole pot into a smooth purée.
steps.fix: Blend a third only; you want body and texture.

steps.do: Bring the soup back to a simmer, add the pasta and cook directly in the soup, stirring often so it does not stick, for the pasta's packet time, usually 9 to 11 minutes. Add hot water a ladle at a time if it gets too thick.
steps.look: Pasta tender with a slight bite, the broth noticeably thicker and silkier from the pasta's starch.
steps.mistake: Not stirring, so the pasta sticks to the bottom of the pot.
steps.fix: Stir every minute, scraping the base.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt and pepper. The soup should be thick enough that a spoon almost stands in it, but still loose. Ladle into warm bowls, drizzle with good olive oil and top with grated cheese.
steps.look: A thick, glossy soup with whole beans and pasta, a golden thread of oil and white cheese on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving it to stand, as the pasta keeps drinking the broth until the soup turns solid.
steps.fix: Serve at once; if making ahead, cook the pasta separately and add it to each bowl.

science: A soffritto builds flavour by slowly softening onion, carrot and celery in oil. Gentle heat breaks down cell walls, releasing sugars and converting the onion's sharp sulphur compounds into sweeter ones, while the fat dissolves aroma compounds and carries them through the soup. Tomato paste, fried briefly, caramelises and adds concentrated savoury depth. A Parmigiano rind contributes glutamates and some protein and fat as it softens in the simmering broth. Pasta cooked directly in the soup releases starch from its surface into the liquid; those starch molecules swell and thicken the broth into a silky body, which is why pasta boiled separately leaves a thinner soup. Blending some beans adds their broken starch for further body.
plating: Ladle into warm, wide bowls so the pasta and beans sit evenly. Finish with a generous thread of peppery olive oil in a spiral, a mound of finely grated Parmigiano in the centre, a turn of black pepper and a few rosemary needles.

pairing.drink: A young Chianti Classico: cherry fruit and fresh acidity, with gentle tannin for beans and cheese.
pairing.brennans: Fattoria di Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022: a Tuscan red from the Brennan's list made for a bowl of beans and pasta.

variations: Add 2 oz (55 g) of diced pancetta to the soffritto for a richer, smoky soup.
Use dried borlotti beans simmered from scratch with sage and garlic, and use their cooking liquid as part of the stock.
Make it greener with a handful of chopped cavolo nero added with the pasta.
safety: Stir starchy soups often; they stick and can scorch.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; the pasta will absorb liquid, so add water when reheating.

title: Spaghetti Aglio, Olio e Peperoncino
summary: Spaghetti tossed with olive oil in which sliced garlic has turned slowly golden, dried chilli and parsley, bound into a glossy sauce with starchy pasta water. equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) frying pan with sloping sides
sharp paring knife or chef's knife

ingredients.note: A bronze-cut brand releases more starch.
Less water than usual makes starchier pasta water.
About 1 percent of the water's weight.
Plus a little to finish.

ingredients.item: garlic cloves, thinly and evenly sliced
dried chilli flakes, or 1 to 2 whole dried peperoncini crumbled

mise: Bring the water to the boil in the pot; weigh the salt.
Peel the garlic and slice it as thinly and evenly as you can, about 1/16 inch (2 mm).
Chop the parsley.
Measure the oil and chilli.
Have the tongs and the jug ready by the pasta pot; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Water on to boil; slice garlic; chop parsley.
Salt the water; pasta in; set a timer 2 minutes short of the packet time.
Garlic into cold oil; heat gently to pale gold over 5 to 7 minutes.
Chilli in; stop the garlic with a ladle of pasta water.
Move the pasta to the pan; toss with pasta water until glossy.
Parsley, a thread of oil, serve at once.

steps.do: When the water is at a rolling boil, add the 4 tsp (20 g) salt and stir. Taste the water once it dissolves: it should taste pleasantly salty, like a well seasoned broth, not like the sea.
steps.look: Water boiling hard; a clear, salty taste.
steps.mistake: Unsalted water, which leaves the pasta bland however good the sauce.
steps.fix: Weigh the salt at about 1 percent of the water; the pasta absorbs seasoning only while it cooks.

steps.do: Add the spaghetti, pushing it under as it softens, and stir for the first minute so it does not stick. Set a timer for 2 minutes less than the packet time.
steps.look: Strands separate and moving freely in the boiling water.
steps.mistake: Breaking the spaghetti, or not stirring so it clumps.
steps.fix: Stir with tongs during the first minute, when sticking happens.

steps.do: Meanwhile put the olive oil and sliced garlic into the cold frying pan, then set it over medium low heat. Let the garlic sizzle gently, swirling the pan often, for 5 to 7 minutes.
steps.look: Small, steady bubbles around the garlic; it turns from white to pale straw and then light gold, smelling sweet and nutty.
steps.mistake: Adding garlic to hot oil, where it browns in seconds and turns bitter.
steps.fix: Start cold and go slowly; if any slices turn dark brown, the oil is ruined, so start again.

steps.do: When the garlic is pale gold, add the chilli flakes, swirl for 10 seconds, then immediately add a ladle, about 1/2 cup (120 ml), of the boiling pasta water to the pan. It will sputter.
steps.look: The sizzle stops at once; the oil and water bubble together into a cloudy liquid.
steps.mistake: Waiting until the garlic looks perfectly golden, by which time carryover heat takes it too far.
steps.fix: Stop it a shade lighter than you want; the hot oil keeps cooking it.

steps.do: When the timer goes, lift the spaghetti out of the pot with tongs straight into the frying pan, letting some water cling to it. Keep the pot of pasta water.
steps.look: Pasta still a little firm in the centre, with a thin white core when one strand is bitten.
steps.mistake: Draining the pasta in a colander and losing all the starchy water.
steps.fix: Transfer with tongs; keep the cooking water until the dish is served.

steps.do: Turn the heat under the frying pan to medium high. Toss the pasta constantly with tongs, lifting and turning, adding pasta water a splash at a time, for 2 to 3 minutes until the pasta is al dente and the sauce turns creamy and coats every strand.
steps.look: A glossy, slightly cloudy sauce clinging to the spaghetti, with no pool of oil left in the pan.
steps.mistake: Not tossing vigorously, so the oil stays separate and the pasta is greasy.
steps.fix: Keep tossing and add a little more pasta water; the starch and agitation together make the emulsion.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, add the parsley and a thread of fresh olive oil and toss once more. Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed.
steps.look: Glossy pasta flecked with gold garlic, red chilli and green parsley.
steps.mistake: The sauce tightening and drying out while you plate.
steps.fix: Loosen with one more splash of pasta water just before serving.

steps.do: Twist each portion into a nest with the tongs, lift into a warm bowl, spoon over any sauce and garlic left in the pan and serve immediately.
steps.look: A neat, glossy nest with the garlic slices on top.
steps.mistake: Waiting, as the sauce soaks in and the pasta goes dry.
steps.fix: Eat it the moment it is ready; this is a dish that waits for no one.

science: Salting the water at about 1 percent seasons the pasta from within, because the dry pasta absorbs salty water as its starch swells. Garlic browns fast because of its sugars; started in cold oil, it heats gradually, its sharp compounds mellow and it turns golden evenly before the outsides scorch. Above deep gold, its sugars burn and turn bitter, which is why water is added to stop the frying. The sauce is an emulsion: oil and water do not mix on their own, but starch released by the pasta into its cooking water coats tiny oil droplets and keeps them suspended. Tossing vigorously breaks the oil into droplets, and using less cooking water concentrates the starch, producing a creamy sauce with no cream.
plating: Use warm, shallow bowls. Twirl the spaghetti around a carving fork or tongs into a tall nest, set it in the centre, spoon the garlic slices and chilli from the pan over the top, and finish with a little chopped parsley and a final thread of olive oil.

pairing.drink: A crisp, dry Italian white such as Vermentino or Verdicchio: citrus and almond notes for garlic and oil.

variations: Add a few anchovy fillets to the oil with the garlic; they melt into the sauce.
Finish with toasted breadcrumbs fried in olive oil for crunch, the southern Italian way.
Add a handful of chopped rocket or lemon zest with the parsley.
safety: Pasta water spits when it hits hot oil; add it away from you.
Move pasta from boiling water with long tongs and keep your arm clear of the steam.
Keep children away from the stove when moving pots of boiling water.

title: Quesadillas with Pico de Gallo
summary: Corn tortillas folded around melting cheese and crisped on a dry comal, served with pico de gallo, a fresh hand-cut salsa of tomato, onion, chilli, coriander and lime, and a guacamole mashed by hand. A fresh salsa cut by hand and a tortilla crisped on a dry pan bring knife work and heat together.
skills: melting cheese on a dry comal
equipment: molcajete or a bowl and a fork for the guacamole
cast iron pan, griddle or comal, 10 to 12 inches (25 to 30 cm)

ingredients.note: Firm but ripe.
Divided between salsa and guacamole.
Seeded for milder heat.
Divided.
About 4 tbsp (60 ml) juice.
They yield to gentle pressure.
Or 4 large flour tortillas.

ingredients.item: Oaxaca cheese or Monterey Jack, grated or pulled into threads
epazote or a few coriander leaves, for the filling
ingredients.note: Optional.

mise: Dice the onion; rinse half of it in the sieve under cold water and shake dry.
Seed and mince the chillies.
Chop the coriander.
Halve the limes.
Grate or pull apart the cheese.
Warm the pan over medium heat.

timeline.do: Knife work: onion, chillies, coriander, tomatoes.
Mix the pico de gallo; leave 10 minutes for the flavours to meet.
Mash the guacamole.
Cook the quesadillas in batches, 2 to 3 minutes a side.
Serve hot with pico and guacamole.

steps.do: Dice the onion finely, about 1/8 inch (3 mm). Put half in the sieve and rinse under cold running water for 20 seconds, then shake dry. This removes the harsh bite while keeping the crunch.
steps.look: Small, even pieces of onion; the rinsed onion tastes sweet and crisp, not burning.
steps.mistake: Raw, unrinsed onion that overpowers a fresh salsa.
steps.fix: Rinse it; this is a classic Mexican habit for raw salsas.

steps.do: Core the tomatoes, cut into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, then strips, then dice. Keep some seeds for juiciness but discard watery pulp if the tomatoes are very wet.
steps.look: Even red cubes with clean edges.
steps.mistake: Mashing soft tomatoes into pulp with a blunt knife.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife and a gentle sawing stroke.

steps.do: In a bowl, combine the tomatoes, rinsed onion, half the chilli, half the coriander, the juice of 1 lime and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt. Stir and leave for 10 minutes, then taste and adjust with more chilli, lime or salt.
steps.look: A bright, juicy salsa: red, white and green, glistening.
steps.mistake: Making it hours ahead, so it turns watery and loses its crunch.
steps.fix: Make it within half an hour of eating; drain off excess liquid before serving.

steps.do: For the guacamole, halve the avocados, remove the stones and scoop the flesh into the molcajete or bowl. First crush the remaining onion, chilli and a pinch of salt into a rough paste, then add the avocado and mash with a fork or pestle, leaving some chunks. Stir in the remaining coriander, lime juice to taste and salt.
steps.look: A creamy guacamole with small chunks of avocado, flecked green and white.
steps.mistake: Blending to a smooth purée, which loses the texture.
steps.fix: Mash by hand only, and leave some pieces.

steps.do: Press a piece of cling film directly onto the guacamole's surface if it must wait.
steps.look: Bright green guacamole with no brown surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered so the top browns.
steps.fix: Cover tightly against the surface; scrape off any brown layer before serving.

steps.do: Heat the dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes. Warm a tortilla for 15 seconds each side until pliable. Sprinkle 1/4 cup (about 28 g) of cheese over one half, add a leaf of epazote if using, and fold the tortilla over.
steps.look: A soft tortilla folding without cracking, cheese sitting on one half.
steps.mistake: Folding a cold, stiff corn tortilla, which cracks.
steps.fix: Warm each tortilla briefly first, then fill on the pan.

steps.do: Cook the folded quesadilla for 2 to 3 minutes per side, pressing lightly once with the spatula, until the tortilla is crisp with brown spots and the cheese has melted completely. Cook two or three at a time.
steps.look: Crisp, blistered tortilla with dark freckles; cheese oozing at the edge.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the tortilla before the cheese melts.
steps.fix: Medium heat and patience; cover the pan for 30 seconds to speed the melting if needed.

steps.do: Serve the quesadillas hot, two per person, cut in half if you like, with the pico de gallo and guacamole on the side.
steps.look: Crisp golden half-moons with molten cheese, and bowls of fresh salsa and guacamole.
steps.mistake: Stacking hot quesadillas, so they steam and turn soft.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the pan or keep warm in a single layer in a low oven.

science: A dry comal or cast iron pan cooks by direct contact, so the tortilla's surface dries, crisps and browns through the Maillard reaction, while the trapped heat inside the fold melts the cheese. Oaxaca cheese and Monterey Jack melt smoothly because their moisture and fat let the proteins relax and flow at moderate heat. Rinsing raw onion washes away the sulphur compounds released when it is cut, softening its bite. Salt and lime draw juice from the tomatoes in pico de gallo by osmosis, which is why it becomes juicier as it sits and soggy if left too long. Avocado browns when its cut cells meet oxygen, as enzymes oxidise phenolic compounds; lime juice slows this and cling film blocks the air.
plating: Cut each quesadilla into two wedges and lean them against each other on a warm plate, cut edges showing the melted cheese. Spoon the pico de gallo into one small bowl and the guacamole into another, garnish both with a coriander sprig and set a lime wedge on the plate.

pairing.drink: A classic Margarita on the rocks with a salted rim: lime and salt echo the salsa and refresh after melted cheese.

variations: Quesadillas de flor de calabaza: add sautéed courgette flowers and a little onion with the cheese.
Mushroom and chilli quesadillas: fill with sautéed mushrooms, garlic and strips of roasted poblano.
Make them with fresh masa: press masa into rounds, fill and fold, and cook on the comal, the Mexico City way.
safety: Wash hands after handling chillies and keep them away from your eyes.
Hold avocados on the board, not in your hand, when removing the stone: tap the knife into it on the board or scoop it out with a spoon.
A dry cast iron pan stays very hot; handle with a cloth.

title: Arepas Reina Pepiada
summary: Venezuelan corn cakes made from precooked white corn flour, shaped by hand, griddled until crusted and finished in the oven, then split and stuffed with reina pepiada, a filling of poached shredded chicken, avocado, mayonnaise, coriander and lime. The arepa is the simplest dough in the course and a lesson in hydration and shaping by hand.
equipment: cast iron pan or griddle, 10 to 12 inches (25 to 30 cm)
small bowl of water for your hands

ingredients.item: bay leaf and half an onion, for poaching
precooked white corn flour (masarepa), such as P.A.N.
ingredients.note: Not masa harina, which will not work.
You may need a little more or less.

ingredients.item: salt and white pepper, for the filling

mise: Put the chicken in the saucepan with the bay, onion, salt and cold water to cover by 1 inch (2.5 cm).
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Measure the warm water with a thermometer or by feel: comfortably warm on the wrist.
Halve the avocado; chop coriander; slice spring onions; squeeze the lime.
Set a bowl of water by the board for wetting your hands.

timeline.do: Poach the chicken; cool it in its liquid.
Mix the dough; rest 5 minutes; knead and shape.
Griddle the arepas about 6 minutes a side.
Into the oven for 12 to 15 minutes; shred chicken and make the filling.
Split the hot arepas.
Fill generously and serve.

steps.do: Bring the chicken and its water slowly to a bare simmer over medium heat, then turn it down so the water just trembles. Poach for 15 to 18 minutes, until the thickest part reads 165°F (74°C). Let the chicken cool in the liquid for 15 minutes.
steps.look: Water barely moving; chicken white throughout with clear juices when cut at the thickest point.
steps.mistake: Boiling the chicken hard, which makes it dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Keep the water at a tremble; check the temperature rather than guessing.

steps.do: Whisk the salt into the warm water in the large bowl. Rain in the masarepa with one hand while stirring with the other, so no lumps form. Leave it for 5 minutes.
steps.look: It starts as a loose batter and swells into a soft dough that holds a fingerprint.
steps.mistake: Kneading straight away before the flour has absorbed the water, which gives a dough that cracks and cooks dense.
steps.fix: Let it rest the full 5 minutes; the rest is when the flour hydrates.

steps.do: With wet hands, knead the dough in the bowl for 2 minutes until smooth and soft, like play dough. Pinch off a piece and flatten it: if the edge cracks, work in water a tablespoon at a time; if it sticks badly, add a little masarepa.
steps.look: A smooth, soft dough whose edges stay smooth when pressed flat.
steps.mistake: A dry dough that cracks at the rim, which splits on the griddle and never forms the steam pocket that lets it open.
steps.fix: Add water until the edge of a pressed disc stays smooth.

steps.do: Divide into 6 equal balls, each about 1/2 cup (150 g). Roll each into a smooth ball between wet palms, then press and turn it into a disc about 3 1/2 inches (9 cm) across and 5/8 inch (1.5 cm) thick, smoothing any cracks at the edges with a wet finger.
steps.look: Even, round discs with smooth tops and smooth, crack-free sides.
steps.mistake: Discs of different thicknesses, which cook unevenly.
steps.fix: Weigh the balls, and press each to the same thickness, checking with a ruler at first.

steps.do: Heat the cast iron pan over medium heat and brush with oil. Cook the arepas, leaving space between them, for about 6 minutes per side, until each face is matte, freckled with brown spots and releases easily.
steps.look: A dry, crusted surface with golden brown patches; they lift cleanly with a spatula.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, which tears the surface; or heat too high, which burns the outside before a crust forms.
steps.fix: Wait until they release on their own; adjust to medium low if they brown fast.

steps.do: Move the arepas to the baking sheet and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 12 to 15 minutes, until they sound hollow when tapped and puff slightly.
steps.look: Slightly puffed with a firm crust; a hollow sound when you tap the underside.
steps.mistake: Skipping the oven, so the centre stays raw and doughy.
steps.fix: Bake until they sound hollow; this is what forms the pocket inside.

steps.do: While they bake, shred the chicken into long threads with two forks. Mash the avocado with the mayonnaise and lime juice until smooth, then fold in the chicken, coriander and spring onion. Season with salt and white pepper until it tastes slightly over-seasoned, because it will be eaten inside plain corn.
steps.look: A creamy, pale green filling holding plenty of chicken threads.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning the filling, which then tastes flat inside the arepa.
steps.fix: Season boldly and taste again.

steps.do: Hold each hot arepa in a towel and split it around its edge with the serrated knife, leaving a hinge on one side like a pitta. Scrape out a little of the soft dough inside if it is thick, then stuff generously with the filling and serve.
steps.look: A golden, crusted arepa open like a book, overflowing with green filling.
steps.mistake: Burning your fingers on the steam inside.
steps.fix: Hold it in a folded towel and open it away from your face.

science: Masarepa is corn that has been cooked, dried and ground, so its starch is already gelatinised and it absorbs water readily without further cooking. It needs well over twice its weight in water, and the rest gives it time to soak in; a dough that has not hydrated properly cracks and seals into a hard crust before steam can build inside. On the griddle, the surface dries and browns through the Maillard reaction, forming a crust. In the oven, water inside the arepa turns to steam, which is trapped by that crust and pushes the dough apart into a pocket. Masa harina is different: it is nixtamalised with lime, has a different starch structure and flavour, and will not behave the same way.
plating: Stand the stuffed arepas upright, hinge down, side by side on a board or plate so the green filling shows at the opening. Add a small bowl of extra filling, a lime wedge and a few coriander sprigs.

pairing.drink: A rum Daiquiri of white rum, lime and sugar: crisp, sour and refreshing beside creamy avocado and corn.

variations: Arepa de pabellón: fill with shredded beef, black beans, fried plantain and white cheese.
Arepa con queso: knead 1/2 cup (50 g) grated white cheese into the dough and fill with more cheese and butter.
Arepa dómino: fill with black beans and crumbled white cheese.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; check with a thermometer.
Wash hands, board and knife after handling raw chicken.
Steam inside a hot arepa can scald; split it in a towel and away from your face.
Refrigerate the filling and use within 1 day, as it contains mayonnaise and chicken.

title: Dal Tadka
summary: Yellow lentils simmered with turmeric until they collapse into a creamy dal, then finished at the table with a tadka of whole spices, garlic and curry leaves bloomed in sizzling ghee. Tadka teaches the cook to hear spices bloom in hot fat, a technique that runs through Indian cooking.
skills: pouring the tadka at the end
equipment: small frying pan or tadka pan

ingredients.item: toor dal (split pigeon peas) or a mix of toor and red lentils
ingredients.note: Red lentils alone cook faster, in 20 minutes.
Or neutral oil with a knob of butter.
Optional.
Optional; it smells strong raw and mellows in fat.
Optional; from Indian grocers.

mise: Rinse the dal in several changes of water until clear; soak 30 minutes if using toor dal.
Chop the tomato, grate the ginger, slice the garlic.
Measure all the tadka spices into a small dish next to the stove, in the order they go in.
Pat the curry leaves dry; wet leaves spit violently.
Chop the coriander; squeeze the lemon.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the toor dal.
Simmer dal with water and turmeric 35 to 40 minutes.
Whisk the dal; add salt, tomato, ginger; simmer 5 minutes.
Make the tadka.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal at the table.

steps.do: Rinse the dal in a bowl, rubbing it between your fingers and pouring off the cloudy water, four or five times until the water runs nearly clear. Soak toor dal in fresh water for 30 minutes, then drain.
steps.look: Clean, bright yellow lentils and clear rinsing water.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rinse, so the dal foams heavily and tastes dusty.
steps.fix: Rinse well and skim foam as it cooks.

steps.do: Put the dal, 4 cups (950 ml) water and turmeric in the pot. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam, then simmer partly covered for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the lentils are completely soft and collapsing.
steps.look: Lentils breaking apart into a thick, creamy, golden mixture.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil hard with the lid on, which foams over.
steps.fix: Keep the lid ajar and the heat low; add hot water if it gets too thick.

steps.do: Whisk the dal vigorously for 30 seconds to break up the lentils into a creamy texture. Add the salt, tomato and ginger and simmer 5 minutes more. Adjust with hot water until it flows like a thick soup.
steps.look: A smooth, pourable dal, golden yellow, with soft pieces of tomato.
steps.mistake: A stiff, pasty dal.
steps.fix: Thin with hot water; dal thickens as it cools.

steps.do: For the tadka, heat the ghee in the small pan over medium high heat until it shimmers. Add the mustard seeds first: they should crackle and pop within seconds. Then add the cumin seeds.
steps.look: Mustard seeds popping and jumping; cumin sizzling and darkening a shade within 10 to 15 seconds, smelling toasty.
steps.mistake: Ghee not hot enough, so the seeds sit and soak up fat without blooming.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer; drop in one cumin seed as a test, and when it sizzles at once, the fat is ready.

steps.do: Add the dried chillies, asafoetida and garlic, and stir for 30 to 60 seconds until the garlic is golden bronze.
steps.look: Garlic edges turning golden, the chillies darkening, a nutty smell.
steps.mistake: Taking the garlic to dark brown, which tastes bitter; the difference is a few seconds.
steps.fix: Lift the pan off the heat the moment the garlic is golden; it keeps cooking in the hot ghee.

steps.do: Off the heat, add the curry leaves, standing back as they crackle, then stir in the Kashmiri chilli powder for 5 seconds.
steps.look: Curry leaves turning glossy and crisp, the ghee stained red.
steps.mistake: Adding the chilli powder over high heat, where it burns in seconds.
steps.fix: Always off the heat for ground spices.

steps.do: Pour the dal into a warm serving bowl. Pour the sizzling tadka over the surface, listening to it hiss, then scatter coriander and add a squeeze of lemon. Serve with rice or chapatis.
steps.look: Red-gold ghee pooling over yellow dal, spices and leaves on top, a loud sizzle on contact.
steps.mistake: Stirring the tadka into the pot long before serving, where its aroma fades.
steps.fix: Add it at the last moment, ideally at the table.

science: Many of the aroma compounds in cumin, mustard, chilli and garlic dissolve in fat rather than water. Heating whole spices in hot ghee, around 325°F to 350°F (160°C to 175°C), releases those compounds into the fat and creates new toasted flavours through the Maillard reaction, while the seeds' moisture flashes to steam, which is the crackle you hear. Simmered for long in a watery dal, these aromas would evaporate or dull, so the tadka goes on last for maximum impact. Ghee has had its milk solids and water removed, so it can be heated well above butter's burning point. Lentils collapse because simmering dissolves the pectin binding their cells and swells their starch, so a vigorous whisk turns them creamy.
plating: Pour the dal into a wide, warm bowl and smooth the surface. Pour the tadka over the centre so the ghee spreads in a red-gold pool with the spices, chillies and curry leaves visible on top. Scatter coriander around the edge and serve rice in a separate bowl.

pairing.drink: A salted lassi, or an Alsace Pinot Gris whose spicy richness and soft fruit suit cumin, garlic and ghee.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: an Alsace Pinot Gris on the Brennan's list, rich enough for ghee and spice.

variations: Dal fry: cook onion, tomato, ginger, garlic and spices first and stir the cooked dal into them before a lighter tadka.
Add a handful of spinach to the dal for the last 3 minutes for dal palak.
Use whole spices such as cloves and cinnamon in the tadka for a deeper, warmer flavour.
safety: Hot ghee is far hotter than boiling water; keep the tadka pan handle turned in and pour slowly.
Curry leaves spit violently in hot fat: dry them and add them off the heat while standing back.
Lentils foam and boil over; keep the lid ajar and the heat moderate.

title: Mujadara
summary: The Levantine staple of lentils and rice cooked together with cumin and crowned with onions fried slowly to deep mahogany, half folded through and half kept crisp on top, served with yoghurt and a chopped salad. Patiently browned onions are the whole flavour of this dish and the cook's first long lesson in caramelising.
equipment: wide 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
heavy 4 quart (3.8 litre) pot with a tight lid

ingredients.note: Not red lentils, which collapse.
Rinsed and soaked 15 minutes.

ingredients.item: large onions, halved and thinly sliced
ingredients.note: Slice 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick.
Mujadara needs plenty.

ingredients.item: salad: cucumber, tomato, parsley, lemon, olive oil
ingredients.us: 1 cucumber, 2 tomatoes, a handful of parsley, 1/2 lemon
ingredients.metric: about 250 g cucumber, 250 g tomato, 10 g parsley, 1/2 lemon
ingredients.note: Diced and dressed.

mise: Pick over and rinse the lentils.
Rinse the rice until clear and soak it 15 minutes; drain.
Slice the onions evenly; this is the longest job.
Measure the spices and salt.
Dice the salad vegetables and keep them separate until serving.

timeline.do: Slice onions; rinse lentils and rice.
Fry the onions low and slow, 30 to 40 minutes.
Simmer the lentils 12 to 15 minutes in the pot.
Add rice, spices, half the onions, water; cover and cook 15 to 18 minutes.
Rest off the heat, lid on, 10 minutes; dress the salad.
Fluff, top with crisp onions, serve with yoghurt and salad.

steps.do: Halve the onions through the root, peel and slice them evenly into half moons 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Even slices brown evenly.
steps.look: A large pile of thin, even crescents.
steps.mistake: Uneven slices, so thin ones burn while thick ones stay pale.
steps.fix: Take care with the knife or use a mandoline with its guard.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt. They will fill the pan; stir to coat them in oil. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, as they collapse.
steps.look: Onions wilting and shrinking to half their volume, turning translucent, releasing steam.
steps.mistake: A small pan that crowds the onions, so they stew instead of browning.
steps.fix: Use the widest pan you have, or cook in two pans.

steps.do: Turn the heat to medium low and keep cooking for another 20 to 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the brown film from the pan into the onions, until they are deep mahogany brown and some are crisp.
steps.look: Onions dark reddish brown, sweet and nutty smelling, some edges crisp; the volume a fraction of where you started.
steps.mistake: Stopping at golden, which gives none of the deep flavour the dish depends on.
steps.fix: Keep going; if they catch, add a spoonful of water and scrape. Mahogany, not blond.

steps.do: With the slotted spoon, lift half the onions onto paper towel and spread them out: they will crisp as they cool. Leave the rest, and the oil, in the pan.
steps.look: Dark onions crisping on the paper towel; half still in the flavoured oil.
steps.mistake: Piling the onions in a heap on the paper, so they steam soft.
steps.fix: Spread them thinly; they crisp as they cool.

steps.do: Meanwhile, put the lentils in the pot with 3 cups (720 ml) water, bring to the boil and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, until just tender but still holding their shape. Do not drain.
steps.look: Lentils softening but still whole, with a bite in the centre; water partly absorbed.
steps.mistake: Cooking the lentils fully before the rice goes in, so they turn to mush.
steps.fix: Stop when they are three quarters cooked; they finish with the rice.

steps.do: Add the drained rice, cumin, allspice, pepper, remaining 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the onions left in the frying pan with their oil. Add enough water to cover by about 3/4 inch (2 cm). Bring to the boil, then cover tightly, turn to the lowest heat and cook for 15 to 18 minutes.
steps.look: When you check at the end, no liquid left, small steam holes on the surface and the rice tender.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking, which lets the steam out so the rice stays hard.
steps.fix: Trust the time; check only at the end.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat, lay a clean tea towel under the lid and rest for 10 minutes. Then fluff gently with a fork.
steps.look: Fluffy rice and lentils, separate and glossy, flecked with brown onion.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the rice and makes it gluey.
steps.fix: Fluff gently with a fork, lifting from the bottom.

steps.do: Spoon onto a platter and pile the crisp onions on top. Serve warm or at room temperature with yoghurt and the chopped salad dressed with lemon, olive oil and salt.
steps.look: A brown-speckled mound crowned with a tangle of dark, crisp onions, cool white yoghurt beside.
steps.mistake: Adding the crisp onions to the hot pot, where they soften.
steps.fix: Top at the last moment.

science: Slowly browning onions is mostly caramelisation and the Maillard reaction working together. First the onions release their water, which must evaporate before their temperature can rise much above 212°F (100°C). Then their sugars, chiefly fructose and glucose, begin to break down and combine with amino acids into hundreds of new compounds: sweet, nutty, toasty and slightly bitter, with deep brown colour. Low, steady heat lets this happen evenly through the onion rather than burning the surface. Spread thin after frying, the onions lose their remaining surface steam and crisp as they cool. Lentils and rice can share a pot because the lentils are given a head start, so both finish tender at the same moment.
plating: Mound the mujadara on a wide platter, flattening the top slightly. Pile the crisp onions in a tall heap in the centre, spoon yoghurt into a bowl beside it with a thread of olive oil and a pinch of cumin, and serve the salad in another bowl.

pairing.drink: A glass of earthy, aged Lebanese red, whose dried fruit and spice suit lentils and browned onion.
pairing.brennans: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003: the famous Lebanese red on the Brennan's list, a natural partner for this Levantine dish.

variations: Mujadara with bulgur: use coarse bulgur instead of rice, as is done in parts of Syria and Palestine.
Masoor mujadara: use small black beluga lentils, which keep their shape beautifully.
Add a pinch of cinnamon with the spices and serve with a garlic yoghurt.
safety: Hot oil spatters as the onions release water; stir with a long spoon.
A mandoline slices fingers as easily as onions: always use its guard.
Cool leftover rice dishes quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

title: Red Red (Black-Eyed Bean Stew with Plantain)
summary: Ghana's black-eyed bean stew cooked in red palm oil with onion, ginger, chilli and tomato, served with sweet, ripe plantain shallow fried until caramelised and a sprinkle of gari. It adds the shallow frying of fruit to the bean lesson and shows how ripeness changes the way a plantain cooks.
skills: cooking beans in a palm oil tomato base
equipment: 10 inch (25 cm) heavy frying pan for plantains

ingredients.note: Or two 15 oz (425 g) cans, drained.

ingredients.item: half an onion, for the beans
ground dried chilli, or 1 Scotch bonnet left whole
ingredients.note: Start low and build.

ingredients.item: very ripe plantains, skins heavily black spotted
ingredients.note: Ripe plantains are sweet; yellow ones are starchy.

ingredients.item: groundnut or other neutral oil, for frying
ingredients.note: About 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) deep in the pan.
To sprinkle; optional.

mise: The night before, soak the beans.
Drain and rinse them; slice onions, grate ginger, crush garlic.
Chop the tomatoes; measure paste and chilli.
Peel the plantains and cut on a sharp diagonal into slices 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick; sprinkle with a pinch of salt.
Line a plate with paper towel.

timeline.do: Soak the beans.
Simmer the beans with half an onion until tender, 40 to 60 minutes.
Warm palm oil; soften onions; fry ginger, garlic, paste and chilli.
Add tomatoes and beans; simmer to a thick stew.
Fry the plantains in batches.
Serve the stew with plantains and gari.

steps.do: Put the drained beans and half onion in the pot with fresh unsalted water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer gently for 40 to 60 minutes until the skins loosen and a bean crushes easily but holds its shape. Drain, keeping 1 cup (240 ml) of liquid; discard the onion.
steps.look: Creamy, tender beans, mostly whole.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which splits the beans into mush.
steps.fix: Keep a gentle simmer; check from 35 minutes.

steps.do: Warm the palm oil in the wide saucepan over medium heat only until it melts, turns clear and runs bright orange, well short of smoking.
steps.look: Clear, glowing orange oil with a fruity smell.
steps.mistake: Heating palm oil to smoking, which bleaches its colour and turns its flavour acrid.
steps.fix: Keep to medium; if it smokes, let it cool before continuing.

steps.do: Add the sliced onions with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the ginger and garlic and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, glossy onions stained orange, a fragrant smell of ginger.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions hard, which turns the stew bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; soft and sweet is the aim.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato paste and chilli and fry, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until the paste darkens to brick red and oil pools at the edge of the pan. Add the chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they break down.
steps.look: A deep red, thick sauce with red oil separating at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding too much chilli at once.
steps.fix: Start with 1 tsp (2 g); you can add more after tasting, never less.

steps.do: Fold in the beans with enough reserved liquid to loosen, and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Simmer gently for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick and every bean is stained red. Taste for salt and chilli.
steps.look: A thick, glossy red stew, no watery liquid, beans whole and coated.
steps.mistake: A thin stew that floods the plate.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered a little longer, or crush a few beans to thicken.

steps.do: Heat the frying oil in the frying pan over medium heat to about 350°F (175°C), when a piece of plantain dropped in sizzles steadily. Fry the plantain slices in a single layer, without crowding, for 2 to 3 minutes per side.
steps.look: Edges turning deep amber and caramelised, centres soft and creamy when pressed with a spoon.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, which blackens the sugary plantain before the centre softens; or too cool, which gives greasy slices.
steps.fix: Hold the oil at a steady sizzle and adjust the heat between batches.

steps.do: Lift the plantains out with the slotted spoon onto paper towel and sprinkle with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Golden brown, glossy slices with dark caramelised edges.
steps.mistake: Using yellow plantains, which fry pale and dry.
steps.fix: Buy plantains a week ahead and let them blacken; that is ripe.

steps.do: Serve the stew in bowls with the fried plantains alongside and a sprinkle of gari over the beans for crunch.
steps.look: Red stew, golden plantains, a scattering of pale gari.
steps.mistake: Plantains left to sit until soggy.
steps.fix: Fry them last, just before serving.

science: Red palm oil gets its colour from carotenoids such as beta carotene, which break down at high heat; warming it only until it melts and runs keeps the colour and fruity aroma. Frying tomato paste in that oil drives off water and caramelises its sugars, deepening the flavour. Plantains change dramatically as they ripen: green plantains are mostly starch, while black spotted ones have converted much of that starch into sugars. In hot oil around 350°F (175°C), those sugars caramelise at the cut surfaces, giving dark, sticky, sweet edges while the inside turns creamy. Chilli heat comes from capsaicin, which is fat soluble and spreads through oil-rich dishes, so add it gradually and taste.
plating: Spoon the red red into the centre of a warm, shallow bowl. Fan the fried plantain slices in an overlapping arc along one side, sprinkle gari in a line across the beans and finish with a few thin slices of raw spring onion or onion for freshness.

pairing.drink: A Dark and Stormy of dark rum and spicy ginger beer: ginger echoes the stew and sweetness meets the plantain.

variations: Add smoked fish or smoked mackerel flaked into the stew, a common Ghanaian addition.
Kelewele: toss the plantain in ginger, chilli and salt before frying for a spiced street snack.
Use coconut oil with a little paprika if palm oil is not available.
safety: Shallow frying oil at 350°F (175°C) causes severe burns: lay plantains in away from you and never leave the pan.
Keep a lid nearby to smother an oil fire; never use water on burning oil.
Wash hands after handling chilli.

title: Red Beans and Rice
summary: New Orleans' Monday lunch: dried red kidney beans simmered for hours with the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, smoked ham hock, sausage and herbs until creamy, served over long-grain rice with hot sauce. It teaches the trinity, a long bean pot that thickens itself and, crucially, how to cook kidney beans safely.
skills: a long bean simmer to creaminess
equipment: heavy 6 quart (5.7 litre) pot or Dutch oven
medium saucepan with a tight lid for rice

ingredients.note: Soaked overnight; see the safety notes.

ingredients.item: smoked sausage or andouille, sliced into rounds

ingredients.note: Plus more as needed.
Add near the end; the hock is salty.

ingredients.item: spring onions, sliced, and Louisiana hot sauce
ingredients.us: 3 spring onions, hot sauce to taste
ingredients.metric: 45 g spring onions, hot sauce to taste

mise: The night before, pick over the beans and soak them in plenty of cold water.
Drain and rinse the beans; discard the soaking water.
Dice the onion, pepper and celery into even 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice; mince the garlic.
Slice the sausage.
Measure herbs and spices.

timeline.do: Soak the beans.
Brown the sausage; sweat the trinity; add beans, hock, herbs and water.
Boil hard for 10 minutes, then hold at a gentle simmer for 2 to 2 1/2 hours.
Mash some beans against the pot to cream the gravy; pick the hock meat.
Cook the rice; rest it 10 minutes.
Season the beans; serve over rice with spring onion and hot sauce.

steps.do: Dice the trinity: cut the onion, green pepper and celery into even 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice. For the pepper, cut off the top and bottom, slice down one side, unroll it flat, trim the ribs and cut into strips, then dice.
steps.look: Three neat piles of small, even cubes, roughly equal in volume for onion and smaller for pepper and celery.
steps.mistake: Uneven chunks that cook at different speeds.
steps.fix: Go slowly and match the size of every piece.

steps.do: In the heavy pot over medium heat, brown the sausage rounds in the bacon fat for 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until well coloured. Lift them out and set aside.
steps.look: Browned rounds and flavourful fat in the pot.
steps.mistake: Crowding the sausage so it steams instead of browning.
steps.fix: Brown in two batches if needed.

steps.do: Add the trinity to the fat with a pinch of salt and cook over medium low heat, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, thyme, cayenne and both peppers and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, glossy vegetables with no hard edges, smelling sweet and peppery.
steps.mistake: High heat that browns and burns the vegetables.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and scrape the pot as they release moisture.

steps.do: Add the drained beans, ham hock, bay leaves and 10 cups (2.4 litres) of water. Bring to a full rolling boil and keep it boiling hard for 10 minutes.
steps.look: A vigorous, rolling boil across the whole surface for the full 10 minutes.
steps.mistake: Simmering kidney beans gently from the start, or cooking them in a slow cooker, which does not get hot enough to destroy their natural toxin.
steps.fix: Always boil kidney beans hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering; this is non-negotiable.

steps.do: Lower the heat to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook for 2 to 2 1/2 hours, stirring and scraping the base every 20 minutes. Add hot water if the beans become exposed.
steps.look: Beans swelling, becoming soft and creamy, the liquid thickening and turning a rich reddish brown.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot dry out so the beans scorch on the base.
steps.fix: Keep the beans just covered with liquid; if the base catches, do not scrape the burnt layer into the beans.

steps.do: When the beans are completely tender, lift out the ham hock. Mash a cupful of beans against the side of the pot with the back of the spoon and stir them back in. Pull the meat off the hock, discard skin and bone, chop and return it with the browned sausage. Simmer 15 minutes more.
steps.look: A thick, creamy gravy coating whole beans, studded with meat.
steps.mistake: Adding cream or flour to thicken.
steps.fix: The creaminess comes from mashed beans; mash a little more if needed.

steps.do: For the rice, rinse it in the sieve until the water runs clear. Put it in the saucepan with 2 1/4 cups (530 ml) water and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, bring to the boil, cover tightly, turn to the lowest heat and cook 17 minutes. Rest off the heat, covered, for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
steps.look: Separate, fluffy grains with small steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking or stirring the rice, which makes it sticky.
steps.fix: Leave the lid on and rest it; fluff gently with a fork.

steps.do: Remove the bay leaves. Taste the beans and season with salt. Serve the beans ladled over a mound of rice, scattered with spring onions, with hot sauce on the table.
steps.look: Creamy red beans over white rice, bright green onion on top.
steps.mistake: Salting at the start, before the hock has given up its salt, which can over-salt the pot.
steps.fix: Salt at the end, after tasting.

science: Red kidney beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a natural protein that can cause severe stomach upset if the beans are raw or undercooked. Boiling at 212°F (100°C) for at least ten minutes destroys it; gentle heating below the boil, as in some slow cookers, can leave it active or even increase its effect, which is why the hard boil comes first. During the long simmer, the beans' cell walls soften as pectin dissolves and their starch gelatinises; mashing some releases that starch into the liquid, thickening it into a creamy gravy without dairy. The ham hock's collagen melts into gelatin, adding body and smoky flavour. Rice cooked by absorption with the lid closed steams evenly, and resting lets moisture redistribute.
plating: Pack the rice into a small bowl and turn it out into the centre of a warm, shallow bowl. Ladle the beans around and partly over it so the rice peaks through, lay a few slices of the browned sausage on top, and scatter the spring onions. Put the hot sauce bottle on the table.

pairing.drink: A cold, malty Louisiana amber lager: refreshing, with enough body for smoky pork and creamy beans.
pairing.brennans: Seafood Gumbo: Brennan's other Creole classic built on the same holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper.

variations: Use pickled pork, the old New Orleans seasoning meat, in place of the hock.
Vegetarian red beans: leave out the meat, use smoked paprika and a little liquid smoke, and finish with butter.
Serve with cornbread and a side of crisp fried sausage.
safety: Raw or undercooked red kidney beans can make people ill: soak, discard the water, and boil hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering; never cook them from raw in a slow cooker.
Smoked sausage should be heated through to at least 165°F (74°C) when reheated.
Cool leftovers quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat rice until steaming hot.

title: Lecsó
summary: Hungary's summer stew of pale wax peppers and onion softened in fat, coloured with sweet paprika and cooked down with peeled tomatoes until syrupy, finished by stirring in beaten eggs. It shows paprika's character in fat, how long cooking sweetens peppers, and when to salt a watery vegetable.
skills: cooking down with tomato and paprika
equipment: wide 12 inch (30 cm) heavy sauté pan or casserole with a lid
saucepan of boiling water and a bowl of iced water for peeling tomatoes
small bowl and fork for the eggs

ingredients.item: Hungarian wax peppers, banana peppers or pale green Cubanelle peppers
ingredients.note: Thin walled pale peppers collapse beautifully; bell peppers are a poor substitute.
Peeled (step 1) and chopped.
Fresh, bright red paprika matters.
Optional.
Added with the tomatoes.
For finishing.

mise: Bring a saucepan of water to the boil and set a bowl of iced water beside it.
Score a small cross in the base of each tomato.
Halve, seed and cut the peppers lengthways into strips about 3/4 inch (2 cm) wide.
Slice the onions.
Beat the eggs lightly with a pinch of salt.

timeline.do: Blanch and peel the tomatoes; slice peppers and onions.
Soften the onion in fat 8 to 10 minutes.
Paprika off the heat; peppers in, covered, 10 to 15 minutes.
Tomatoes and salt; cook uncovered until syrupy.
Stir in the eggs until just set.
Serve with bread.

steps.do: Drop the scored tomatoes into the boiling water for 20 to 30 seconds, until the skin at the cross starts to curl back. Lift them into the iced water for 1 minute, then slip off the skins, core and chop the flesh roughly.
steps.look: Skins peeling away easily from firm, uncooked flesh.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in the boiling water too long, so the flesh cooks and turns mushy.
steps.fix: Thirty seconds at most; it is the skin you are loosening, not the tomato you are cooking.

steps.do: Heat the oil or lard in the sauté pan over low heat. Add the onions and cook gently, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until glassy and soft but not coloured.
steps.look: Translucent, soft onions, glossy with fat.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions, which changes the clean, sweet character of the dish.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; add a spoonful of water if they begin to colour.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika until the fat turns red. Then return it to low heat and add the pepper strips and hot pepper.
steps.look: Brick red fat coating the onions, smelling sweet and warm.
steps.mistake: Adding paprika over the flame, where it burns in seconds and turns bitter and brown.
steps.fix: Always off the heat; the hot fat blooms it on its own.

steps.do: Cover the pan and let the peppers sweat in their own moisture over low to medium low heat for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.look: Peppers limp and softened, their skins slack, a little liquid in the pan.
steps.mistake: Salting the peppers now, which draws their water out early so they boil to mush before the tomato reduces.
steps.fix: Hold the salt until the tomatoes go in.

steps.do: Add the chopped tomatoes and the salt. Cook uncovered over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 10 to 15 minutes, until the liquid has reduced to a thick red sauce that clings to the strips.
steps.look: No pooling liquid; a thick, glossy red sauce coating soft pepper strips.
steps.mistake: Stopping while it is watery, which makes a thin soup when the eggs go in.
steps.fix: Keep reducing until a spoon dragged across the pan leaves a clear trail.

steps.do: Taste and adjust the salt. Lower the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir gently but constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, until the eggs are just set in soft curds through the peppers.
steps.look: Soft yellow curds of egg threaded through the red peppers, moist and glossy.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the eggs into dry, rubbery pieces.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat while the eggs still look slightly wet; they finish in the pan's heat.

steps.do: Serve hot in warm bowls with crusty bread.
steps.look: A glossy red and yellow stew of soft peppers and egg.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit on the heat, which toughens the eggs.
steps.fix: Serve straight away.

science: Pale wax peppers are thin walled and full of water, so they collapse into silky strips rather than roasting. Salt draws water from vegetable cells by osmosis; added to the peppers alone, it pulls their juices out early so they stew and fall apart before the tomatoes have reduced, which is why it goes in with the tomatoes. Paprika is ground dried pepper whose red carotenoid pigments and flavour compounds dissolve in fat; heating it in the fat blooms that colour and aroma, but paprika's sugars burn quickly, so it goes in off the heat. Blanching tomatoes for seconds heats the layer just beneath the skin, loosening it so it slips off. Long, gentle cooking breaks down the peppers' cell walls and concentrates their sugars.
plating: Spoon the lecsó into warm, shallow bowls, mounding it so the egg curds show among the peppers. Finish with a light dusting of paprika and a few thin rings of fresh hot pepper, and serve thick slices of bread alongside.

pairing.drink: A peppery Austrian Grüner Veltliner or a dry Hungarian Furmint: bright acidity and a white pepper note that match the peppers.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Alte Reben’ Grüner Veltliner 2023: an Austrian Grüner on the Brennan's list with the peppery freshness this dish wants.

variations: Add sliced Hungarian smoked sausage (kolbász), browned first, instead of or as well as the eggs.
Serve without eggs as a side dish for grilled meats.
Stir in a little cooked rice at the end for a heartier version.
safety: Lift tomatoes from boiling water with a slotted spoon, never your fingers.
Eggs stirred until just set are fully cooked through; for vulnerable guests, cook until no wet egg remains.
Wash hands after handling hot peppers.

title: Tomato and Egg Stir-Fry with Rice
summary: The everyday home cooking of China: eggs set in seconds in a smoking wok until puffed and soft, lifted out, then folded back into a quick, sweet and savoury sauce of tomatoes, served over steamed rice. The first wok dish in the course teaches high heat, speed and doing every bit of preparation before the flame goes on.
skills: soft eggs cooked fast in hot oil
equipment: carbon steel wok or a 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
wok spatula or wide metal spatula
medium saucepan with a tight lid for rice

ingredients.note: Optional, beaten into the eggs.

ingredients.item: neutral oil with a high smoke point
spring onions, white and green parts separated, sliced

ingredients.note: To balance the tomatoes' acidity.
Optional, common in Chinese homes for colour and depth.

ingredients.item: cornflour mixed with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water
ingredients.note: Optional, to thicken.

mise: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it 15 minutes.
Beat the eggs with 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt and the Shaoxing wine until smooth.
Cut the tomatoes into wedges about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick.
Mince the garlic; slice the spring onions.
Mix the cornflour slurry; measure sugar, salt and ketchup into a small bowl.
Line everything up beside the wok in the order it goes in.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice.
Cook the rice: boil, cover, lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 10.
Prepare every ingredient; line them up.
Cook the eggs in a smoking wok; lift them out.
Cook the tomatoes; return the eggs; fold together.
Serve over rice.

steps.do: Drain the soaked rice, put it in the saucepan with 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) water, bring to the boil, cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes. Turn off the heat and rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Fluffy, separate grains with steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; the steam is doing the cooking.

steps.do: Put every prepared ingredient within reach of the stove. A stir-fry happens in under five minutes and there is no time to chop once the wok is hot.
steps.look: Bowls of beaten egg, tomato wedges, garlic, spring onion and the seasoning lined up in order.
steps.mistake: Starting to cook before everything is ready.
steps.fix: In Chinese kitchens, preparation is the cooking; the wok is the last few minutes.

steps.do: Heat the wok over the highest heat until it just starts to smoke, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and swirl it round the sides.
steps.look: A wisp of smoke from the wok; the oil shimmering and flowing like water.
steps.mistake: A wok that is not hot enough, so the eggs soak up oil and turn flat and greasy.
steps.fix: Wait for the first smoke before adding oil.

steps.do: Pour in the beaten eggs. They will puff up immediately. Let them set for 5 seconds, then push and fold them gently from the edges into the centre with the spatula for 15 to 20 seconds, until they form large, soft curds that are still wet in places. Tip them onto a plate.
steps.look: Puffy, golden-edged curds, soft and glossy, about two thirds set.
steps.mistake: Cooking the eggs until fully set, so they turn rubbery when returned to the sauce.
steps.fix: Lift them out while they look underdone; they finish in the sauce.

steps.do: Add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil to the wok over high heat. Add the garlic and white spring onion and stir for 10 seconds, then add the tomato wedges and stir-fry for 1 to 2 minutes, pressing a few against the wok, until they soften and release their juices.
steps.look: Tomatoes collapsing at the edges, a red, juicy sauce forming in the wok.
steps.mistake: Cooking the tomatoes until they disappear into a paste.
steps.fix: Stop when some wedges still hold their shape.

steps.do: Add the sugar, the remaining 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, the ketchup if using, and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water. Stir and let it bubble for 30 seconds. Stir the cornflour slurry and add it if you want a glossier, thicker sauce; it thickens in seconds.
steps.look: A glossy, bright red sauce that coats the spatula.
steps.mistake: Too sour a sauce.
steps.fix: Add sugar a little at a time; it should taste sweet, sour and savoury in balance.

steps.do: Return the eggs to the wok and fold gently a few times so they soak up the sauce without breaking into small bits. Turn off the heat, add the sesame oil and green spring onion.
steps.look: Large soft curds of egg coated in red sauce, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks the egg into crumbs.
steps.fix: Fold two or three times only.

steps.do: Fluff the rice and serve it in bowls with the tomato and egg spooned over the top.
steps.look: White rice under glossy red and yellow tomato and egg.
steps.mistake: Leaving the stir-fry in the hot wok while the rice is served.
steps.fix: Serve immediately from the wok.

science: In a smoking wok, eggs meet oil at around 400°F (205°C). Water in the egg flashes to steam, which puffs the curds while the proteins on the outside set almost instantly and brown slightly at the edges. Lifting them out while still partly liquid prevents the proteins from tightening and squeezing out water, so they stay tender when returned to the sauce. Tomatoes are acidic and contain plenty of glutamate; brief, hot cooking breaks their cells and releases juice, and sugar balances their acidity. A cornflour slurry thickens almost instantly when it reaches the boil, because the starch granules swell and bond with water, giving a glossy sauce that clings to the egg.
plating: Fill a bowl with rice, pressing it lightly into a dome, then spoon the tomato and egg over half the rice so both colours show, letting the sauce run down one side. Finish with the green spring onion and serve with chopsticks.

pairing.drink: A light, crisp Chinese lager or a dry Alsace Riesling: refreshing and bright against sweet and sour tomato.

variations: Add a few slices of fresh ginger with the garlic for warmth.
Stir-fried egg with prawns: cook peeled prawns quickly after the eggs and return them with the eggs.
Make it saucier with a little chicken stock to soak into the rice.
safety: Hot oil in a smoking wok can flare; keep the wok handle steady and add wet ingredients carefully.
Have a lid nearby; never put water on an oil fire.
Eggs cooked until set in the sauce are fully cooked.
